questions.title: Choosing Between #Temp Tables, Table Variables, and CTEs Inside a Stored Procedure
questions.prompt: You're writing a complex reporting stored procedure. Partway through, you compute an intermediate result set of roughly 200,000 rows that gets referenced three separate times later in the procedure, filtered differently each time, and would benefit from its own index on one of its columns. A junior developer on your team used a CTE for it because 'that's what we always use.' Explain why that choice is likely to hurt performance here, what you'd use instead and why, and the one scenario where a table variable would actually be the better choice over a temp table.
questions.modelAnswer:
A CTE isn't a stored, materialized result at all -- it's inlined into the statement that references it, and if you reference the same CTE three separate times, SQL Server may well re-run its underlying query three separate times (unless it happens to decide to spool the result on its own, which isn't something you can rely on or control). For a 200,000-row intermediate result referenced three times with different downstream filters, that risks recomputing the same expensive logic three times over, and a CTE also can't carry its own index -- so if the column you'd filter or join on isn't already well-served by indexes on the base tables, every one of those three references pays that cost independently.

A #temp table is the right choice here. It's a real, physically-stored table in tempdb, which means two things that matter directly to this scenario: SQL Server maintains real statistics on it, so the optimizer can build a genuinely informed plan for each of the three later queries against it (rather than guessing), and you can explicitly CREATE INDEX on it -- so the column those three downstream queries filter or join on can actually be indexed, turning three potential scans into three seeks. At 200,000 rows, this is squarely the 'thousands of rows, reused more than once, might need its own index' case.

A table variable would be the better choice only when the intermediate set is small -- a handful to a few hundred rows -- and you're specifically trying to avoid statement recompilation inside a stored procedure. Historically, SQL Server assumed a table variable held exactly one row for costing purposes (pre-2019 compatibility levels, or without the newer deferred-compilation improvements), which is actually fine when the set really is tiny, but would badly under-allocate resources at 200,000 rows -- the opposite of what you want here. Table variables also aren't rolled back by an enclosing ROLLBACK, which occasionally matters for specific logging/auditing patterns, but that's a narrower reason to choose one and isn't the deciding factor in this scenario.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell the junior developer: the CTE choice makes sense as a habit, but it's working against them here specifically because of how many rows there are and how many times it gets used. A CTE doesn't actually store anything -- every time you reference it, SQL Server might just re-run the query behind it from scratch, and it has no index of its own. If we're touching this 200,000-row set three separate times with three different filters, we could be paying for that underlying computation three times, and none of those three references get to use an index on it even if one would help a lot.

My recommendation is a #temp table instead: dump that intermediate result into it once, put an index on whatever column the three downstream queries actually filter or join on, and now each of those three references gets a real seek against real statistics instead of SQL Server guessing. That's exactly the profile -- meaningful row count, reused multiple times, benefits from its own index -- where a temp table wins clearly.

I'd also tell them table variables aren't wrong, just wrong for this case -- they're great when the set is genuinely small and you're inside a procedure trying to avoid a recompile every time row counts shift. The catch is that SQL Server has historically assumed a table variable holds about one row when it's building a plan, which is totally fine for a small set but would be a disaster at 200,000 rows -- the optimizer would badly under-allocate for a set that size, and the plan quality would suffer for every one of those three references, not help it.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to a CTE out of habit regardless of row count or reuse pattern
Not realizing a CTE referenced multiple times may re-run its underlying query each time
Assuming a table variable always outperforms a temp table because it 'sounds lighter weight'
Putting a large, reused intermediate set into a table variable and getting a poor plan from the one-row cardinality assumption
Forgetting that only a #temp table supports an explicit CREATE INDEX statement after the fact
keyPoints: CTEs are inlined and re-evaluated per reference, not materialized or indexed
#Temp tables are physically stored with maintained statistics and support explicit indexes
200,000 rows reused three times with filtering is a textbook #temp table case
Table variables historically get a one-row cardinality assumption, poor for large sets
Table variables fit small sets inside procedures where avoiding recompilation matters most

Recommends a #temp table and justifies it with statistics/indexing
Explains the risk of recomputation across three CTE references
Correctly identifies the scenario where a table variable wins
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Indexed Views: Mechanics and Restrictions
questions.prompt: Explain how an indexed view actually works under the hood in SQL Server — what SQL Server materializes, how it keeps that materialized data in sync with the base tables, and why indexed views come with such a strict list of requirements (deterministic functions only, no outer joins, SCHEMABINDING, etc.).
questions.modelAnswer: A standard view is just a stored query — nothing is persisted, and every time you select from it, SQL Server substitutes the view's definition into your query and compiles a plan against the base tables. An indexed view is fundamentally different: when you create a unique clustered index on a view, SQL Server actually materializes the result set of that view's query onto disk, in exactly the structure a clustered index implies (a b-tree with the data at the leaf level, physically sorted by the clustered index key). From that point on, the view's rows exist as real, maintained data, not a re-run query. Once that materialized data exists, SQL Server has to keep it transactionally consistent with the base tables, so every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE against the underlying tables also triggers maintenance of the indexed view's data as part of the same transaction — this is handled automatically and synchronously, which is why indexed views add write overhead in proportion to how many views depend on the table. The strict rules exist precisely because this maintenance has to be deterministic and unambiguous: SCHEMABINDING is required so the base tables can't be altered out from under the view's materialized structure; aggregate functions need COUNT_BIG rather than COUNT so NULL/overflow semantics are unambiguous; outer joins and subqueries are disallowed because the engine can't always determine, incrementally, exactly which materialized rows need to change when a base row changes; and non-deterministic functions (GETDATE(), RAND()) are banned because the materialized value has to be reproducible and tied only to its deterministic inputs. In short, an indexed view trades write-time cost and a narrow set of allowed constructs for read-time speed, because the expensive aggregation or join work is done once at write time instead of on every read.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I think about indexed views is that they flip a normal view inside out. A regular view is lazy — it's just a saved SELECT statement, and the actual work happens every time someone queries it. An indexed view is the opposite: the moment you put a unique clustered index on it, SQL Server goes and physically builds that result set on disk, like any other table, and from then on it has to maintain it in real time. So if you've got an indexed view that aggregates sales by product, every single insert or update to the Sales table also updates that materialized aggregate behind the scenes, inside the same transaction. That's the trade-off — you're paying extra cost on every write so that reads against the view are basically free, just reading pre-computed data off disk instead of re-aggregating millions of rows. The restrictions make total sense once you see it that way — SCHEMABINDING locks the base tables so nobody can change a column type underneath the materialized structure, you need COUNT_BIG instead of COUNT because the engine needs predictable, deterministic math to maintain the aggregate incrementally, and things like outer joins or non-deterministic functions like GETDATE() are blocked because the engine genuinely can't figure out, row by row, exactly how to patch the materialized result when something changes upstream. I'd tell an interviewer: use indexed views when you have an expensive aggregate that's read far more often than the base data is written — that's the sweet spot — and be honest that they're not free, they add real overhead to every write against the underlying tables.
commonMistakes: Thinking an indexed view is 'just a view with an index for faster lookup' rather than a materialized, physically stored structure
Forgetting that maintenance happens synchronously inside the write transaction, not as an async refresh job
Not knowing why COUNT_BIG is mandatory instead of COUNT or COUNT(*)
Assuming indexed views support the same join/subquery flexibility as regular views
Overusing indexed views on heavy-write tables without weighing the write-amplification cost
keyPoints: Indexed views physically materialize the result set via a unique clustered index
Base table DML synchronously maintains the indexed view's data in the same transaction
SCHEMABINDING prevents base table changes that would break the materialized structure
Deterministic-only functions and no outer joins/subqueries are required for unambiguous incremental maintenance
The performance trade-off is faster reads at the cost of slower writes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains physical materialization via unique clustered index
Explains synchronous maintenance on base table writes
Connects restrictions (SCHEMABINDING, COUNT_BIG, no outer joins) to the underlying reason
Identifies the read-speed vs write-cost trade-off
Clarity and technical precision

questions.title: SCD Type 2 Mechanics in a Star Schema
questions.prompt: Explain exactly what has to happen, mechanically, when you implement a Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2 for a Customer dimension in a star schema — what new columns are needed, what happens to the existing 'current' row when an attribute changes, and how fact table grain and surrogate keys make this work correctly for historical reporting.
questions.modelAnswer: SCD Type 2 preserves history by never overwriting an existing dimension row when a tracked attribute changes — instead it closes out the old row and inserts a brand-new row representing the new state, so the dimension table ends up holding multiple physical rows for the same real-world entity over time. Mechanically, this requires the dimension table to carry a surrogate key (a system-generated, meaningless integer, typically an identity column) that is distinct from the natural/business key (like CustomerID from the source system) — the surrogate key is what's unique per version-row, while the natural key is what ties all historical versions of the same customer together. You also need metadata columns to track validity: typically EffectiveDate/ExpirationDate (or StartDate/EndDate) and a boolean or flag column like IsCurrent. When an attribute change is detected during the ETL/ELT load — say a customer's Region changes from 'East' to 'West' — the process does two things in sequence: it updates the existing row's ExpirationDate to the load date and sets IsCurrent to false (closing it out, not deleting it), and it inserts a new row with a new surrogate key, the same natural key, the updated Region value, an EffectiveDate of the load date, a NULL or far-future ExpirationDate, and IsCurrent set to true. The reason this matters for fact table grain is that fact table rows store the dimension's surrogate key, not the natural key, at load time — so a sales transaction that happened while the customer was in 'East' is permanently linked to the surrogate key representing that specific historical version of the customer row, and a transaction after the change links to the new surrogate key representing 'West'. This is exactly what makes historically accurate reporting possible: if you aggregate sales by Region using the surrogate-key relationship, each transaction is correctly attributed to the region the customer was actually in at the time of that transaction, rather than every historical transaction retroactively being reattributed to the customer's current region (which is what would happen under SCD Type 1, where you simply overwrite the attribute in place).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe SCD Type 2 as 'never update in place, always version instead.' The core structural requirement is that your dimension table needs two different kinds of keys doing two different jobs — a surrogate key that's unique per row, system-generated, meaningless, usually just an identity column, and the natural key from the source system that stays the same across every version of that customer. Then you need a handful of tracking columns — an effective date, an expiration date, and usually an IsCurrent flag — so you can tell, for any point in time, which row represented the 'truth' for that customer. When something changes — say a customer moves regions — the load process doesn't touch the existing row's Region value at all. Instead it closes that row out, sets its expiration date and flips IsCurrent to false, and then inserts a completely new row with a new surrogate key, the same natural key, the new region, and IsCurrent true. So now you've physically got two rows in the dimension table for the same person, representing two different points in their history. The piece that really makes this click for people is understanding what the fact table actually stores — it's not storing the natural CustomerID, it's storing that surrogate key, captured at the moment the transaction was loaded. So a sale that happened back when the customer lived in the East region is forever tied to that East-version surrogate key, even after the customer moves and a new row gets created. That's exactly why SCD Type 2 lets you report history accurately — if I slice historical sales by region, each sale lands in whatever region was true at the time it happened, not wherever the customer happens to live today. Compare that to Type 1, where you'd just overwrite the Region value on the existing row — simpler, but it silently rewrites history, because every past transaction now appears to have happened under the customer's current region.
questions.example:
-- Closing out the old row and inserting the new version:
UPDATE DimCustomer
SET ExpirationDate = @LoadDate, IsCurrent = 0
WHERE CustomerNaturalKey = @CustID AND IsCurrent = 1;

INSERT INTO DimCustomer (CustomerNaturalKey, Region, EffectiveDate, ExpirationDate, IsCurrent)
VALUES (@CustID, @NewRegion, @LoadDate, NULL, 1);
-- FactSales.CustomerSK always points to whichever surrogate key
-- was current at the time the sale was loaded.
commonMistakes: Confusing SCD Type 2 with Type 1 and overwriting the attribute in place, destroying history
Forgetting the dimension needs both a surrogate key and a natural key serving distinct purposes
Storing the natural key in the fact table instead of the surrogate key, which breaks historical attribution
Forgetting to close out the old row's ExpirationDate/IsCurrent when inserting the new version, leaving two 'current' rows
Not handling the case where multiple attributes change simultaneously, or where a late-arriving fact needs to match a historical dimension version rather than the current one
keyPoints: SCD Type 2 preserves history by inserting new versioned rows instead of overwriting attributes
Surrogate keys (system-generated) and natural keys (business keys) serve distinct roles
EffectiveDate/ExpirationDate/IsCurrent track which row represents which time period
Fact tables store the surrogate key, which is what preserves historically accurate attribution
Type 2 vs Type 1 is the key contrast: version history vs. overwrite-in-place

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the close-out-old-row-and-insert-new-row mechanic
Correctly distinguishes surrogate key from natural key and their respective roles
Correctly explains the EffectiveDate/ExpirationDate/IsCurrent tracking columns
Explains why fact tables storing the surrogate key preserves historical accuracy
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: How Purview's Data Map Scanning and Classification Actually Decide What Gets Tagged
questions.prompt: A colleague asks why Microsoft Purview sometimes tags a column as 'U.S. Social Security Number' and sometimes misses an obvious SSN column entirely in the same database. Explain mechanically how a Purview scan combines a scan rule set, classification rules, and sampling to decide what gets classified, the real difference between system and custom classifications, and why a classification applied at scan time is not the same thing as a sensitivity label.
questions.modelAnswer: A Purview scan runs against a registered data source using a scan rule set, which is the configuration object that decides two things: which classification rules are active for this scan, and which file types or structured objects the scanner even looks inside. For structured sources, Purview samples a configurable percentage of rows per column (not the full table by default) and runs each classification rule's pattern against that sample -- a system classification like 'U.S. Social Security Number' is a built-in rule combining a regex pattern (digit grouping matching SSN format) with supporting signals such as the column name and a minimum match-confidence threshold across the sampled rows. If the sampled rows for a column don't clear that confidence threshold -- because the data is sparse, inconsistently formatted, null-heavy in the sample, or the column name doesn't reinforce the pattern -- the classification is skipped for that column even though a human looking at the full data would call it an obvious SSN column. This is exactly why increasing the sample percentage, or adding a custom classification tuned to the real format and column-naming pattern in that specific source, closes gaps system classifications miss. Custom classifications work identically under the hood (regex plus optional supporting rules) but are authored by the organization for patterns Microsoft's built-in library doesn't cover, such as an internal employee ID format. Critically, a classification is Purview's own metadata describing what kind of data was found -- it lives in the catalog, independent of the source system. A sensitivity label (often backed by Microsoft Purview Information Protection) is a separate concept: it can be applied manually, inherited from a classification via an auto-labeling policy, or set directly, and depending on the label and connector, it can actually be written back to the source file or dataset to drive protection (encryption, access restriction) -- classification alone never changes anything about the source data.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as two separate questions Purview is answering, and most confusion comes from assuming they're the same question. First: 'does a sample of this column's values match a known pattern?' That's classification, and it only ever looks at a sample, not the whole table, scored against a confidence threshold per rule. So an SSN column with messy formatting, a lot of nulls in the sampled rows, or a column name that doesn't reinforce the pattern can genuinely get missed by the system classification even though a human scanning the full table would call it obvious. The fix in that case is usually either turning up the sampling percentage in the scan rule set or writing a custom classification tuned to exactly how that source actually stores the value. Second question: 'should this data be protected, and how?' That's a sensitivity label, and it's a distinct layer on top of classification -- it can be assigned manually, inherited automatically from a classification via policy, and in some connectors it can actually write protection back to the source. So when someone asks why a column got classified but doesn't look 'protected,' I'd say: classification is Purview noticing a pattern and recording it in the catalog; a label is the separate decision about what to do about it, and nothing changes on the actual data just because a classification fired.
questions.example: A custom classification for an internal 'EMP-NNNNNN' employee ID format needs its own regex rule in a custom scan rule set, because the built-in system classification library has no pattern for a company-specific ID scheme -- Purview will never classify it correctly out of the box no matter how clean the data is.
commonMistakes: Assuming a Purview scan reads every row of every column instead of a configurable sample
Treating classification and sensitivity labeling as the same action rather than two distinct layers
Assuming a missed classification means the scan failed, rather than a sampling/confidence-threshold miss
Not knowing custom classifications use the same regex-plus-signals mechanism as system classifications
Believing a classification by itself changes or protects the underlying data
keyPoints: Scans sample a configurable percentage of data per column, not the full dataset, by default
Classification rules combine a pattern (often regex) with supporting signals and a confidence threshold
Custom classifications use the same mechanism as system classifications, authored for organization-specific patterns
Classification is catalog metadata; a sensitivity label is a separate, sometimes source-write-back, protection decision
Sampling gaps, not scan failures, are the most common reason an 'obvious' sensitive column gets missed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains scan rule set and sampling mechanics
Correctly explains classification pattern/confidence-threshold mechanism
Correctly distinguishes system vs. custom classification
Correctly distinguishes classification from sensitivity labeling
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Domains vs. Workspaces: Where Fabric Governance Boundaries Actually Live
questions.prompt: A new Fabric administrator asks why their organization needs both 'domains' and 'workspaces' — isn't a workspace already a boundary? Explain mechanically what a domain actually governs versus what a workspace governs, how OneLake security sits underneath both, and give a concrete example of a setting that only a domain can control and one that only a workspace can control.
questions.modelAnswer: A workspace is the operational container in Fabric -- it's where items (lakehouses, warehouses, semantic models, reports) actually live, and workspace roles (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer) govern who can create, edit, or just consume those items inside that one container. A domain is a layer above workspaces: it's a grouping mechanism, typically mapped to a business unit or subject area, that a domain admin uses to apply policy and settings consistently across every workspace assigned to it, without having to touch each workspace individually. Mechanically, assigning a workspace to a domain doesn't change the workspace's own role-based permissions at all -- a domain admin doesn't automatically get Workspace Admin rights inside every workspace in their domain unless that's separately granted -- but it does let the domain admin apply domain-level settings (certain tenant-switchable governance settings scoped to the domain, default workspace settings for new workspaces created under that domain, and domain-level data classification defaults) that cascade as defaults across the whole group. OneLake security sits underneath both layers entirely independently: it governs access to the actual data (folders, tables, files) inside a lakehouse or warehouse, enforced at the storage/data layer regardless of which workspace or domain the item sits in -- so a user can have Workspace Viewer access (can see the item exists, can open the report) while still being denied by a OneLake data access role from reading the underlying table data directly. A concrete domain-only control is which workspaces are even eligible to be assigned to that business-unit grouping and the domain-wide default settings applied to new workspaces created under it; a concrete workspace-only control is the specific role assignment deciding whether an individual user can edit versus merely view a specific report inside that one workspace.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd draw it as two different questions being answered at two different altitudes. The workspace question is: 'inside this one container, who can do what to this specific item?' That's roles -- Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer -- scoped to that single workspace. The domain question is: 'across this whole business unit's worth of workspaces, what governance defaults and settings apply consistently?' A domain admin isn't automatically a workspace admin everywhere in their domain -- those are separate permission layers, and conflating them is the mistake I see most. What a domain uniquely controls is things like which workspaces get grouped under Marketing versus Finance, and what default settings and classification apply to any new workspace created under that domain going forward -- you set it once at the domain level instead of chasing down every individual workspace. What a workspace uniquely controls is the fine-grained 'can this specific person edit this specific report' decision, which a domain has no mechanism to override directly. And I'd make sure to call out that OneLake security is its own separate layer underneath all of that -- someone can have Viewer access at the workspace level and still be completely blocked from reading the raw table data in the lakehouse if a OneLake data access role says no, because OneLake enforces at the data layer, independent of whatever workspace or domain the item happens to be organized under.
commonMistakes: Assuming domain admin rights automatically grant workspace admin rights inside every workspace in the domain
Treating domains as just a folder/label with no real governance mechanism behind them
Assuming workspace role assignment also controls access to the underlying OneLake data
Not realizing OneLake security is enforced independently of workspace roles
Confusing domain-level default settings with settings that can be individually overridden per workspace
keyPoints: Workspaces hold items and enforce fine-grained roles (Admin/Member/Contributor/Viewer) per container
Domains group workspaces by business unit and apply consistent governance defaults across that group
Domain admin rights and workspace admin rights are separate, not automatically inherited
OneLake security governs actual data access independently of workspace or domain settings
Domain-only control: cross-workspace defaults/classification; workspace-only control: per-item role assignment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes what a workspace governs vs. what a domain governs
Correctly explains domain admin rights are not automatic workspace admin rights
Correctly explains OneLake security as an independent underlying layer
Gives accurate concrete domain-only and workspace-only examples
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: How Unity Catalog's Three-Level Namespace Decides What a GRANT Actually Covers
questions.prompt: A Databricks admin grants a group USE CATALOG on a catalog and SELECT on one specific table inside it, then is confused when the group still can't query that table. Explain mechanically how Unity Catalog's catalog-schema-table namespace and its privilege model work together, what inheritance actually means here, and exactly what's missing from the grants described.
questions.modelAnswer: Unity Catalog organizes every data object under a three-level namespace -- catalog.schema.table -- and each level in that chain is its own securable object with its own independent set of grantable privileges; a privilege granted at one level is not automatically a privilege at the level below it, with one specific exception: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA exist purely as 'can traverse this container to reach what's inside it' privileges, and they're required at every level in the path before a privilege granted deeper in the hierarchy (like SELECT on a table) can actually take effect. Granting SELECT on a table gives permission to read that table's data once the principal is actually able to resolve the full path down to it, but it does not implicitly grant USE SCHEMA on the schema that table lives in -- that's a separate grant that has to be made explicitly. In the scenario described, the group has USE CATALOG (so it can see/traverse the catalog) and SELECT on the table (so it's permitted to read that table's data), but nobody granted USE SCHEMA on the schema the table lives inside -- without that, the group can't resolve the path through the schema to reach the table at all, so the SELECT grant is effectively unreachable and the query fails as if no permission existed. This is intentionally not automatic: Unity Catalog's model treats 'can see this container exists and traverse it' and 'can act on this specific object' as two orthogonal questions, so that an admin can grant deep object-level access without silently exposing every other object in the same schema -- but it does mean every grant needs its full chain of USE privileges explicitly set, from catalog down through schema, before the terminal object-level privilege does anything.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the admin: you've granted the destination but not the road to get there. Unity Catalog treats catalog, schema, and table as three separate things you grant privileges on independently -- granting SELECT on the table only answers 'are you allowed to read this table's data,' it says nothing about whether you can actually navigate down to it. USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are the 'can you even get into this container' privileges, and they're required at every level along the path before a deeper grant like SELECT means anything. In this case, the group got USE CATALOG at the top and SELECT way down at the table, but nobody granted USE SCHEMA on the schema sitting in between those two -- so the group can see the catalog exists, is allowed to read that specific table once it gets there, but has no way to actually traverse through the schema to reach it. The fix is just adding GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA catalog.schema TO group. I'd also explain why Unity Catalog designed it this way instead of making it automatic: it lets you grant someone access to one specific table deep in a schema without silently exposing visibility into every other table in that same schema just because they happen to share a parent container.
commonMistakes: Assuming a privilege granted at one namespace level automatically applies to levels below it
Forgetting USE SCHEMA is a required, separate grant distinct from USE CATALOG
Treating USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA as read privileges rather than pure traversal privileges
Not realizing SELECT on a table is unreachable without the full chain of USE grants above it
Granting broad schema-level SELECT when only one table needs access, over-exposing the schema
keyPoints: Catalog, schema, and table are each independent securable objects with their own grants
USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are traversal privileges, required at every level in the path
A deeper object-level privilege (e.g. SELECT) does nothing without the full USE chain above it
The missing grant in this scenario is USE SCHEMA on the table's containing schema
This design deliberately separates 'can traverse' from 'can act on,' to avoid over-exposing sibling objects

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the three-level namespace as independently securable objects
Correctly explains USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA as traversal privileges
Correctly identifies the missing USE SCHEMA grant as the root cause
Explains the design rationale for not making this automatic
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: How Snowflake's Role Hierarchy Actually Resolves Effective Privileges
questions.prompt: A Snowflake admin is confused that a user with only the ANALYST role assigned appears to have privileges that were only ever granted to the ADMIN role. Explain mechanically how Snowflake's role hierarchy works — what GRANT ROLE TO ROLE actually does, how privilege inheritance flows, and why this makes role design, not just user-to-role assignment, the real access control surface in Snowflake.
questions.modelAnswer: In Snowflake, a role is not just a bucket of privileges assigned to users -- roles can be granted to other roles, forming a directed hierarchy, and a role inherits every privilege held by any role beneath it in that hierarchy, recursively, all the way down. GRANT ROLE child_role TO ROLE parent_role doesn't give the child role anything; it does the opposite -- it makes the parent role inherit everything the child role can do, as if the parent held those privileges directly. So if ANALYST was granted to ADMIN at some point (GRANT ROLE ANALYST TO ROLE ADMIN), that only flows privileges upward from ANALYST into ADMIN -- it would not explain a user with just ANALYST seeing ADMIN-only privileges. The actual explanation for the scenario described is almost certainly the reverse relationship: at some point someone ran GRANT ROLE ADMIN TO ROLE ANALYST, making ANALYST a parent of ADMIN in the hierarchy, so ANALYST now inherits every privilege ADMIN holds. This is exactly why role hierarchy design is the real access control surface in Snowflake, more so than which role a given user is assigned: a user's effective privileges are the union of everything inherited through every role reachable downward from their directly assigned role, so a single misplaced GRANT ROLE ... TO ROLE statement can silently flow a powerful role's entire privilege set into a role many ordinary users hold, without ever touching a single user-level grant. Auditing Snowflake access correctly means walking the full role graph with SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE and SHOW GRANTS OF ROLE for every role in the chain, not just checking what was granted directly to the user or to the role they're nominally assigned.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mental model I'd give them is: think of roles as nodes in a tree, and GRANT ROLE X TO ROLE Y means 'Y now inherits everything X can do' -- the privileges flow upward from the child into the parent, not the other way around. So if someone's confused that ANALYST seems to have ADMIN-level access, my first instinct isn't to go look at what's granted directly to ANALYST -- it's to check whether ADMIN was ever granted to ANALYST, meaning ANALYST became ADMIN's parent in the hierarchy, and now inherits its entire privilege set. That's almost certainly what happened here, probably by accident, maybe someone trying to let an admin 'use' the analyst role and getting the GRANT direction backwards. The bigger point I'd make is that in Snowflake, who you assign a role to is almost the less interesting question -- the real access control surface is the shape of the role hierarchy itself, because one GRANT ROLE ... TO ROLE statement can quietly pipe a powerful role's privileges into a role dozens of ordinary users hold. So when I audit access, I never just check what's granted straight to a user -- I walk the whole graph, SHOW GRANTS OF ROLE on every role in the chain, to see exactly what flows into what before I trust any single role assignment at face value.
questions.example:
-- This is the likely accidental root cause:
GRANT ROLE ADMIN TO ROLE ANALYST;
-- Now ANALYST inherits every privilege ADMIN holds, flowing upward.

-- Correct direction, if the intent was the opposite:
-- GRANT ROLE ANALYST TO ROLE ADMIN;  -- ADMIN inherits ANALYST's privileges instead
commonMistakes: Assuming GRANT ROLE X TO ROLE Y grants X's privileges to Y's members in the wrong direction
Auditing only what's granted directly to a user instead of walking the full role hierarchy
Treating user-to-role assignment as the primary access control surface instead of role hierarchy design
Not using SHOW GRANTS OF ROLE / SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE to trace inherited privileges
Assuming privilege inheritance is one level deep rather than fully recursive down the hierarchy
keyPoints: GRANT ROLE child TO ROLE parent makes the parent inherit the child's privileges, not the reverse
Inheritance is recursive through the entire role hierarchy, not just one level
A reversed or accidental GRANT ROLE statement explains privileges appearing where they shouldn't
Role hierarchy design, not just user-to-role assignment, is the real access control surface
Auditing requires walking the full graph (SHOW GRANTS OF/TO ROLE), not just direct user grants

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the direction of inheritance in GRANT ROLE TO ROLE
Correctly diagnoses the likely root cause of the scenario
Explains recursive inheritance through the full hierarchy

questions.title: Masking Policies vs. Row Access Policies: What Each One Actually Evaluates
questions.prompt: A teammate wants to hide credit card numbers from most analysts and also restrict which sales regions each analyst can see, and proposes using one masking policy to do both. Explain mechanically what a Snowflake masking policy versus a row access policy each actually evaluate and at what point in query execution, why one policy type can't substitute for the other, and how CURRENT_ROLE() is used differently by each.
questions.modelAnswer: A masking policy is attached to a single column and evaluates per-value, at query time, deciding what that column's value should look like to the querying session -- it's a CASE-style expression (commonly gated on CURRENT_ROLE() or a context function) that returns either the real value or a masked substitute (NULL, a hash, a redacted string, or a partially-revealed value), and it never removes rows from the result set, only transforms the contents of that one column. A row access policy is attached to a table (or view) and evaluates per-row, during query execution, deciding whether each row is included in the result set at all -- it's a boolean expression evaluated against row data (often compared against CURRENT_ROLE() or a mapping table of role-to-region access) that either lets the row through or filters it out entirely, and it has no mechanism to alter column values for rows that do pass through. Because these operate on two orthogonal dimensions of the same query -- which columns look like what, versus which rows exist at all -- one genuinely cannot substitute for the other: a masking policy could hide the credit card number for everyone but can't make an analyst's query simply never return out-of-region rows, and a row access policy could restrict region visibility but can't selectively blank out one column's value for the rows it does let through. The correct design is both policies applied simultaneously to the same table: a masking policy on the CreditCardNumber column referencing CURRENT_ROLE() to decide who sees the real digits versus a masked string, and a separate row access policy on the table (or a row access policy driven by a mapping table) referencing CURRENT_ROLE() to decide which SalesRegion rows that role is allowed to see -- Snowflake applies both independently and simultaneously against every query, in either order, since they don't interact with each other's logic.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them these solve two completely different problems and Snowflake doesn't let one stand in for the other. A masking policy lives on one specific column and only ever changes what that column's value looks like -- real digits or a masked string -- it has zero ability to remove a row from the results. A row access policy lives on the table and only ever decides whether a given row shows up at all -- it has zero ability to touch what any column's value looks like for the rows it does let through. So 'hide credit card numbers' and 'restrict which regions someone can see' are actually two separate governance questions, and they need two separate policies, both attached to the same table at the same time -- Snowflake evaluates both of them on every query, completely independently of each other. In practice I'd write a masking policy on just the CreditCardNumber column, checking CURRENT_ROLE() to decide who gets the real number versus a masked version, and a row access policy on the table itself -- often backed by a small mapping table of role-to-allowed-region rather than hardcoding roles into the policy logic -- that filters out rows for regions the calling role isn't permitted to see. Neither one does the other's job, and trying to force one policy to do both just means you'll either expose data you meant to hide or hide data you meant to show.
commonMistakes: Trying to use one masking policy to both hide a column value and restrict row visibility
Assuming a row access policy can transform column values for rows it lets through
Assuming a masking policy can remove rows from a result set
Hardcoding role names directly into policy logic instead of using a maintainable mapping table
Forgetting both policy types can and should be applied simultaneously to the same table independently
keyPoints: Masking policies operate per-column, per-value, transforming content without removing rows
Row access policies operate per-row, deciding inclusion/exclusion, without altering column content
The two operate on orthogonal dimensions and cannot substitute for each other
Both can and should be applied together on the same table, evaluated independently
CURRENT_ROLE() (often via a mapping table) commonly drives both, but for different decisions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains masking policy mechanics (per-column, per-value)
Correctly explains row access policy mechanics (per-row, inclusion/exclusion)
Explains why neither can substitute for the other
Proposes a correct combined design using both policies together
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Row-Level Security vs. Object-Level Security in Power BI: Two Different Enforcement Points
questions.prompt: A Power BI developer built row-level security (RLS) rules so each regional manager only sees their own region's rows, and separately wants to hide an entire 'Internal Cost' table from everyone except Finance. They ask why the RLS role they already built can't also just hide that table. Explain mechanically how RLS and object-level security (OLS) each enforce restrictions, why they operate at different layers of the model, and why both are often needed together.
questions.modelAnswer: RLS enforces at the row level: a role defines a DAX filter expression against one or more tables, and at query time Power BI's engine applies that filter transparently to every query the report issues, so a user assigned to a role only ever sees rows that satisfy the DAX expression -- but every table, column, and measure in the model is still structurally visible to them; they simply can't see rows the filter excludes. OLS enforces at the schema/structural level entirely independently of any row filtering: it restricts visibility of whole tables, columns, or measures themselves, so a user with OLS restrictions applied can't see that the object exists at all in field lists, visuals, or even DAX queries against the model -- there's no 'filtered row' concept involved because OLS isn't filtering data, it's removing the object from the user's view of the schema. These operate at genuinely different layers precisely because they answer different questions: RLS answers 'of the rows that exist in this visible table, which ones is this user allowed to see,' while OLS answers 'is this table/column/measure even part of this user's model at all.' That's why the existing RLS role can't also hide the Internal Cost table -- a DAX row filter has no mechanism to remove an entire table from the schema, only to filter which rows within a visible table are returned. The correct design applies both independently: the existing RLS role continues filtering regional rows for everyone it applies to, and a separate OLS configuration (set in the model, typically via an external tool like Tabular Editor since Power BI Desktop's native UI support for OLS is limited) hides the Internal Cost table from every role except the ones Finance belongs to -- Power BI evaluates both simultaneously, with OLS determining what's visible in the schema at all, and RLS filtering whatever rows remain visible within it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain to the developer that RLS and OLS are answering two different questions, and that's exactly why one role definition can't do both jobs. RLS is a row filter -- it's a DAX expression that quietly trims which rows come back for a given role, but the table itself, every column, every measure, is still fully visible in the schema; the user just gets fewer rows out of it. OLS is a different mechanism entirely -- it actually removes a table, column, or measure from the model as far as that user is concerned, so it doesn't show up in the field list, in a visual, or even if someone tries to write a DAX query against it directly. There's no filtering happening with OLS, there's nothing to filter -- the object just isn't part of their model. So when they ask why the existing RLS role can't also hide the Internal Cost table, the honest answer is that a row filter has no concept of 'hide this whole table' -- it only ever filters rows within tables that are already visible. What they actually need is both mechanisms running side by side: keep the RLS role doing exactly what it's doing for regional filtering, and separately configure OLS, usually through Tabular Editor since the native Power BI Desktop experience for OLS is limited, to remove the Internal Cost table from the schema for every role except Finance. Power BI applies both at the same time without conflict, because they're operating on completely different layers of the model.
commonMistakes: Assuming a single RLS role definition can also hide entire tables or columns
Treating OLS as 'RLS but for columns' rather than a structurally different, schema-level mechanism
Not knowing OLS typically requires an external tool (e.g. Tabular Editor) beyond Power BI Desktop's native UI
Assuming RLS-filtered rows means the table itself becomes invisible, when the table structure remains visible
Forgetting that RLS and OLS are independent and must both be explicitly configured to work together
keyPoints: RLS filters which rows are returned via a DAX expression; the table/columns remain structurally visible
OLS removes whole tables/columns/measures from the schema itself, with no row-filtering concept
RLS answers 'which rows,' OLS answers 'is this object part of the model at all'
A DAX row filter cannot hide an entire table; that requires OLS
Both can and should be configured together, enforced independently and simultaneously

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains RLS as DAX-based row filtering
Correctly explains OLS as schema-level object visibility restriction
Explains why RLS cannot substitute for OLS in this scenario
Proposes correctly combining both mechanisms
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Azure RBAC vs. Azure Policy: Access Control and Guardrails Are Not the Same Thing
questions.prompt: A cloud governance lead tells their team 'we've locked down the storage account with RBAC, so we're covered on governance.' Explain mechanically what Azure RBAC actually controls versus what Azure Policy controls, when each is evaluated, and why RBAC alone leaves a real governance gap that only Azure Policy can close — with a concrete example of something RBAC cannot prevent but Policy can.
questions.modelAnswer: Azure RBAC answers 'who is allowed to perform this action on this resource' -- it's evaluated at the moment a security principal attempts a management-plane or data-plane operation, checking role assignments (built-in or custom roles granting specific permissions) scoped to a management group, subscription, resource group, or individual resource. If the caller holds a role assignment with the needed permission at or above the target scope, the action is allowed; RBAC has no concept of what the resource's configuration should look like, only who may act on it. Azure Policy answers a completely different question: 'does this resource's actual configuration comply with an organizational rule,' and it's evaluated both at resource creation/update time (via a deny effect, which can block a non-compliant change outright) and on an ongoing compliance-scan basis against resources that already exist (flagging or, with certain effects like deployIfNotExists or modify, actively remediating drift) -- it has no concept of who performed the action, only whether the resulting resource state satisfies the rule. This creates a real gap RBAC cannot close on its own: a fully authorized user -- someone correctly granted Contributor or Storage Account Contributor via RBAC -- can still create a storage account with public blob access enabled, no encryption enforcement, or without the required network restrictions, because RBAC already answered 'yes, this person may modify storage accounts' and has nothing further to say about whether the specific configuration they chose is acceptable. Only an Azure Policy assignment (for example, denying storage account creation unless allowPublicBlobAccess is false, or requiring a specific minimum TLS version) actually prevents that specific unsafe configuration, regardless of how legitimately authorized the person creating it is. Genuine cloud governance requires both layers deliberately: RBAC to restrict who can act, and Policy to constrain what the result of any permitted action is allowed to look like.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on 'RBAC means we're covered' directly, because RBAC and Policy are answering two completely different questions and only one layer of protection doesn't cover you against the other's gap. RBAC is entirely about identity and permission -- is this person allowed to touch this resource at all. It says nothing about what they actually do once they're allowed in. Policy is the opposite -- it doesn't care who you are, it cares whether the resource you just created or modified actually matches the rules the organization has decided on, and it gets evaluated both at the moment of creation, where it can outright block a non-compliant change, and continuously afterward, flagging or even auto-remediating drift on resources that already exist. The gap that leaves if you only have RBAC: someone with totally legitimate Contributor access -- exactly the access you wanted them to have for their job -- can still spin up a storage account with public blob access wide open, or skip the encryption and network restrictions you assumed were standard, because RBAC already said yes to 'can this person manage storage accounts' and has no further opinion on how they configure it. The only thing standing between a fully authorized person and that unsafe configuration is a Policy assignment that denies creation unless the setting matches what's required. So I'd tell the team: RBAC answers who, Policy answers what the result looks like, and real governance needs an explicit Policy layer on top of RBAC, not instead of it.
questions.example: A user with Contributor via RBAC is fully authorized to create a storage account with Allow Blob Public Access enabled -- RBAC permits the action entirely. Only an Azure Policy definition with a deny effect on storageAccounts where allowBlobPublicAccess equals true actually stops that specific unsafe configuration from being created.
commonMistakes: Treating RBAC alone as sufficient governance coverage
Confusing 'who can act' (RBAC) with 'what the result must look like' (Policy)
Not knowing Policy evaluates both at creation time (deny) and continuously (compliance scanning/remediation)
Assuming a fully authorized user's actions are automatically safe or compliant
Not recognizing that Policy has no concept of identity, only resource configuration state
keyPoints: RBAC controls who may perform an action, evaluated at the time of the attempted action
Policy controls what a resource's configuration must look like, evaluated at creation and on an ongoing basis
RBAC has no opinion on configuration; Policy has no opinion on identity
A fully RBAC-authorized user can still create a non-compliant/unsafe resource without Policy
Real governance requires both layers deliberately combined, not one substituting for the other

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what RBAC controls and when it's evaluated
Correctly explains what Azure Policy controls and when it's evaluated
Articulates the specific governance gap RBAC alone leaves open
Gives a correct, concrete example of something only Policy prevents
Clear, accurate overall explanation
