questions.title: Walking a Bill-of-Materials Hierarchy with a Recursive CTE
questions.prompt: AdventureWorks2012's Production.BillOfMaterials table models a bicycle's bill of materials: a top-level assembly (ProductAssemblyID) is built from component products (ComponentID), and some of those components are themselves sub-assemblies built from further components, to an unknown depth. Write a query that returns the full multi-level component tree for a given assembly, including each component's depth level, using only currently-active BOM rows. Then explain the two required parts of a recursive CTE, why one particular set operator is mandatory, and what safety valve you'd put in place before running this against unfamiliar data.
questions.modelAnswer:
A recursive CTE has exactly two parts joined by UNION ALL: an anchor member that seeds the recursion (here, the direct components of the requested assembly), and a recursive member that references the CTE by its own name and joins the next level down onto the previous pass's results. SQL Server keeps re-executing the recursive member, feeding each pass's output back in as input to the next, until a pass produces zero new rows -- that's the only termination condition, which is exactly why cyclic data (a component that is, transitively, its own ancestor) can spin forever without a guard.

UNION ALL is mandatory, not a style choice: SQL Server's recursive CTE syntax does not permit plain UNION for the member union, because UNION's deduplication would have to compare against the full accumulated result set on every pass, which conflicts with how the recursive expansion is implemented. You also cannot put TOP, DISTINCT, GROUP BY/HAVING, or an outer join against the CTE itself inside the recursive member -- the recursive member is restricted to a simple SELECT...FROM CTE JOIN base-table shape.

The safety valve is OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) on the outer statement. The default limit is 100 levels; set it explicitly (or to 0, meaning unlimited, only when you're certain the data is acyclic) so a bad BOM row with a circular reference fails fast with error 530 instead of running away. Finally, filter EndDate IS NULL in both the anchor and the recursive member's join predicate -- Production.BillOfMaterials keeps historical, retired component relationships, and without that filter the hierarchy walk includes assemblies that no longer apply.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for a recursive CTE here because this is a classic parent-child walk of unknown depth -- you can't write a fixed number of self-joins when you don't know how many sub-assembly levels exist. I'd structure it as an anchor that grabs the direct components of the assembly I'm given, filtered to EndDate IS NULL so I'm not pulling in retired BOM relationships, starting at level zero. Then the recursive part joins BillOfMaterials back onto the CTE itself, matching the previous level's ComponentID to the new row's ProductAssemblyID, bumping the level each time. I always remind people UNION ALL isn't optional there -- SQL Server's recursive CTE syntax simply won't accept a plain UNION on that join. And before I'd run this against a BOM table I didn't already trust, I'd tack on OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100) or some sane number, because if there's ever a circular reference in that data -- a component that loops back to one of its own ancestors -- I want a clean error, not a query that just hangs.
questions.example:
WITH BOMHierarchy AS (
    -- Anchor: direct components of the requested assembly
    SELECT ProductAssemblyID, ComponentID, 0 AS Level,
           CAST(ComponentID AS VARCHAR(400)) AS Path
    FROM Production.BillOfMaterials
    WHERE ProductAssemblyID = 800 AND EndDate IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive member: references BOMHierarchy by its own name
    SELECT bom.ProductAssemblyID, bom.ComponentID, bh.Level + 1,
           bh.Path + '/' + CAST(bom.ComponentID AS VARCHAR(20))
    FROM Production.BillOfMaterials AS bom
    INNER JOIN BOMHierarchy AS bh
        ON bom.ProductAssemblyID = bh.ComponentID
    WHERE bom.EndDate IS NULL
)
SELECT ProductAssemblyID, ComponentID, Level, Path
FROM BOMHierarchy
ORDER BY Level
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100);
commonMistakes: Using UNION instead of UNION ALL, which T-SQL rejects for recursive CTEs
Forgetting to filter EndDate IS NULL, pulling in retired BOM relationships
Not setting MAXRECURSION, so a circular reference in the data hangs instead of erroring cleanly
Assuming the CTE itself is indexed or materialized, when it's really re-expanded pass by pass
Putting DISTINCT, TOP, or an outer join against the CTE inside the recursive member, which T-SQL disallows
keyPoints: Anchor member seeds the recursion; recursive member references the CTE by its own name
UNION ALL is required between anchor and recursive member -- plain UNION is disallowed
Recursion stops automatically when a pass produces zero new rows
OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) is the safety valve against circular/cyclic data
Filter EndDate IS NULL to exclude retired BOM relationships
The recursive member cannot contain TOP, DISTINCT, GROUP BY/HAVING, or an outer join against the CTE

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct anchor/recursive member structure in the query
Explains why UNION ALL is mandatory, not a preference
Addresses recursion depth/cycle safety via MAXRECURSION
Filters to active BOM rows (EndDate IS NULL)
Correctly describes recursive CTE syntax restrictions
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Removing Duplicate Staging Rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)
questions.prompt: A failed, partially-retried ETL load left Staging.SalesOrderDetail with duplicate rows sharing the same (SalesOrderID, ProductID), each with a different SalesOrderDetailID. Write a set-based query that deletes every duplicate except the one with the lowest SalesOrderDetailID for each key combination. Then explain why this approach is preferred over a cursor-based row-by-row deletion, and what would change in your query if you needed to keep the duplicate with the highest, rather than lowest, SalesOrderDetailID.
questions.modelAnswer:
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) is the right tool because it assigns a unique, strictly sequential number to every row within each partition without collapsing any rows the way GROUP BY would -- each duplicate row survives in the result set, just tagged with its position within its own (SalesOrderID, ProductID) group, ordered however I specify. Wrapping that in a CTE lets me then DELETE directly against the CTE wherever the assigned row number is greater than 1 -- SQL Server treats the CTE as a view onto the same underlying rows, so deleting from it deletes the real staging rows.

This beats a cursor for the same reason any row-by-row approach loses to a set-based one: a cursor would FETCH one row at a time, decide whether to delete it, and round-trip through the query engine's overhead for every single row -- on a staging table with any real volume, that's dramatically slower than a single set-based operation the engine can plan and execute as one pass (or a small number of passes) over the data, using whatever indexes exist on the partition/order columns.

To keep the highest SalesOrderDetailID instead of the lowest, the only change needed is the ORDER BY inside OVER(): ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID DESC instead of ascending (or no direction, since ascending is the default) -- row number 1 then lands on the highest ID in each partition, and everything else (the PARTITION BY, the DELETE WHERE rn > 1) stays identical. It's worth noting RANK() or DENSE_RANK() would be the wrong choice here specifically because they assign the same rank to true ties -- I want exactly one designated "keeper" row per key no matter what, which is precisely what ROW_NUMBER()'s strict, no-ties-allowed numbering guarantees.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move is to reach for ROW_NUMBER partitioned by the duplicate key -- SalesOrderID and ProductID together -- ordered by SalesOrderDetailID ascending, so within each duplicate group the row I want to keep gets numbered 1 and everything else gets 2, 3, and so on. I put that inside a CTE, and then I can delete straight from the CTE wherever that row number is greater than one -- SQL Server lets you do that because the CTE is really just a lens onto the same underlying staging rows.

I'd explain to someone why I didn't write this as a cursor: a cursor processes one row at a time, and every one of those iterations carries its own overhead -- that's exactly the row-by-row anti-pattern this course warns about. SQL Server's engine is built to work on whole sets of rows at once, so a single set-based DELETE against the CTE lets the optimizer handle this as one efficient operation instead of forcing it into thousands of tiny ones.

And if someone asked me to flip it around and keep the highest ID instead of the lowest, that's a one-word change -- just add DESC to the ORDER BY inside the OVER() clause. I'd also mention I specifically didn't reach for RANK or DENSE_RANK here, because those can tie two rows at the same rank, and I need exactly one row designated as the keeper every time -- ROW_NUMBER is the only one of the three that guarantees that.
questions.example:
WITH Duplicates AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY SalesOrderID, ProductID
               ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID ASC
           ) AS rn
    FROM Staging.SalesOrderDetail
)
DELETE FROM Duplicates
WHERE rn > 1;

-- To keep the HIGHEST SalesOrderDetailID instead, only the ORDER BY direction changes:
-- ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID DESC
commonMistakes: Using a cursor or WHILE loop to delete duplicates row by row
Using RANK() or DENSE_RANK() instead of ROW_NUMBER(), which can tie and leave more than one 'keeper' row
Forgetting that DELETE works against the CTE because it's a direct view onto the base rows, not a copy
Omitting an explicit ORDER BY inside OVER(), leaving which row survives undefined
Running the DELETE without first running the SELECT version to verify which rows would be removed
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) numbers every row without collapsing the result set
DELETE can run directly against a CTE wrapping the window function
Set-based deletion beats row-by-row cursor processing for performance at volume
ROW_NUMBER guarantees a single keeper per partition; RANK/DENSE_RANK do not
Flipping ASC/DESC in the ORDER BY changes which duplicate is kept

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct ROW_NUMBER/PARTITION BY/DELETE query
Explains why set-based beats cursor-based deletion
Correctly identifies the ORDER BY change needed to keep the highest ID
Explains why ROW_NUMBER is preferred over RANK/DENSE_RANK here
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Fix the Non-SARGable Order Lookup
questions.prompt: The query below is used in a nightly dashboard refresh and is now the slowest query in the job, taking almost 4 minutes against the Orders table (60M rows, nonclustered index on OrderDate). Rewrite it so it can use an index seek instead of a scan, without changing what it returns.
questions.code:
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, TotalAmount
FROM Orders
WHERE CONVERT(varchar(10), OrderDate, 120) = '2026-03-15'
   OR DATEADD(day, 1, OrderDate) = '2026-03-16';
questions.modelAnswer: This query has two separate non-SARGable predicates combined with OR, each of which independently forces a full scan: CONVERT(varchar(10), OrderDate, 120) wraps the column in a string conversion before comparing it, and DATEADD(day, 1, OrderDate) performs arithmetic on the column before comparing it — both require per-row evaluation across all 60 million rows, and the OR compounds the cost further because the optimizer can't cleanly combine two non-seekable branches into a single seek plan. Both predicates are actually expressing the exact same intent (rows where OrderDate falls on March 15, 2026), so the correct fix is to collapse them into a single SARGable range predicate that leaves OrderDate bare on one side of the comparison, using a half-open interval to correctly capture the entire day regardless of time-of-day values stored in the column.
questions.professionalAnswer: Looking at this, both of these predicates are just two different, overcomplicated ways of saying 'OrderDate is March 15th, 2026' — one converts the column to a string and compares it to a string literal, the other adds a day and compares to the 16th, and both of those operations have to run against the column before SQL Server can even check the condition, which means it can't seek, it has to scan every row and compute the expression first. I'd collapse this down to a plain date range using the raw column, written as a half-open interval so it still works correctly even if OrderDate has a time component — that keeps the column bare on the left side of the comparison so the optimizer can seek straight into the nonclustered index on OrderDate instead of touching all 60 million rows.
questions.example:
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, TotalAmount
FROM Orders
WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-03-15'
  AND OrderDate < '2026-03-16';
commonMistakes: Only fixing one of the two predicates and leaving the other non-SARGable branch in the OR
Using OrderDate = '2026-03-15' directly, which silently misses rows with a non-midnight time component
Not recognizing that both predicates express the same logical condition and can be merged into one range
Adding an index hint instead of fixing the predicate, which doesn't solve the underlying non-SARGable issue
Forgetting the half-open interval pattern and using BETWEEN with an inclusive end date/time that can miss late-day rows
keyPoints: Both original predicates wrap the column in a function/arithmetic, forcing per-row evaluation and a scan
Recognize that both branches express the same underlying date condition
Rewrite as a single SARGable half-open range on the bare column
Half-open range correctly handles any time-of-day component on OrderDate
Resulting plan should allow an index seek on the nonclustered OrderDate index

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies both predicates as non-SARGable and explains why
Produces a correct, equivalent SARGable rewrite
Uses a half-open interval that correctly handles time components
Explains expected improvement (seek vs scan)
Clean, correct SQL syntax

questions.title: Writing a Custom Classification Rule for an Internal Employee ID Format
questions.prompt: Your organization's HR extracts and finance exports contain an internal employee ID in the format EMP-123456 (always the literal prefix, a hyphen, then exactly six digits). Microsoft Purview's built-in classification library has nothing that recognizes this pattern. Walk through exactly how you'd build and deploy a custom classification for it in Purview — the regex rule itself, how you'd attach supporting evidence so it doesn't over-match, which scan rule set it needs to be added to, and how you'd verify it actually fired after a scan.
questions.modelAnswer:
First I'd define the custom classification itself in Purview's management center: a name like MICROSOFT.CUSTOM.EMPLOYEE_ID, a data pattern rule using a regular expression anchored tightly to the known format -- something like ^EMP-\d{6}$ -- rather than a loose pattern that could false-positive on unrelated six-digit codes elsewhere in the data. Regex alone is rarely enough to avoid over-matching, so I'd also configure a column-name (or 'name pattern') supporting rule -- requiring the column name to contain something like 'employee' or 'empid' -- and set the minimum match percentage/confidence threshold high enough that a column only gets classified if a strong majority of its sampled values match the pattern, not just a handful of coincidental hits.

Once the classification rule exists, it does nothing on its own -- it has to be added to a scan rule set (either a new custom scan rule set or an existing one scoped to the HR/finance sources) under the structured file types or database object types section, specifically the classification list for that rule set. I'd then either run a new scan or re-run an existing scheduled scan using that rule set against the registered HR/finance sources -- classifications are only assigned during an actual scan, they don't retroactively apply to data cataloged before the rule existed.

To verify it fired, I'd open the specific asset in the Data Catalog after the scan completes and check its Schema/classification tab for the column in question -- it should list the custom classification by name. I'd also spot-check a column that intentionally doesn't match the pattern (wrong format, wrong column name) to confirm it was correctly skipped, and check the scan's run history/diagnostics for any errors if the classification doesn't show up as expected.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start in the Purview governance portal's classification management area and create a new custom classification, giving it a clear name and a regex pattern locked down to exactly EMP- followed by six digits, not something loose that could match other numeric codes. Regex by itself tends to over-match, so I'd add a second layer -- a column-name hint requiring something like 'employee' or 'empid' to appear in the column name -- and push the confidence threshold up so it only fires when most of the sampled values actually match, not just a stray coincidence.

Then the part people sometimes forget: creating the classification doesn't make it active anywhere. I have to go add it into the actual scan rule set that governs the HR and finance sources, under the classification list for whatever file or database types those sources use. And classifications only get assigned during a scan run, so I'd either trigger a fresh scan or wait for the next scheduled one using that updated rule set -- existing catalog entries from before the rule existed won't retroactively pick it up.

To prove it worked, I'd open the asset in the catalog, look at its column-level classification tags, and confirm EMP-123456-style columns show the new custom classification while an unrelated six-digit column without the right name context doesn't. If it's missing where I expect it, my first suspect is the confidence threshold being too strict or the sample just not containing enough matching values.
questions.example:
Custom classification rule sketch:
Pattern: ^EMP-\d{6}$
Supporting rule: column name contains 'employee' OR 'empid' (case-insensitive)
Minimum match confidence: High (most sampled values must match)
Added to: HR-Finance custom scan rule set, under structured file/database classification list
Verification: Data Catalog asset > Schema tab > column shows classification 'EMP_EMPLOYEE_ID'
commonMistakes: Writing a regex loose enough to false-positive on unrelated numeric codes
Forgetting a custom classification does nothing until it's added to the scan rule set actually used against the source
Expecting classifications to retroactively apply to assets cataloged before the rule existed, without a new scan
Not adding a supporting column-name rule, relying on regex alone
Not verifying with both a positive match and a deliberate negative (non-matching) case
keyPoints: Custom classifications use a regex pattern plus optional supporting evidence (column name, confidence threshold)
A classification rule must be added to the scan rule set actually used against the target source
Classifications are only assigned during a scan run, not retroactively applied to existing catalog entries
Tight regex anchoring plus supporting rules reduces false-positive over-matching
Verification means checking the asset's column-level classification tags after a fresh scan, including a negative test case

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Defines a correctly anchored, specific regex pattern
Adds supporting evidence (column name/confidence) to reduce over-matching
Correctly explains adding the rule to the relevant scan rule set
Correctly explains that a new scan run is required, not retroactive application
Describes a concrete verification method including a negative test case

questions.title: Configuring OneLake Data Access Roles for a Folder-Level Security Boundary
questions.prompt: A Fabric lakehouse contains a 'raw' folder (unprocessed vendor files, sensitive) and a 'curated' folder (cleaned, business-ready tables) inside the same workspace. The whole analytics team has Workspace Viewer access so they can use the curated tables in Power BI, but only a small data engineering group should be able to read the raw folder directly. Walk through how you'd configure this using OneLake data access roles, and explain why workspace-level roles alone can't achieve this split.
questions.modelAnswer:
Workspace roles (Viewer, Contributor, Member, Admin) are an all-or-nothing grant on the item level inside that workspace -- a Viewer can see and use every item they're permitted to see, and by default that includes reading the underlying data of a lakehouse they have access to, with no built-in mechanism in the workspace role itself to say 'but not this one specific folder.' That's exactly the gap OneLake data access roles close: they let you define custom, folder-scoped roles directly on the lakehouse that grant read (and optionally write) access to specific paths within OneLake, independent of the coarser workspace role.

Concretely, I'd open the lakehouse's OneLake data access roles configuration and create a new role -- say 'RawFolderReaders' -- scoped to the /Files/raw (or equivalent Tables/raw) path, and assign only the data engineering security group to it. Critically, OneLake data access roles work as an allow-list on top of whatever default access exists: by default, anyone with sufficient workspace permission can read the whole lakehouse, so to actually restrict the raw folder I need to also configure the default/built-in access appropriately -- either by scoping a specific role that the broader analytics team falls into (granting them explicitly only the curated path) or by ensuring the raw folder isn't covered by any role the wider group belongs to while the data engineering group has its own explicit role covering it.

The reason workspace-level roles alone can't do this is that they have no concept of a sub-item boundary -- Viewer is scoped to 'the lakehouse,' not to 'this folder within the lakehouse.' OneLake data access roles are specifically the mechanism built to add that finer-grained, path-level boundary underneath the coarser workspace role, which is why both layers are configured together: workspace roles decide who can see the lakehouse exists and use it at all, OneLake data access roles decide exactly which paths within it they can actually read.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the gap first: Workspace Viewer is a blunt instrument -- it says 'this person can use items in this workspace,' and by default that includes reading everything in a lakehouse they can see, with no folder-level granularity built into the workspace role itself. To get the split this scenario needs, I'd go into the lakehouse's OneLake data access roles settings and define a custom role scoped specifically to the raw folder's path, and assign only the data engineering security group to that role. Then I'd make sure the broader analytics team's access is structured so they're not inadvertently covered by that raw-folder role -- either by giving them their own role scoped just to the curated path, or by relying on the fact that OneLake access roles are additive grants, so simply not including them in any role that touches 'raw' keeps them out of it, provided the lakehouse's default access posture doesn't quietly grant broader read access underneath. I'd double check that specifically, because it's the part people get wrong -- assuming the folder-level role is automatically restrictive rather than additive. The core thing I'd tell the team is that workspace roles and OneLake data access roles are two different layers solving two different problems: workspace roles gate 'can you use this lakehouse at all,' OneLake data access roles gate 'exactly which paths inside it can you actually read,' and you need the second layer specifically because the first one has no sub-item concept whatsoever.
questions.example:
OneLake data access role 'RawFolderReaders':
Scope: Files/raw (and/or Tables/raw if structured)
Permission: Read
Assigned security principal: DataEngineering-SG (Azure AD group)
-- Broader analytics team keeps Workspace Viewer for the lakehouse item,
-- but is not included in any role covering the raw path, limiting them
-- in practice to the curated tables surfaced through Power BI.
commonMistakes: Assuming Workspace Viewer access can be restricted to specific folders without OneLake data access roles
Treating OneLake data access roles as restrictive overrides rather than additive allow-list grants
Forgetting to verify the lakehouse's default access posture doesn't already grant broad read access underneath
Scoping the custom role to the wrong path (e.g. the lakehouse root instead of the specific raw subfolder)
Not assigning the role to a security group, leading to unmaintainable individual user assignments
keyPoints: Workspace roles are item-level, with no built-in concept of a folder-level boundary inside a lakehouse
OneLake data access roles add a path-scoped, additive permission layer underneath workspace roles
Roles must be scoped precisely to the intended path (e.g. raw folder only) and assigned to groups
Default/broad access must be checked so it doesn't silently override the intended restriction
Workspace roles and OneLake data access roles are configured together, not as substitutes for each other

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why workspace roles alone can't achieve folder-level restriction
Correctly describes configuring a scoped OneLake data access role
Correctly notes OneLake data access roles are additive, not automatically restrictive
Addresses verifying default/broad access doesn't undermine the restriction
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Granting a BI Analyst Group Read Access While Denying PII Columns in Unity Catalog
questions.prompt: A new BI analyst group needs to query the sales schema in Unity Catalog for reporting, but must never see the customer_ssn and customer_email columns on the customers table. Write the full sequence of GRANT statements needed to give the group working access to the schema, and explain the additional mechanism required to actually hide those two columns, since a table-level GRANT has no concept of per-column denial.
questions.modelAnswer:
The GRANT sequence has to establish the full traversal chain before the terminal read privilege means anything: USE CATALOG on the catalog, USE SCHEMA on the sales schema, and SELECT on the relevant tables (or on the schema as a whole if every table in it should be readable). None of these GRANT statements have any concept of per-column restriction -- GRANT SELECT ON TABLE is all-or-nothing for every column in that table's current schema, so the analyst group would see customer_ssn and customer_email in full once granted SELECT directly on the base table.

To actually hide those two columns, the base table itself has to not be the object the analyst group queries. The standard Unity Catalog pattern is to create a secure view (or a view with column masks, depending on edition/feature availability) that selects every column except the restricted two -- or that applies a masking expression to them -- and grant the analyst group SELECT on that view instead of on the base table, while explicitly not granting them SELECT on the underlying table itself. Because Unity Catalog views carry their own object-level ACLs, the group can be fully authorized to query the view and have zero privileges on the base table it's built from, which is what actually enforces the column restriction: there's no code path for them to reach the raw table and see the sensitive columns, and the view only ever exposes the columns its definition includes.
questions.professionalAnswer:
First, the plumbing: GRANT USE CATALOG, then GRANT USE SCHEMA on sales, then whatever SELECT grant gives them working table access -- and I'd point out right away that none of those three statements have any notion of 'except these two columns.' A table-level SELECT grant is all or nothing for the current schema of that table; there's no column-exclusion clause on GRANT SELECT ON TABLE.

So the real work is building a view that doesn't include customer_ssn and customer_email at all -- just a SELECT of everything else from customers -- and granting the analyst group SELECT on that view specifically, while making sure they never get SELECT on the base customers table itself. Unity Catalog views have their own independent ACLs, so the group can be completely authorized to read the view and have zero access to the underlying table, which is exactly what makes the column hiding actually stick -- it's not a display trick, they genuinely have no privilege path to the raw table where those columns live.
commonMistakes: Granting SELECT directly on the base table, exposing every column including the restricted two
Assuming a table-level GRANT supports a column-exclusion clause
Creating the restricting view but still leaving a SELECT grant on the base table for the same group
Forgetting the full USE CATALOG / USE SCHEMA traversal chain before the view-level grant takes effect
Not using a security group for the grant, leading to unmaintainable per-user access
keyPoints: GRANT statements establish traversal (USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA) before any object-level grant is reachable
Table-level SELECT has no per-column denial mechanism -- it's all-or-nothing
A secure view excluding the sensitive columns, with its own independent grant, is the enforcement mechanism
The group must not also hold SELECT on the base table, or the view restriction is bypassable
Grants should target security groups, not individual users, for maintainability

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct full GRANT sequence (USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, view SELECT)
Correctly explains table-level GRANT has no column-exclusion mechanism
Correctly proposes a restricting view as the enforcement mechanism
Notes the base table must not also be independently granted to the same group
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Building a Dynamic View That Masks SSN Based on Group Membership
questions.prompt: Rather than hiding customer_ssn entirely, Compliance wants most analysts to see a masked version (last 4 digits only) while a small Compliance-Review group sees the full value — all through a single shared view everyone queries, not two separate views. Write the dynamic view definition that does this using group-membership checks, and explain why this pattern is preferable to maintaining two near-duplicate views.
questions.modelAnswer:
A dynamic view embeds the access-control logic directly inside the view's SELECT using Unity Catalog's built-in functions for checking the calling principal's group membership -- most commonly is_account_group_member('group_name') -- wrapped in a CASE expression against the column being protected. The view is defined once, granted to every analyst who needs any access to it, and the masking decision is evaluated per query, per calling user, at query time, rather than being baked into two separate static view definitions that both have to be kept in sync with the base table's schema.

This single-view pattern is preferable to maintaining two near-duplicate views for a concrete maintenance reason: every time the base customers table's schema changes -- a new column added, a column renamed -- two separate views mean two separate places that have to be updated, and any time someone forgets to update one of them, it silently drifts out of sync with the other (different column lists, different ordering), creating confusing inconsistencies for whoever queries the 'wrong' one. A single dynamic view has exactly one definition to maintain, and the only thing that varies by caller is the masking expression's CASE result, not the overall structure of the query -- so schema drift between two parallel objects simply isn't possible, because there's only one object.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd build this as one view where the masking decision is a CASE expression right inside the SELECT, checking is_account_group_member against the Compliance-Review group -- if you're in that group, you get the real ssn column value; if you're not, you get a masked version showing only the last four digits. Everyone who needs any access to this view gets the same SELECT grant on the same object; what changes per person is purely what the CASE expression resolves to when their query runs.

The reason I'd push back on 'just make two views' is maintenance drift, plainly. The moment the base customers table's schema changes -- a new column, a renamed one -- you now have two view definitions that both need updating, and the two of them will eventually get out of sync because somebody updates one and forgets the other, or updates them slightly differently. With one dynamic view, there's exactly one definition to keep current, and the only per-user difference lives in a single CASE expression, not in two parallel, slowly diverging objects.
questions.example:
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW sales_catalog.sales.customers_masked AS
SELECT
  customer_id,
  first_name,
  last_name,
  CASE
    WHEN is_account_group_member('compliance_review') THEN customer_ssn
    ELSE CONCAT('XXX-XX-', RIGHT(customer_ssn, 4))
  END AS customer_ssn,
  region
FROM sales_catalog.sales.customers;

GRANT SELECT ON VIEW sales_catalog.sales.customers_masked TO `bi_analysts`, `compliance_review`;
commonMistakes: Maintaining two near-duplicate views instead of one dynamic view, risking schema drift between them
Hardcoding usernames instead of checking group membership via is_account_group_member
Forgetting SELECT must still be granted on the view, not the base table, to every intended consumer
Applying the masking logic to the wrong column or producing an inconsistent masked format across rows
Not re-testing the view after a base table schema change to confirm the masking expression still references the correct column
keyPoints: A dynamic view embeds a CASE expression using group-membership checks to vary output per calling user
is_account_group_member() evaluates the actual querying principal's group membership at query time
One dynamic view avoids schema drift risk inherent in maintaining two near-duplicate views
The masking decision varies; the underlying query structure and grant surface stay single and consistent
Grants are made on the view, not the base table, for every group needing any level of access

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct dynamic view definition using group-membership check and CASE masking
Correctly explains the schema-drift maintenance risk of two near-duplicate views
Correct GRANT structure on the view for all intended consumers
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Creating a Masking Policy for a Credit Card Column With Role-Based Unmasking
questions.prompt: Write the Snowflake DDL to create a masking policy that fully redacts a credit_card_number column for every role except FINANCE_ADMIN and PAYMENTS_OPS, which should see the real value, and apply it to the orders table's credit_card_number column. Explain what happens if the column already had a masking policy attached from an earlier project, and how you'd confirm the policy is actually active.
questions.modelAnswer:
The masking policy is created as its own schema-level object with CREATE MASKING POLICY, defined once with an input type and return type matching the column it will protect, and a CASE expression driven by CURRENT_ROLE() that returns the real value for the two privileged roles and a fully redacted string otherwise. Creating the policy object does nothing to any table by itself -- it has to then be explicitly attached with ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN ... SET MASKING POLICY, which is the step that actually activates enforcement on that specific column.

If the column already has a masking policy attached from an earlier project, Snowflake does not allow two masking policies to be simultaneously active on the same column -- attempting to SET a new masking policy on a column that already has one attached fails with an error unless the existing one is first removed via ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN ... UNSET MASKING POLICY. So the correct sequence when replacing an existing policy is: unset the old one, then set the new one -- there's a brief window where the column is unprotected between those two statements, which matters for anyone running a sensitive migration and should be done in a maintenance window or wrapped tightly together.

To confirm the policy is actually active, I'd query INFORMATION_SCHEMA or run SHOW MASKING POLICIES combined with a check of the specific column's policy references (e.g. via SELECT * FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.POLICY_REFERENCES(REF_ENTITY_NAME => 'orders', REF_ENTITY_DOMAIN => 'table'))), and then do the practical test: run SELECT credit_card_number FROM orders as a session using a non-privileged role and confirm it returns the redacted value, then switch to FINANCE_ADMIN and confirm it returns the real value.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd write the masking policy as its own object first -- CREATE MASKING POLICY with a CASE on CURRENT_ROLE(), returning the real value for FINANCE_ADMIN and PAYMENTS_OPS and a redacted string for everyone else. That alone does nothing until I explicitly attach it to the column with ALTER TABLE orders MODIFY COLUMN credit_card_number SET MASKING POLICY -- that's the step that flips enforcement on.

If there's already a policy on that column from an earlier project, Snowflake won't just let me layer a second one on top -- I have to unset the existing policy first, then set the new one, as two separate statements. I'd flag that there's a small gap between those two steps where the column has no masking policy active at all, so I'd want to do that swap quickly and ideally during a lower-traffic window if the data's genuinely sensitive.

To actually prove it's working, I wouldn't just trust that the ALTER succeeded -- I'd query the policy references through INFORMATION_SCHEMA to confirm the column shows the new policy attached, and then do the real test: query the table as a role that isn't FINANCE_ADMIN or PAYMENTS_OPS and confirm I get the redacted value, then switch to FINANCE_ADMIN and confirm I get the real number.
commonMistakes: Assuming CREATE MASKING POLICY alone activates enforcement without a SET MASKING POLICY on the column
Trying to attach a new masking policy to a column that already has one, without unsetting it first
Not accounting for the brief unprotected window between unsetting the old policy and setting the new one
Verifying only that the ALTER TABLE statement succeeded instead of confirming behavior with an actual query test
Hardcoding role checks without considering role hierarchy inheritance into CURRENT_ROLE()
keyPoints: A masking policy is a standalone object; it must be explicitly attached to a column to take effect
A column can only have one masking policy at a time; the existing one must be unset before setting a new one
There is a brief unprotected window during a policy swap that should be handled carefully
INFORMATION_SCHEMA.POLICY_REFERENCES confirms which policy is attached to which object
Real verification requires testing the actual query result under privileged and non-privileged roles

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct CREATE MASKING POLICY and ALTER TABLE SET MASKING POLICY DDL
Correctly explains the unset-then-set requirement for an existing policy
Flags the unprotected window during policy replacement
Describes a concrete, correct verification method
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Writing a Row Access Policy That Restricts Rows by Sales Region
questions.prompt: Each regional sales role (SALES_EAST, SALES_WEST, SALES_CENTRAL) should only see rows in the orders table matching their own region, while SALES_ADMIN should see every region. Rather than hardcoding region logic directly into the policy, use a mapping table of role-to-region so new regions can be added without touching the policy definition. Write the mapping table, the row access policy, and the statement attaching it to the table.
questions.modelAnswer:
The mapping table approach separates 'who is allowed to see what' (data, which changes often as the business adds regions or reassigns roles) from 'how is that decision enforced' (policy logic, which should stay stable). I'd create a small table, say region_access(role_name STRING, sales_region STRING), with one row per role-region pairing the business wants to allow, plus a dedicated row (or a wildcard sentinel handled in the policy) representing SALES_ADMIN's all-region access -- the cleanest way to express 'sees everything' without special-casing it inside the policy itself is to insert a row for SALES_ADMIN against every region value, or add an OR CURRENT_ROLE() = 'SALES_ADMIN' escape clause directly in the policy for exactly that one role.

The row access policy itself then does nothing but look up whether a row exists in that mapping table matching the calling role and the row's region -- EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM region_access WHERE role_name = CURRENT_ROLE() AND sales_region = orders.sales_region). Attaching it with ALTER TABLE ... ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY ... ON (sales_region) makes every query against orders -- regardless of who wrote it or how -- automatically filtered through this lookup, with no way for a report author to accidentally bypass it, since it's enforced inside the table's own access path, not inside each individual query.

Adding a new region going forward requires only an INSERT into region_access -- zero changes to the policy definition, zero redeployment risk, and the pattern scales cleanly as the organization adds regions or changes which roles can see which ones.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd deliberately keep the actual region-to-role logic out of the policy and put it in a small lookup table instead -- role_name and sales_region, one row per combination that should be allowed. For SALES_ADMIN seeing everything, I'd either add a row for every region against that role, or just add a straightforward CURRENT_ROLE() = 'SALES_ADMIN' OR clause in the policy as the one deliberate exception -- either way works, I'd pick whichever the team finds easier to maintain.

The policy itself then just asks one question: does a row exist in that mapping table for the role running this query and the region on this particular row? That's an EXISTS subquery against the mapping table, nothing more. I attach that policy to the orders table on the sales_region column, and from that point forward every single query against orders gets filtered through it automatically -- there's no way for someone to write around it, because it's enforced at the table's access layer, not something each report author has to remember to add themselves.

The payoff of doing it this way is that when the business adds a new region next quarter, I don't touch the policy at all -- I just insert new rows into the mapping table, and the existing policy logic picks it up with zero redeployment.
commonMistakes: Hardcoding region-to-role logic directly into the policy, requiring redeployment for every new region
Forgetting to handle SALES_ADMIN's all-region access explicitly, either via a wildcard or a role check
Assuming a row access policy can be bypassed by writing a 'clever' query -- it's enforced at the table's access path
Not indexing or sizing the mapping table appropriately, causing it to become a performance bottleneck on every query
Confusing a row access policy's evaluation (EXISTS/boolean per row) with a masking policy's content-transformation logic
keyPoints: A mapping table separates maintainable access data from stable policy logic
The row access policy is a boolean expression evaluated per row via an EXISTS lookup against the mapping table
SALES_ADMIN's all-region access needs an explicit mechanism (wildcard rows or a role check)
Attaching the policy with ALTER TABLE enforces it transparently on every query, with no bypass path
Adding a new region requires only a data change (INSERT), never a policy redeployment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct mapping table design and data
Correct row access policy using EXISTS against the mapping table
Correctly handles SALES_ADMIN's all-region access
Correct ALTER TABLE ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY attachment
Explains the maintainability benefit of the mapping-table pattern

questions.title: Building Tag-Based Masking So New PII Columns Are Protected Automatically
questions.prompt: Rather than attaching a masking policy to every PII column individually (and risking new columns going unprotected until someone remembers), set up tag-based masking in Snowflake: create a classification tag, attach a masking policy to the tag itself instead of to individual columns, and apply the tag to an existing email column. Explain exactly what happens the next time a new column is tagged the same way, without any further policy work.
questions.modelAnswer:
Tag-based masking inverts the normal attachment direction: instead of a masking policy being set directly on each column (ALTER TABLE ... SET MASKING POLICY, repeated per column, per table, forever), the policy is associated with a tag object via ALTER TAG ... SET MASKING POLICY, and any column that later has that tag applied to it -- via ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN ... SET TAG -- automatically inherits enforcement of every masking policy associated with that tag, with no separate per-column masking-policy statement required.

Concretely: create the tag (CREATE TAG pii_classification), create the masking policy with an input/return type matching the columns it will be used on, associate the policy with the tag (ALTER TAG pii_classification SET MASKING POLICY email_mask), and then apply the tag to the existing email column (ALTER TABLE customers MODIFY COLUMN email SET TAG pii_classification = 'EMAIL'). From that point, the email column is masked according to the policy, exactly as if it had been set directly.

The real payoff is the next step: if a new table is created six months later with its own email-type column, and someone (or an automated classification process) tags that new column with the same pii_classification tag, masking enforcement applies to it immediately and automatically -- no one has to remember to write or attach a new masking policy statement for that specific column. This is precisely the governance-at-scale pattern that closes the gap of 'new sensitive columns go unprotected until someone remembers to lock them down': protection is now a consequence of correct classification/tagging, not a separate manual step that has to happen in parallel with every new table or column.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The mental shift here is: instead of tying a masking policy to a specific column, I tie it to a tag, and then tagging becomes the thing that actually turns protection on. So I create the tag first -- something like pii_classification -- then I create the masking policy as usual, and instead of attaching it to a column with SET MASKING POLICY, I attach it to the tag itself with ALTER TAG ... SET MASKING POLICY. Only then do I apply the tag to the existing email column.

The part worth emphasizing is what happens next, with zero extra work: if six months from now someone builds a brand-new table with its own email column, and that column gets tagged pii_classification -- whether by a person doing it manually or by an automated classification process -- it's masked immediately, because the masking policy was never actually tied to that specific column, it's tied to the tag, and the tag just showed up on a new object. Nobody has to remember to go write a fresh masking-policy statement for every new sensitive column that gets created going forward. That's the whole point of doing it this way instead of column-by-column -- it turns 'is this new column protected' into a direct consequence of 'was it correctly classified,' which is a much easier thing to actually keep up with at scale than remembering every individual ALTER TABLE statement.
commonMistakes: Attaching the masking policy directly to each column instead of to the tag, losing the automatic-inheritance benefit
Forgetting the masking policy's input/return type must be compatible with every column type the tag might later be applied to
Assuming tagging a column automatically classifies it correctly without any validation step
Not realizing a column can only have one masking policy effectively enforced even if reached via a tag
Treating tag-based masking as optional 'nice to have' rather than the mechanism that actually closes the new-column protection gap
keyPoints: A masking policy can be associated with a tag object instead of (or in addition to) a specific column
Applying the tag to any column automatically enforces every masking policy associated with that tag
New columns tagged the same way are protected immediately, with no new per-column policy statement
This turns protection into a consequence of correct classification/tagging rather than a separate manual step
The policy's input/return type must remain compatible with the range of column types the tag may be applied to

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct CREATE TAG / ALTER TAG SET MASKING POLICY / apply tag sequence
Correctly explains automatic enforcement on newly tagged columns
Explains the governance-at-scale benefit over per-column policy attachment
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Configuring and Testing Row-Level Security Roles in a Power BI Semantic Model
questions.prompt: Walk through, step by step, how you'd configure row-level security in a Power BI Desktop semantic model so that a 'RegionalManager' role only sees rows where the Region column matches a value derived from the viewing user's email, and how you'd thoroughly test it before publishing — including the one testing step people skip that causes production surprises.
questions.modelAnswer:
In Power BI Desktop, I'd open Modeling > Manage Roles and create a new role, say RegionalManager, then define a DAX filter expression on the fact or dimension table that should be restricted -- typically on a Region dimension table rather than the fact table directly, since filtering the dimension cascades through any relationship to the fact table and is both simpler and usually cheaper than filtering a large fact table row by row. The filter expression would be something like [RegionManagerEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(), which compares the dimension row's assigned manager email against the identity of whoever is actually viewing the report at query time -- USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns the UPN of the Power BI Service's authenticated viewer once published (in Desktop, it falls back to the Windows account unless overridden by a test role).

To test thoroughly before publishing, I'd use Modeling > View As and select the RegionalManager role, entering a specific UPN of a known regional manager to simulate their view -- this is the step that most closely replicates production behavior. Critically, the skipped step that causes surprises is testing with more than one representative UPN and testing the 'no match' case: picking a UPN that doesn't correspond to any row in the Region table at all, to confirm the user correctly sees zero rows rather than accidentally seeing everything (which happens if the DAX filter is written in a way that evaluates to TRUE when no match exists, or if the role isn't actually being enforced on the right table). I'd also test with a UPN whose casing differs from what's stored in the dimension, since UPN comparisons can be case-sensitive depending on the exact DAX functions used, and a silent case mismatch is a very common reason RLS appears to work in testing with one 'clean' test account but breaks for real users whose email casing varies.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd go into Manage Roles, create RegionalManager, and write the DAX filter against the Region dimension table rather than the fact table -- filtering the dimension and letting the relationship cascade the restriction is simpler and almost always the right call unless there's a specific reason the relationship direction doesn't support it. The filter itself compares the row's assigned manager email to USERPRINCIPALNAME(), which is Power BI's way of asking 'who is actually looking at this report right now.'

For testing, View As Role with a specific UPN is the obvious first step, and most people stop there. The thing I always do that catches real problems: test a UPN that doesn't match any row at all, and confirm the result is zero rows, not everything -- because if the DAX expression has any subtle logic bug, the failure mode is often 'nobody matches, so nothing filters, so they see all of it,' which is the worst possible silent failure for a security feature. I'd also deliberately test a UPN with different letter casing than what's actually stored in the table, because UPN comparisons can be case-sensitive depending on which DAX function and data type you're working with, and that's exactly the kind of thing that passes testing with one clean internal test account and then quietly breaks for a real user whose email happens to be stored with different capitalization somewhere upstream.
questions.example:
RegionalManager role DAX filter on the Region dimension table:
[RegionManagerEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()

Test matrix before publishing:
1. View As Role, UPN = a known manager -- expect only their region's rows
2. View As Role, UPN = not present in RegionManagerEmail at all -- expect zero rows, not all rows
3. View As Role, UPN = same manager but different letter casing -- expect identical result to test 1
commonMistakes: Filtering the large fact table directly instead of the smaller dimension table that cascades through relationships
Testing only one 'known good' UPN and never testing a non-matching UPN
Not testing for case-sensitivity mismatches between the stored value and the real UPN format
Assuming Desktop's View As behaves identically to the Service's enforcement without separately verifying after publish
Forgetting that a non-matching user seeing everything, rather than nothing, is a silent, dangerous failure mode
keyPoints: RLS roles are defined with a DAX filter, ideally against a dimension table that cascades to the fact table
USERPRINCIPALNAME() identifies the actual viewing user at query time
View As Role in Desktop with a specific UPN is the primary pre-publish testing tool
Testing a non-matching UPN to confirm zero rows (not all rows) is the critical, often-skipped test
Case-sensitivity mismatches in UPN comparison are a common, easily-missed production failure mode

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes creating the role and DAX filter, ideally on the dimension table
Correctly uses USERPRINCIPALNAME() for identity-based filtering
Describes View As Role testing with a specific UPN
Identifies testing the non-matching-UPN zero-rows case as the critical skipped step
Addresses case-sensitivity risk in UPN comparison

questions.title: Configuring a Dev/Test/Prod Deployment Pipeline With Data Source Rules
questions.prompt: Set up a Power BI deployment pipeline with Development, Test, and Production stages for a semantic model and its reports, where each stage must point to a different underlying SQL database (dev_db, test_db, prod_db) without manually editing the connection after every deployment. Walk through the configuration, including the specific mechanism that makes the data source swap automatic.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd create the pipeline in the Power BI Service, assigning three existing (or new) workspaces to the Development, Test, and Production stages respectively, then deploy the semantic model and reports forward from Development into Test, and from Test into Production, using the pipeline's deploy action, which compares content between stages and only moves what's changed. The piece that actually makes the data source swap automatic is deployment rules: on the Test and Production stages specifically (deployment rules can't be set on Development, since it's the origin stage), I'd open the pipeline's deployment rules for the semantic model and define a parameter rule or data source rule that overrides the connection string/server and database values to point at test_db for the Test stage and prod_db for the Production stage.

This only works cleanly if the semantic model's data source is parameterized -- using Power Query parameters for the server and database names rather than a hardcoded connection string baked into each query -- because deployment rules operate by overriding parameter values per stage, not by rewriting M code. Once that's set up, every subsequent deployment into Test or Production automatically applies that stage's rule and repoints the model at the correct database without anyone touching the connection manually -- the rule persists across deployments until someone changes it, so this is a one-time setup cost per stage, not a per-deployment task.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd set up the pipeline with three workspaces mapped to Development, Test, and Production, and do my first deploy forward from Dev into Test, then Test into Production, letting the pipeline's comparison view show me exactly what's different before I confirm each deploy. The actual mechanism that avoids manually re-pointing the connection every time is deployment rules -- these live on the Test and Production stages only, not on Development, since Development is where content originates. For the semantic model, I'd configure a parameter rule that overrides the server and database parameter values for that specific stage: test_db for Test, prod_db for Production.

The catch, and it's an important one: this only works if the model's connection is built on parameters in the first place -- Power Query parameters for server name and database name, not a connection string typed directly into each query. Deployment rules override parameter values; they don't rewrite the underlying M code.
