questions.title: Granting Fine-Grained S3 Access Through AWS Lake Formation Using LF-Tags
questions.prompt: An analytics team needs read access to every table tagged 'department=finance' across dozens of databases in the Glue Data Catalog, without an admin having to individually grant access table by table or update grants every time a new finance table is added. Walk through configuring this with AWS Lake Formation LF-Tags, and explain why this scales better than resource-based (table-by-table) grants.
questions.modelAnswer:
LF-Tags (Lake Formation tag-based access control) let an administrator define a tag -- say department with allowed values including finance -- in the Lake Formation console, assign that tag to the relevant databases or individual tables in the Glue Data Catalog, and then grant a principal (an IAM role or user) access based on the tag expression (department = finance) rather than by naming each table individually. Concretely: create the LF-Tag and its allowed values, assign department = finance to every current finance table (or at the database level if every table in that database should inherit it), then grant the analytics team's IAM role SELECT permission scoped to the LF-Tag expression department = finance, rather than a list of specific table ARNs.

This scales better than resource-based, table-by-table grants for the same reason tag-based masking scales better than per-column masking policies: the grant is attached to a tag expression, not to a fixed enumeration of resources, so when a new finance table is created next quarter and tagged department = finance by whoever owns it (ideally as a required step in the table creation process, or automated via a Glue crawler classification step), the analytics team's existing grant automatically covers it -- no admin has to remember to add a new grant for that specific new table. Without LF-Tags, an admin maintaining table-by-table grants would need to proactively find and grant access to every new finance table as it's created, which is exactly the kind of manual, easily-forgotten step that leads to either over-broad standing grants (to avoid the hassle) or analysts missing access to legitimately relevant new data.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd set this up with LF-Tags rather than naming tables one by one. First step is defining the tag itself in Lake Formation -- a key like department with finance as one of its allowed values -- then assigning department = finance to the existing finance tables, or to the whole database if every table in it belongs to finance. The grant itself then targets the tag expression, not a list of table names: I grant the analytics team's IAM role SELECT where department = finance, and that's the entire access decision from that point forward.

The reason this beats table-by-table grants becomes obvious the moment a new finance table shows up. If I'd granted access by naming specific tables, someone has to remember to add a new grant every single time a finance table gets created -- and in practice, that step gets missed constantly, either leaving analysts without access to new data they should have, or pushing admins toward overly broad standing grants just to avoid the maintenance burden. With LF-Tags, as long as whoever creates the new table tags it department = finance -- which I'd make a required step in the table creation process -- the analytics team's existing grant covers it automatically, with zero additional admin work. The access decision becomes a consequence of correct tagging, not a thing anyone has to separately remember to maintain.
questions.example:
1. Create LF-Tag: key = department, values = [finance, marketing, supply_chain]
2. Assign tag: department=finance to each finance database/table in Glue Data Catalog
3. Grant: analytics_team_role -> SELECT -> LF-Tag expression department=finance
-- New finance table created next quarter, tagged department=finance by its owner
-- -> covered by the existing grant automatically, no new grant needed.
commonMistakes: Granting access table-by-table (resource-based) instead of via an LF-Tag expression
Forgetting that new resources must still be tagged correctly to inherit existing tag-based grants
Not making tagging a required, enforced step in the table creation/onboarding process
Assuming LF-Tags remove the need for any access review, rather than just removing the per-resource grant maintenance burden
Confusing LF-Tags with plain Glue Data Catalog table properties, which have no bearing on Lake Formation access decisions
keyPoints: LF-Tags let grants target a tag expression (e.g. department=finance) rather than an enumerated list of resources
New resources tagged with the matching value automatically inherit existing tag-based grants
This avoids the maintenance burden and missed-grant risk inherent in table-by-table access control
Tagging must be a consistently enforced step when new tables/databases are created
Access decisions become a consequence of correct classification/tagging, scaling without proportional admin effort

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes defining and assigning an LF-Tag
Correctly describes granting access via the tag expression rather than per-table
Correctly explains why this scales better than table-by-table grants
Notes the dependency on consistent tagging of new resources
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Fixing a SQL-Injectable Dynamic Search Procedure
questions.prompt: A teammate wrote the stored procedure below to let a reporting UI search products by color with a user-selectable sort column. Identify every injection vector in it, then rewrite it safely. Explain specifically why the color value and the sort column name have to be handled differently -- one can be parameterized directly, the other cannot.
questions.modelAnswer:
There are two separate injection vectors here, and they need two different fixes.

The first is @Color: it's concatenated directly into the string inside quotes, so a value like `Red'; DROP TABLE Production.Product; --` gets executed as part of the statement. This is the classic case sp_executesql exists to solve -- @Color is a data value, so it belongs in sp_executesql's parameter list, where SQL Server treats it strictly as data and never as executable text, no matter what characters it contains.

The second is @SortColumn, and it's actually the more dangerous one because it can't be fixed the same way. sp_executesql's parameters only substitute values -- they cannot substitute an identifier like a column name, because `ORDER BY @Param` isn't valid T-SQL (SQL Server would try to sort by a constant, not by a column). That means @SortColumn has to be handled by validation, not parameterization: either whitelist it against a known, fixed list of legal column names before it ever reaches the dynamic string, or at minimum wrap it in QUOTENAME() to neutralize bracket-based injection tricks -- and I'd do both, since QUOTENAME alone doesn't stop someone passing a syntactically valid but unintended column name.

The corrected version below parameterizes @Color through sp_executesql and validates @SortColumn against an explicit allow-list before concatenating it (safely, as an identifier, not a value).
questions.professionalAnswer:
Looking at this procedure, I'd flag it immediately in a code review -- it's building the entire WHERE and ORDER BY clause by gluing strings together, and that's a textbook SQL injection hole. There are actually two different problems stacked on top of each other, and I'd want to be clear they need different fixes. The Color value is a data value, so the right move is sp_executesql with a proper parameter -- that's the whole reason sp_executesql exists, it treats whatever gets passed in purely as data, so even something like a stray apostrophe or an embedded DROP TABLE just becomes a literal string being compared, not code getting executed.

The sort column is trickier, and I'd explain why it can't get the same treatment: you physically cannot parameterize an identifier the way you parameterize a value -- ORDER BY @SomeParam just doesn't do what you'd want, it won't sort by a column, it'll try to sort by whatever that one value is. So for something like a sort column, I always reach for a whitelist -- check the incoming value against the small, fixed list of columns we actually allow sorting by, fall back to a safe default if it's not on the list, and only then build it into the dynamic SQL as an identifier, wrapped in QUOTENAME for good measure.
commonMistakes: Parameterizing only the value and missing that the sort column is a second, separate injection vector
Trying to pass the sort column as an sp_executesql parameter, which doesn't work for identifiers
Relying on QUOTENAME alone for the sort column without an allow-list behind it
Using EXEC() with concatenated strings instead of sp_executesql
Assuming input validation on the UI side is sufficient and skipping server-side protection
keyPoints: sp_executesql parameterizes data values safely; EXEC() with concatenation does not
Identifiers (column/table names) cannot be parameterized -- only values can
Dynamic identifiers must be validated against a whitelist, optionally plus QUOTENAME
Reach for dynamic SQL only when a real identifier or structural element must vary at runtime
SQL injection risk exists even inside stored procedures, not just at the application layer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies both injection vectors (value and identifier)
Explains why sp_executesql parameters can't substitute identifiers
Provides a correct, safe rewrite using sp_executesql
Includes identifier whitelisting/QUOTENAME for the sort column
Clear overall explanation of the fix

questions.title: Diagnosing a Recurring Deadlock Between Two Order-Processing Procedures
questions.prompt: Two stored procedures are both involved in order processing: usp_UpdateOrderStatus updates the Orders table first, then OrderDetails; usp_ApplyDiscount updates OrderDetails first, then Orders. Under heavy load during a sale event, both start failing intermittently with error 1205. Walk through how you'd confirm this is a genuine deadlock rather than ordinary blocking, what SQL Server already did automatically before you even got paged, how you'd capture the diagnostic evidence, and how you'd redesign the two procedures so this stops recurring.
questions.modelAnswer:
Error 1205 is the giveaway on its own -- it's SQL Server's specific "transaction was deadlocked" error, distinct from ordinary blocking (which doesn't raise an error at all; it just makes the waiting session sit there until the lock is released or the query times out). So the first confirmation is simply that message text and code, not a guess.

Before anyone got paged, SQL Server's lock monitor already detected the cycle automatically and picked one of the two transactions as the deadlock victim, rolling it back on its own and raising 1205 in that session, while letting the other transaction proceed normally. That's expected, automatic behavior -- the problem isn't that SQL Server handled a deadlock; it's that the application design is creating deadlocks in the first place.

To get real evidence instead of guessing, I'd capture the actual deadlock graph: either the system_health Extended Events session (which captures deadlock graphs by default on every modern SQL Server instance with zero setup), or trace flag 1222 writing deadlock graphs to the error log, or a live SQL Server Profiler trace with the Deadlock graph event if I need to reproduce it under controlled load. The graph shows exactly which two sessions were involved, which resources (specific rows/keys/pages) each one held and was waiting on, and which queries were running -- that's what turns "it deadlocks sometimes" into "usp_UpdateOrderStatus held a lock on Orders row X while waiting on OrderDetails row Y, and usp_ApplyDiscount had the exact opposite."

The root cause here is visible just from the procedure descriptions, independent of the graph: the two procedures touch the same two tables in opposite order. usp_UpdateOrderStatus locks Orders then OrderDetails; usp_ApplyDiscount locks OrderDetails then Orders. Under enough concurrent load, it's inevitable that one session grabs the first lock each procedure needs right as the other grabs the second, and neither can proceed. The fix is to enforce a single, consistent access order across every procedure that touches both tables -- rewrite usp_ApplyDiscount to update Orders before OrderDetails, matching usp_UpdateOrderStatus. I'd also shorten both transactions to only what genuinely needs to be atomic, consider whether the default isolation level is adding unnecessary lock duration for this workload, and add application-side retry logic that catches 1205 specifically and retries the transaction once, since even with consistent ordering, some contention under extreme load is still possible.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd point to is that error 1205 is specific -- it's SQL Server's deadlock error, not generic blocking, so I already know what category of problem this is before I even look at the code. And something people sometimes miss: by the time I'm looking at this, SQL Server has already handled the immediate crisis on its own -- it detected the cycle, picked a victim, rolled that one transaction back, and let the other one finish. So I'm not firefighting an active deadlock; I'm investigating why this keeps happening.

To get real evidence I'd go straight to the deadlock graph -- these days that's usually just querying the system_health Extended Events session, since it captures deadlock graphs automatically without me having to turn anything on ahead of time. If I needed something more targeted I'd reach for trace flag 1222 or a Profiler trace with the deadlock graph event. That graph tells me exactly which resources each session was holding and waiting on, which is the proof, not just a theory.

But honestly, in this specific case, I could probably guess the root cause just from the procedure descriptions: one updates Orders then OrderDetails, the other does it backwards. That's the single most common cause of a deadlock -- two pieces of code locking the same two tables in opposite order. My fix is to make every procedure that touches both tables agree on one consistent order, keep the transactions as short as possible so the window for collision is small, and add retry logic around 1205 specifically on the application side as a safety net, since consistent ordering reduces deadlocks dramatically but doesn't mathematically guarantee zero under extreme concurrency.
commonMistakes: Treating ordinary blocking and a deadlock (error 1205) as the same thing
Assuming a deadlock means SQL Server malfunctioned rather than handled an application design flaw
Guessing at the cause instead of capturing the actual deadlock graph
Fixing only the symptom (retrying) without addressing the inconsistent table access order
Wrapping the entire procedure in one long transaction instead of minimizing what's actually atomic
keyPoints: Error 1205 specifically identifies a deadlock, distinct from ordinary blocking
SQL Server automatically detects deadlocks and rolls back a chosen victim
system_health Extended Events / trace flag 1222 / Profiler capture the deadlock graph for real evidence
Root cause here is inconsistent table access order across the two procedures
Fix: enforce consistent access order, keep transactions short, add retry logic for 1205

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes deadlock (1205) from ordinary blocking
Describes SQL Server's automatic deadlock detection and victim rollback
Names a real diagnostic method for capturing the deadlock graph
Identifies inconsistent access order as the root cause
Proposes a concrete redesign (consistent order, shorter transactions, retry logic)
Clear, structured troubleshooting narrative

questions.title: A Nightly Procedure That Used to Finish in Minutes Now Takes Hours
questions.prompt: A nightly stored procedure that updates loyalty points for every customer who made a purchase that day used to finish in under five minutes. Over the last two months it's crept up to three hours, and nobody changed the procedure's code. When you open it, you find it's built around a cursor that loops through qualifying customers one at a time, calling an UPDATE inside the loop. Walk through how you'd confirm the cursor is the real problem, why its cost grows disproportionately as the table grows, and how you'd rewrite it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I wouldn't assume the cursor is guilty just because cursors have a bad reputation -- I'd confirm it with SET STATISTICS TIME and IO around the existing procedure, and separately time a rewritten set-based version against the same day's data, so the comparison is based on actual numbers rather than instinct. I'd also check whether the cursor's own underlying SELECT has degraded (stale statistics causing a scan instead of a seek on the qualifying-customers query), since that's a second, compounding problem that's easy to miss if you only blame the loop itself.

The reason a cursor's cost grows disproportionately as a table grows isn't just that there are more rows to loop over -- it's that every iteration carries fixed per-row overhead (a context switch between the engine and the cursor machinery, its own mini-transaction and log record for each UPDATE, lock acquisition and release every single time) that a single set-based statement pays only once, not once per row. As the qualifying-customer count has grown month over month with the business, that per-row overhead has been multiplying against a growing row count, which is exactly the kind of cost curve that looks fine for a long time and then visibly takes off -- nobody changed the code, but the data volume the same code runs against did.

The rewrite replaces the entire loop with a single set-based UPDATE ... FROM that joins the same filtering logic the cursor used to decide which customers qualify, letting the engine process the whole batch as one operation instead of thousands of tiny ones.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is to actually prove it's the cursor rather than just assuming it, because cursors get blamed a lot but I want real numbers. I'd run STATISTICS TIME and IO on the existing procedure, and time a rewritten set-based version against the same data, and compare. I'd also take a look at the cursor's own underlying query, because sometimes the real second problem is that it's degraded from a seek to a scan as the table's grown, on top of the cursor overhead itself. As for why this crept up without the code changing -- a cursor pays a fixed cost per row, every iteration, things like its own mini-transaction and locking overhead, and a single set-based statement only pays that cost once for the whole batch. As the number of qualifying customers has grown with the business over the last couple months, that per-row cost has been compounding against a bigger row count every single night, which is exactly the kind of thing that looks fine for a long time and then suddenly doesn't. The actual fix is just replacing the whole loop with one UPDATE statement that joins against the same qualifying criteria the cursor used, so the engine handles it as a single batch operation instead of thousands of small ones.
commonMistakes: Assuming 'nobody changed the code' rules out a regression, missing that growing data volume is itself the real cause
Not profiling with STATISTICS TIME/IO before concluding the cursor is the bottleneck
Rewriting to a WHILE loop over a temp table instead of a true single set-based statement, which is still slow
Not checking whether the cursor's underlying SELECT has also degraded due to stale statistics
keyPoints: Confirm the cause with STATISTICS TIME/IO or direct timing, not assumption
Cursor cost scales with fixed per-row overhead that compounds as row counts grow month over month
Check the cursor's own driving query for separate degradation (stale stats, scan vs. seek)
Rewrite as one set-based UPDATE ... FROM statement
Validate the rewrite produces identical results before replacing the original in production

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a concrete way to confirm the cursor is the bottleneck
Explains why cursor cost compounds as data grows
Correctly rewrites the loop as a set-based UPDATE
Addresses validation before production rollout

questions.title: A Purview Scan Fails Against Azure SQL Database With an Authentication Error
questions.prompt: A nightly Purview scan against an Azure SQL Database source has started failing every run with an authentication error, right after the DBA team rotated credentials on the source during a routine security hardening pass. The scan was working fine for months beforehand. Walk through your diagnostic process to find exactly which authentication layer broke, and how you'd fix it in a way that survives the next credential rotation.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd start by opening the failed scan run's details in Purview and reading the actual error message rather than assuming -- Purview surfaces a specific failure reason (authentication failed, firewall blocked, timeout, etc.), and 'authentication error' right after a credential rotation points straight at the registered data source's credential configuration, not at Purview's own managed identity or network path, which wouldn't be affected by the source team rotating its own credentials.

Purview can authenticate to Azure SQL Database one of two common ways: via SQL authentication using a credential stored in Azure Key Vault (referenced by a Purview credential object pointing at a specific secret), or via Purview's system/user-assigned managed identity granted a SQL role directly on the database. Given the timing lines up exactly with the DBA team's credential rotation, the most likely scenario is SQL-authentication-based: the scan's registered credential in Purview points at a Key Vault secret holding the old SQL login's password, and the DBA team rotated the actual SQL login's password without updating that Key Vault secret to match -- so Purview is still presenting the old password. I'd confirm by checking the Key Vault secret's last-modified timestamp against the rotation date, and by testing the same SQL login/password combination independently (e.g. via SSMS) to confirm whether it's actually the credential that's stale.

The immediate fix is updating the Key Vault secret to the new password (or re-pointing the Purview credential object at a new secret), then re-running the scan to confirm success. The fix that survives the next rotation is architectural: switch the data source registration to authenticate via Purview's managed identity instead of a SQL login/password pair, with the managed identity granted appropriate read permissions directly on the database -- that removes password rotation from the picture for this scan entirely, since managed identity credentials are handled by Azure AD and never need manual secret updates. If managed identity isn't viable for this source, the second-best fix is coordinating with the DBA team so any future credential rotation includes updating the specific Key Vault secret Purview's scan depends on, as an explicit, documented step in their rotation runbook.
questions.professionalAnswer:
First thing I'd do is actually read the scan failure details in Purview instead of guessing -- it tells you specifically what kind of failure happened, and 'authentication error' right after a credential rotation is a pretty strong signal pointing at the source's credential, not at Purview's own network path or managed identity, since rotating a SQL Server login's password has nothing to do with Purview's own identity.

Purview typically talks to Azure SQL Database either with a SQL login and password stored in Key Vault, or through its managed identity granted a role directly on the database. Given the timing, my first bet is that the registered credential is a Key Vault secret holding the old password, and the DBA team rotated the actual database login without updating that specific secret to match -- so Purview's still trying the old password and getting rejected. I'd check the Key Vault secret's last-modified date against the rotation date to confirm, and separately test the old credential by hand to make sure that really is what's stale.

Short term, I just update the Key Vault secret to the new password and re-run the scan. Longer term, the fix that actually survives the next rotation is switching this source to authenticate via Purview's managed identity instead of a password-based login at all -- that takes password rotation out of the equation completely for this scan, since Azure AD handles the managed identity's credentials, not a secret someone has to remember to update. If managed identity genuinely isn't an option here, the fallback is making sure the DBA team's rotation runbook explicitly includes updating this Key Vault secret every time, instead of relying on someone remembering.
commonMistakes: Assuming the failure is Purview's own managed identity or network/firewall issue without checking the actual error detail
Not correlating the failure's start time precisely with the credential rotation event
Fixing only the immediate Key Vault secret without addressing why it will break again at the next rotation
Not testing the suspected stale credential independently to confirm the diagnosis before changing anything
Overlooking managed identity as the more durable long-term authentication method for this source type
keyPoints: Read the actual scan failure detail in Purview rather than assuming the cause
Azure SQL Database sources commonly authenticate via a Key Vault-stored SQL credential or via managed identity
Timing correlation with the credential rotation points at a stale Key Vault secret as the likely cause
Immediate fix: update the Key Vault secret to match the new password and re-run the scan
Durable fix: switch to managed identity authentication, or add the secret update to the rotation runbook

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Starts diagnosis from the actual scan error detail, not assumption
Correctly identifies the likely stale Key Vault credential as root cause
Proposes a concrete immediate fix
Proposes a durable fix (managed identity or runbook change) surviving future rotations
Clear, structured troubleshooting narrative

questions.title: New Files in a Data Lake Aren't Getting Classified Even Though the Scan Succeeded
questions.prompt: An ADLS Gen2 container has been scanning successfully every night in Purview for months, with existing files correctly classified. A new batch of vendor files was added to the container last week in a new subfolder, the scan reports success with no errors, but none of the new files show any classification at all in the Data Catalog. Walk through your diagnostic process to find out why.
questions.modelAnswer:
A clean scan with zero errors but zero classification on new files means the scan is doing something -- it's not failing outright -- but whatever it's doing to the new files isn't resulting in classification, which narrows this to a handful of specific, checkable causes rather than a general scan failure.

First, I'd check the scan's scope configuration: many ADLS scans are set up against a specific path or set of paths rather than the whole container recursively, and if the new vendor files landed in a subfolder outside the configured scan scope, the scan would genuinely succeed (it scanned everything it was told to) while silently never touching the new folder at all. Second, I'd check file type support in the scan rule set being used: if the new vendor files are in a format (a less common file extension, a compressed or proprietary format) that isn't included in the scan rule set's enabled file types, Purview will register the files as assets but has nothing to apply classification logic against, since classification rules in that rule set are typically tied to specific supported file types. Third, I'd check whether the new files' actual content just doesn't match any active classification rule's pattern or confidence threshold at all -- genuinely possible if the vendor's file format or field layout is different enough from what the existing, already-classified files look like, in which case 'no classification' is technically correct behavior, not a bug, and the real work is writing a custom classification for the new vendor's format. I'd distinguish between these by opening one specific new file's asset page in the Data Catalog: if the asset doesn't exist in the catalog at all, that points at scan scope; if the asset exists with its schema but zero classifications, that points at file type support or classification pattern mismatch, and I'd compare the new files' actual structure against the scan rule set's classification coverage to confirm which one.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The fact that the scan reports success with no errors tells me this isn't a scan failure -- the scan ran fine, it's something more specific about these particular new files. I'd check three things in order. First, scope: is the scan actually configured to recurse into every subfolder of this container, or is it pointed at a specific set of paths that doesn't include where the new vendor files landed? That's a very common and very silent gap -- the scan succeeds because it genuinely scanned everything it was told to, it just wasn't told about the new subfolder.

Second, if scope checks out and the files do show up as assets in the catalog, I'd look at file type support in the scan rule set -- if these vendor files are in a format that isn't enabled in the rule set being used, Purview catalogs them as assets but has no classification logic to even run against that file type.

Third, if the assets exist, the file type is supported, and there's still no classification, then it's possible the vendor's actual data format or field layout just genuinely doesn't match any existing classification rule's pattern -- which isn't a bug, it just means this new vendor's data needs its own custom classification written for it. I'd figure out which of the three it is by opening one new file's asset page directly: no asset at all means scope; an asset with schema info but zero classification tags means file type or pattern mismatch, and from there I'd compare the vendor file's actual structure against what the rule set is actually looking for.
commonMistakes: Assuming a 'successful' scan status rules out any gap, when scope, file type, and pattern mismatch can all cause silent non-classification
Not checking whether the scan's configured path actually includes the new subfolder
Forgetting that unsupported file types get cataloged as assets but never run through classification logic
Assuming a classification gap always means a bug rather than a genuinely new data format needing a new custom rule
Not isolating the diagnosis by checking one specific new file's asset page directly in the catalog
keyPoints: A clean scan result does not guarantee classification occurred -- several silent gaps are possible
Scan scope (path/recursion configuration) can exclude new subfolders while still reporting success
Unsupported file types in the scan rule set are cataloged but never classified
A genuine pattern/format mismatch means a new custom classification is needed, not a bug fix
Checking one new file's asset page directly isolates which of the three causes applies

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons that scan success doesn't guarantee classification occurred
Correctly identifies scan scope/path configuration as a cause to check
Correctly identifies unsupported file type in the scan rule set as a cause to check
Correctly identifies a genuine pattern mismatch requiring a new custom classification
Describes a concrete method to isolate which cause applies

questions.title: A OneLake Shortcut Returns 'Access Denied' Even Though the User Has Workspace Access
questions.prompt: A user has Viewer access to WorkspaceB and is trying to query a shortcut inside a lakehouse there that points at a table physically stored in WorkspaceA's lakehouse. The user can see the shortcut exists and open the item, but every query against it fails with a permission error. The same user has never been individually granted anything in WorkspaceA. Diagnose why this is happening and fix it.
questions.modelAnswer:
A OneLake shortcut is a pointer, not a copy -- when a query resolves data through a shortcut, it's actually reading the real data at its original physical location, which means OneLake security is evaluated against the target location's permissions, not against the permissions of the workspace the shortcut was created in. The user has Viewer access to WorkspaceB, which is enough to see that the shortcut item exists and to open it, but opening a shortcut and actually reading the data it points to are two different authorization checks -- the second one requires the calling user to have read access to the original data in WorkspaceA, independent of whatever access they have in WorkspaceB.

Since this user has never been granted anything in WorkspaceA -- no workspace role there, and no OneLake data access role scoped to the underlying path -- the query fails at the point where OneLake tries to authorize the read against the actual source location and finds no grant for this user there at all. This is a very common point of confusion specifically because the shortcut's existence and metadata are visible through WorkspaceB's permissions, which makes it look like a WorkspaceB-only concern, while the actual data access decision happens entirely at the other end.

The fix is granting this user (or, better, the security group they belong to) read access to the underlying data in WorkspaceA -- either Workspace Viewer-equivalent access there if that's an acceptable scope, or more precisely, a OneLake data access role in WorkspaceA scoped to just the specific path the shortcut points at, which avoids granting the user broader access to everything else in WorkspaceA beyond what the shortcut actually needs.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The key thing to explain here is that a shortcut doesn't copy data -- it's a pointer, and when someone actually queries through it, OneLake checks permissions against where the data really lives, not against the workspace where the shortcut itself sits. So having Viewer access in WorkspaceB is enough to see the shortcut exists and open it, but that's a completely separate authorization check from 'can this user actually read the data the shortcut points to,' which gets evaluated against WorkspaceA.

Since this user's never been granted anything in WorkspaceA at all, that second check fails every time, which is exactly the 'I can see it but can't query it' symptom described. People get tripped up by this because the shortcut is visible and the permissions feel like they should be local to the workspace you're sitting in, when the real gate is at the other end entirely.

The fix is to grant this user, or ideally their security group, read access over in WorkspaceA -- and I'd lean toward a OneLake data access role scoped specifically to the path the shortcut targets rather than a broad workspace role there, so they get exactly what the shortcut needs and nothing more in a workspace they otherwise have no business being in.

Not realizing OneLake evaluates permission against the shortcut's target location, not its container workspace
Granting the user broad Workspace Admin/Member access to WorkspaceA instead of a narrowly scoped data access role
Troubleshooting only WorkspaceB's permissions when the actual gap is in WorkspaceA
Granting access to the individual user instead of their security group, creating unmaintainable one-off grants

Seeing/opening a shortcut item and reading its underlying data are two separate authorization checks
The user needs access granted in the target workspace (WorkspaceA), independent of their access in WorkspaceB
A narrowly scoped OneLake data access role in WorkspaceA is preferable to a broad workspace role there
This is a common, easily-missed source of 'visible but inaccessible' shortcut errors

Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: A Domain Admin Can't See a Workspace That Should Belong to Their Domain
questions.prompt: The Marketing domain admin reports they can't see a workspace called 'Campaign-Analytics' in the Fabric admin portal's domain view, even though the workspace owner insists they assigned it to the Marketing domain weeks ago. Walk through the specific places you'd check to find out why the assignment isn't taking effect from the domain admin's point of view.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd start by actually checking the workspace's current domain assignment from the Fabric admin portal directly, rather than trusting the workspace owner's memory of what they did weeks ago -- the most common explanation for this exact symptom is that the assignment never actually completed or was later changed, not that it's correctly assigned but somehow hidden from the domain admin. A few specific things to check in order: first, confirm in the admin portal's workspace list that Campaign-Analytics shows Marketing as its domain right now -- if it shows 'unassigned' or a different domain, the assignment simply didn't take, possibly because the owner only started the assignment flow but didn't complete/save it, or a later reorganization moved it elsewhere without telling this team.

Second, if the assignment does correctly show Marketing, I'd check whether this specific domain admin's role is actually scoped to the Marketing domain -- domain admin rights are assigned per domain, and it's possible this person is a domain admin for a different domain, or was never actually granted the Marketing domain admin role at all despite being treated informally as 'the Marketing domain admin' by the team.

Third, I'd check whether the workspace is explicitly excluded from domain-wide visibility by some other setting, or whether there's tenant-level restriction on which domains certain workspace types can be assigned to (for example, some workspace types or capacities may have assignment restrictions). Fourth, I'd rule out a simple caching/propagation delay by having the domain admin refresh or wait a short period and re-check, since some admin portal views don't refresh instantaneously after an assignment change. The fix depends entirely on which of these turns out to be true: re-assign the workspace if it never took, correct the domain admin role assignment if that's the gap, or escalate to tenant-level configuration if a broader restriction is blocking it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move is to stop trusting the secondhand account of 'I assigned it weeks ago' and go look at the actual current state in the admin portal myself. I'd check the workspace's domain field directly -- if Campaign-Analytics doesn't show Marketing right now, the assignment either never completed or got changed since, and that alone explains everything; no further mystery needed.

If it does correctly show Marketing, my next check is whether this specific person's domain admin role is actually scoped to the Marketing domain in the system, not just informally understood by the team to be 'the Marketing domain admin.' I've seen cases where someone's treated as the domain admin socially but was never actually granted that role for the right domain.

After that I'd check for any tenant-level restriction on domain assignment for this particular workspace type or capacity, since some configurations do limit what can be assigned where. And I wouldn't rule out a boring answer either -- a short propagation delay in the admin portal's view after an assignment change. I'd nail down which of these it actually is before touching anything, because the fix is completely different depending on whether the workspace assignment itself is wrong versus the admin's own role assignment being wrong.

questions.title: A User With SELECT Granted Still Can't Query the Table in Unity Catalog
questions.prompt: A data engineer granted a new contractor group `SELECT ON TABLE sales_catalog.reporting.orders`, confirmed the grant exists with SHOW GRANTS, and the contractor still gets a permission denied error running a plain SELECT against that exact table. Diagnose the likely cause and the exact fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
This is almost certainly the missing-traversal-grant pattern: SELECT on the table is necessary but not sufficient, because Unity Catalog requires USE CATALOG on sales_catalog and USE SCHEMA on sales_catalog.reporting before the contractor's session can even resolve the path down to the table -- without both of those, the table-level SELECT grant exists but is unreachable, and the error surfaces as a generic permission denial rather than anything that explicitly says 'missing USE SCHEMA.'

I'd confirm by running SHOW GRANTS ON CATALOG sales_catalog and SHOW GRANTS ON SCHEMA sales_catalog.reporting for the contractor's group specifically, not just SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE -- if either USE CATALOG or USE SCHEMA is missing from those two outputs, that's the exact gap. The fix is granting both explicitly: GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG sales_catalog TO the group, and GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA sales_catalog.reporting TO the group, after which the existing SELECT grant on the table becomes reachable and the query should succeed with no other changes needed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't stop at confirming the SELECT grant exists -- that's exactly the step that looks reassuring but doesn't tell the whole story. My bet is the group has SELECT on the table but is missing USE CATALOG and/or USE SCHEMA on the containing catalog and schema, and without those, there's no way for their session to actually traverse down to the table at all, so the SELECT grant just sits there unreachable. I'd check SHOW GRANTS at the catalog level and the schema level specifically, not just at the table -- if either USE CATALOG or USE SCHEMA is missing from those two, that's the fix: grant both of those explicitly, and the existing table-level SELECT starts working immediately with nothing else needed.

Granting broader catalog/schema-level privileges than USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA when only traversal is needed

questions.title: A Row Filter Unexpectedly Filters Out the Table Owner's Own Queries
questions.prompt: A Unity Catalog admin applied a row filter function to the orders table restricting rows by region, tested it successfully as a regional analyst, then was alarmed to find their own ad hoc queries against the same table -- run as the table's owner and a workspace admin -- are also being filtered down to a seemingly random subset of rows. Diagnose why this is happening and how to fix it if full visibility for admins is actually required.
questions.modelAnswer:
A row filter function in Unity Catalog applies to every principal who queries the table through normal SQL access, including the table's owner and workspace/account admins, unless the filter function's own logic explicitly carves out an exception for them -- row filters are not automatically bypassed by elevated roles the way some other permission checks are, because the row filter is evaluated as part of query execution against whatever the function's boolean expression returns for the current calling user, and ownership/admin status isn't automatically part of that expression unless someone wrote it in. The 'seemingly random subset' the admin is seeing is actually completely deterministic -- it's whatever region the filter function's logic resolves for their calling identity, likely because their own role or identity doesn't match any row in whatever mapping table or role-check logic the filter was built against, so they're getting whichever rows (possibly zero, possibly a coincidental subset) the filter's fallback or default logic happens to produce for an unmatched caller.

The fix, if full visibility for admins is a genuine requirement, is to explicitly add that exception inside the row filter function's own logic -- for example, an OR clause checking is_account_group_member('admins') or a specific admin role check, returning TRUE unconditionally for that case, alongside the existing region-matching logic for everyone else. This has to be done inside the filter function itself; there's no separate Unity Catalog setting that exempts owners or admins from a row filter after the fact, because the row filter doesn't know anything about who's asking beyond what its own expression chooses to evaluate.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd explain is that this isn't a bug -- row filters apply to everyone who queries through normal SQL access, and being the table owner or a workspace admin doesn't automatically exempt you, because nothing about ownership or admin status is special-cased unless the filter's own logic explicitly checks for it. So what looks like a random subset to the admin is actually totally deterministic -- it's whatever the filter function resolves for their specific calling identity, and since their identity probably doesn't match any row in whatever region-mapping logic the filter uses, they're seeing whatever that unmatched case happens to produce.

If full visibility for admins is actually a real requirement, the fix has to live inside the filter function itself -- add an explicit OR condition checking something like is_account_group_member for an admins group, returning true unconditionally for that case before falling through to the normal region-matching logic for everyone else. There's no toggle anywhere in Unity Catalog that says 'exempt owners or admins from this row filter' after the fact -- the filter function is the entire decision, so any exception has to be written into that same expression.

Treating the filtered subset as a bug or random behavior instead of deterministic unmatched-case logic
Looking for a Unity Catalog setting to exempt admins, when the exception must be written into the filter function itself
Adding the admin exception as a separate grant instead of inside the filter function's boolean expression
Not testing the admin exception explicitly after adding it, assuming it works without verification

The filtered result for an unmatched identity is deterministic, driven by the filter's fallback/unmatched-case logic
There is no separate setting to exempt admins from a row filter after the fact

Testing must explicitly cover the admin/owner case, not just the regular-user case

questions.title: A Masking Policy Isn't Hiding Data for a Role That Should Be Restricted
questions.prompt: An analyst assigned only the ANALYST role can see unmasked credit card numbers in a Snowflake table, even though the masking policy explicitly only allows FINANCE_ADMIN and PAYMENTS_OPS to see real values, and ANALYST was never directly listed in the policy. Diagnose why the masking isn't working for this role.
questions.modelAnswer:
Since the masking policy's CASE expression checks CURRENT_ROLE() against an explicit list that doesn't include ANALYST, the policy logic itself isn't the problem -- the far more likely explanation is role hierarchy: CURRENT_ROLE() reflects whatever role the session is currently operating as, and if ANALYST has, at some point, been granted one of FINANCE_ADMIN or PAYMENTS_OPS as a child role (GRANT ROLE FINANCE_ADMIN TO ROLE ANALYST), that doesn't change what CURRENT_ROLE() returns when someone is using ANALYST directly -- so the masking policy comparing CURRENT_ROLE() against a fixed list wouldn't normally be fooled by hierarchy on its own. The actual mechanism I'd suspect first is that the masking policy's CASE logic might be checking something broader than CURRENT_ROLE(), such as IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION() or a privilege-based check instead of an exact CURRENT_ROLE() string match -- IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION() returns true for any role reachable through the session's current role hierarchy, not just the exact active role, so if ANALYST inherits FINANCE_ADMIN through the hierarchy, a policy written with IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('FINANCE_ADMIN') would incorrectly unmask for the analyst even though CURRENT_ROLE() itself would show ANALYST.

I'd confirm by inspecting the actual masking policy definition (DESCRIBE MASKING POLICY or the policy's DDL) to see exactly which function it uses, then separately run SHOW GRANTS OF ROLE FINANCE_ADMIN to check whether ANALYST is listed as having that role granted to it anywhere in the hierarchy. If the policy does use IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION, the fix is either tightening the policy to check CURRENT_ROLE() explicitly against the exact allowed roles (accepting that this means a user must explicitly switch to FINANCE_ADMIN to see real data, rather than inheriting it silently), or -- if the hierarchy itself is the actual mistake -- removing the accidental GRANT ROLE FINANCE_ADMIN TO ROLE ANALYST so ANALYST no longer inherits that privilege at all.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Since ANALYST isn't explicitly named in the policy, my first suspicion isn't the policy text itself -- it's whether ANALYST somehow inherits FINANCE_ADMIN through the role hierarchy, and whether the masking policy was written using IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION instead of CURRENT_ROLE(). That distinction matters a lot here: CURRENT_ROLE() only ever returns the exact role the session is actively using, but IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION() returns true for any role reachable through that session's hierarchy, including roles inherited indirectly. If someone wrote the masking policy against IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('FINANCE_ADMIN') and ANALYST happens to have inherited FINANCE_ADMIN at some point through a GRANT ROLE statement, the policy would unmask for an analyst even though they never directly hold FINANCE_ADMIN and CURRENT_ROLE() would still say ANALYST.

I'd check the actual policy DDL to see which function it's using, and separately run SHOW GRANTS OF ROLE FINANCE_ADMIN to see if ANALYST shows up anywhere in that chain. Depending on what I find, the fix is either tightening the policy to use a strict CURRENT_ROLE() check instead of IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION, or removing whatever accidental grant gave ANALYST that inherited privilege in the first place -- those are two different fixes for two different root causes, and I wouldn't guess which one without actually looking at both pieces.

Not distinguishing CURRENT_ROLE() (exact active role) from IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION() (any inherited role in the hierarchy)
Not checking the role hierarchy (SHOW GRANTS OF ROLE) to see whether an unintended inheritance exists
Fixing the symptom by adding ANALYST to an explicit deny list instead of finding the actual root cause
Assuming CURRENT_ROLE()-based policies can also be fooled by hierarchy inheritance, which they generally cannot
keyPoints: CURRENT_ROLE() reflects only the exact active role; IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION() reflects any inherited role in the hierarchy
A masking policy written with IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION can unmask for a role that merely inherits a privileged role
Checking the actual policy DDL and SHOW GRANTS OF ROLE together isolates which mechanism is responsible
The fix differs depending on whether the policy logic or the role hierarchy itself is the actual problem
An accidental GRANT ROLE statement can silently flow privileged access into a much broader role

questions.title: A Secure View's Performance Collapsed Right After Adding a Row Access Policy
questions.prompt: A secure view in Snowflake used to return results in under two seconds. Right after a row access policy was added to its underlying table, the same view now takes over a minute, even for queries that return very few rows. Walk through how you'd diagnose the cause and how you'd fix it without removing the row access policy.
questions.modelAnswer:
A row access policy's boolean expression is evaluated for every row the underlying table could produce before Snowflake's optimizer can apply other filters, so the first thing I'd check is exactly what that policy expression actually does -- if it's a simple, indexed-style lookup against a small mapping table, the per-row cost should be trivial, but if it contains a non-deterministic function, a correlated subquery that itself scans a large table, or a join against a poorly-sized/unindexed mapping table, that expensive logic now runs once per row of the underlying table on every single query against the view, regardless of how selective the final result is. I'd pull up the query profile for a run against the view and look specifically at which operator dominates total execution time -- if a large portion of time is attributed to evaluating the row access policy's expression (visible as part of the scan/filter operators feeding the view), that confirms the policy itself as the bottleneck rather than anything else that changed.

Second, I'd check whether the row access policy's expression can see and push down filters the way a normal WHERE clause can -- a row access policy with a complex EXISTS subquery against a large table may not get the same optimization treatmentas a simple equality check, so simplifying the policy expression's logic (for example, pre-joining or pre-aggregating a large mapping table into a smaller, purpose-built lookup table restricted to just role-to-permission pairs) often restores much of the lost performance. Third, I'd verify the mapping table the policy references is appropriately small and, if large, consider whether a clustering key or search optimization on it would help, since the policy's lookup runs against it on every row evaluation. The fix should preserve the row access policy's security guarantee entirely -- the goal is making its expression efficient, not removing or weakening the actual access control it provides.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move is to actually look at what the row access policy's expression is doing, because that's almost certainly where the new cost is coming from -- a row access policy's boolean logic runs per row of the underlying table, before the optimizer gets to apply the query's own selective filters, so an expensive expression here gets paid everywhere, even for a query that should only return a handful of rows. I'd pull the query profile and see how much total time is attributed to evaluating that policy versus everything else -- if it's dominating the runtime, that confirms it.

From there, I'd look specifically at whether the policy's logic is something lightweight, like a simple lookup against a small table, or something heavier, like a correlated subquery against a big, unindexed mapping table. If it's the heavier case, my fix is to simplify that lookup -- shrink the mapping table down to just the role-to-permission pairs it actually needs, and make sure it's small and well-structured rather than a large table the policy has to search through on every row. I'd be explicit that the goal here is making the policy's logic efficient, not loosening or removing it -- the security guarantee it provides has to stay exactly as strong; we're just making the mechanism that enforces it cheaper to evaluate.

-- Check what's actually expensive inside the policy
DESCRIBE ROW ACCESS POLICY region_filter;

-- Likely heavy: correlated subquery against a large, unindexed table
-- Likely fix: a small, purpose-built mapping table
CREATE TABLE region_access_lookup AS
SELECT DISTINCT role_name, sales_region FROM region_access;
-- Re-point the policy at the smaller, purpose-built lookup table instead of a larger source table.

Not checking the query profile to confirm the policy evaluation is actually the dominant cost
Assuming row access policy overhead is fixed and unavoidable regardless of its own internal logic
Leaving an expensive correlated subquery or large unindexed mapping table inside the policy expression
Not verifying the fix with a before/after query profile comparison

An expensive expression (large unindexed mapping table, correlated subquery) compounds across every row
The query profile isolates whether policy evaluation is the dominant cost

A small, purpose-built mapping table is preferable to a large general-purpose table inside the policy

questions.title: RLS Works in Power BI Desktop but Fails to Restrict Anything After Publishing
questions.prompt: A semantic model's RLS role was thoroughly tested with View As Role in Power BI Desktop and worked perfectly. After publishing to the Power BI Service, every user -- regardless of role assignment -- sees all rows with no restriction at all. Walk through the specific places this breaks down after publish and how you'd fix it.
questions.modelAnswer:
RLS enforcement in the Service depends on two things that have nothing to do with the DAX filter's correctness, and both are extremely common post-publish gaps: role membership assignment, and the connection/storage mode the model actually uses once published.

First, and most common: creating an RLS role in Desktop does not automatically assign any users to it after publishing -- role membership has to be explicitly configured in the Power BI Service under the semantic model's Security settings, adding specific users or groups to each role. If nobody did that step after publishing, every viewer is effectively not a member of any role, and Power BI's default behavior for someone with normal workspace access who isn't assigned to any RLS role is typically to see unrestricted data if they have a level of access (like being a workspace member/admin) that bypasses RLS entirely, or to see nothing if RLS is being enforced but they're in no role -- 'everyone sees everything' specifically points at role assignment never having been configured, or at the affected users being workspace Admins/Members (roles that bypass RLS by design, since internally they have edit-level access to the model, not just consumption through a report).

Second, if role assignment is confirmed correct, I'd check the model's connection/storage mode: RLS defined via DAX filters works natively with Import mode and most DirectQuery scenarios, but RLS enforcement behavior can differ for live connections to Analysis Services/Azure Analysis Services or for certain DirectQuery configurations where the underlying data source needs its own security configured (or where USERPRINCIPALNAME() doesn't resolve the way it did in Desktop's test harness) -- if the published model is actually a live connection rather than the model the RLS role was defined on, the role defined in Desktop may not even be the operative security layer at all. I'd confirm by checking exactly which users saw unrestricted data -- if it's specifically workspace Admins/Members, that's role-bypass-by-design and expected; if it's everyone including Viewers who were supposedly assigned to a restrictive role, that's a role assignment configuration gap in the Service that needs to be fixed directly in the model's Security settings.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The DAX filter working perfectly in Desktop tells me the logic itself is fine, so I wouldn't go back and re-check the filter expression first -- I'd go straight to the two things that are genuinely different between Desktop testing and a real published report. First and most likely: did anyone actually assign users to the RLS role in the Service after publishing? Creating the role in Desktop doesn't assign a single person to it -- that's a separate step done afterward in the model's Security settings in the Service, and if it never happened, nobody's actually in any role, which usually means either everyone sees everything or everyone sees nothing, depending on their underlying workspace access level.

That leads to the second thing I'd check specifically: is it workspace Admins and Members who are seeing everything? Because that's actually expected behavior, not a bug -- those roles have edit-level access to the model itself, which bypasses RLS by design, since RLS is a report-consumption restriction, not a hard data lock against people who can edit the model. If it's genuinely everyone, including people who should just be Viewers assigned to a restrictive role, then I'd go confirm role membership was actually configured in the Service, because that's the step I'd bet got skipped.
questions.example:
Common post-publish RLS gap checklist:
1. Power BI Service > Semantic model > Security > is anyone actually assigned to the RLS role?
2. Are the unrestricted users Workspace Admins/Members (expected RLS bypass) or Viewers (a real gap)?
3. Is the published model Import/DirectQuery with the same RLS role, or a live connection where RLS behaves differently?

Not checking whether the published model's connection/storage mode changes how RLS is enforced
Assuming View As Role in Desktop fully replicates the Service's real enforcement behavior

questions.title: A Certified Dataset Loses Its Endorsement Badge After a Workspace Migration
questions.prompt: A semantic model was certified by the BI Center of Excellence months ago and consistently showed the certified badge. After the workspace it lived in was migrated to a new capacity and renamed as part of an org restructuring, the exact same semantic model (same content, same owner) no longer shows any endorsement badge at all in the catalog. Diagnose why, and what you'd check before assuming it needs to be re-certified from scratch.
questions.modelAnswer:
Endorsement status (Promoted or Certified) is metadata attached directly to the specific semantic model item itself, not to the workspace it lives in -- so a workspace rename or capacity migration alone should not, by itself, strip certification from an item that physically moved or was renamed along with its container. The fact that the badge disappeared points at one of a few more specific causes tied to how the migration was actually performed, rather than the rename/capacity-move being the direct cause.

First, I'd check whether the migration was a true in-place move (the same item, same unique identifier, relocated to a different capacity) versus an export/republish or a copy-based migration -- some migration approaches recreate the semantic model as a new item with a new identity rather than truly moving the existing one, and endorsement metadata does not carry over to a newly-created item even if its content is identical; it would need to be re-certified because, as far as Power BI's object model is concerned, it's a different item, not the same one relocated. Second, I'd check whether certification in this tenant requires the containing workspace to meet certain criteria (some organizations configure certification policies that are tied to specific workspace types or require the workspace itself to carry a specific designation) -- if the new workspace, post-restructuring, doesn't meet whatever criteria the tenant's certification policy enforces, the badge could be suppressed even though the underlying certification metadata technically still exists on the item. Third, I'd confirm the certifying authority/reviewer attribution didn't get invalidated by an ownership or workspace-admin change during the migration, since some certification workflows re-validate the certifying reviewer's continued authority at render time. Before assuming a full re-certification is needed, I'd check the model's current endorsement setting directly in its item settings in the new workspace -- if the setting itself still shows 'Certified,' the badge-rendering issue may be a propagation delay or a workspace-policy mismatch rather than lost metadata, which is a very different, usually much faster fix than redoing the certification review from scratch.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd establish is whether this was a true move of the existing item or something that effectively recreated it, because that distinction changes everything. Endorsement is metadata on the specific item itself, not on the workspace -- a workspace rename or capacity change alone shouldn't strip it. But if the migration approach was actually export-and-republish, or some kind of copy-based move, Power BI may be treating the result as a brand-new item with a new identity, and a new item simply doesn't inherit certification metadata from whatever it was copied from, no matter how identical the content looks.

Before I'd assume it needs a full re-certification review, I'd go check the model's own item settings in the new workspace directly and see what the endorsement setting actually says right now. If it still says Certified there, then the badge not rendering might be a workspace-policy mismatch -- some tenants tie certification eligibility to specific workspace criteria, and if the restructured workspace doesn't meet that criteria anymore, the badge can get suppressed even though the underlying metadata is technically intact -- or it could just be a propagation delay. That's a very different, much faster fix than redoing the whole certification process, so I wouldn't jump straight to 're-certify from scratch' without checking what the item's actual current setting says first.

Not distinguishing a true in-place move from an export/republish or copy-based migration that creates a new item identity

questions.title: A Purview Access Policy Denies Access Despite a Valid Azure RBAC Grant
questions.prompt: A data engineer was granted Storage Blob Data Reader via Azure RBAC on a storage account, which should let them read blob data directly. They can browse the storage account's properties in the Azure portal fine, but every attempt to actually read blob data fails with an authorization error. The storage account is registered in Purview with an access policy configured. Diagnose the likely cause.
questions.modelAnswer:
The specific detail that changes this diagnosis is that the storage account is registered in Purview with an access policy configured -- once a storage account has Purview's policy enforcement enabled on it, Purview access policies and native Azure RBAC operate as two layers that both have to permit the action, not as alternatives where either one being satisfied is enough. Enabling policy enforcement for Purview on a resource (a deliberate, explicit setting that has to be turned on for that storage account) effectively lets Purview's own access policies participate in the authorization decision alongside RBAC -- if no Purview access policy explicitly grants this specific user data-plane read access, the Purview policy layer can still deny the request even though the native Azure RBAC role assignment would, on its own, have been sufficient before policy enforcement was enabled.

I'd confirm by checking two things: first, whether policy enforcement is actually turned on for this storage account in Purview (a setting distinct from simply having the account registered/scanned) -- if it's on, that's almost certainly the layer causing the denial; second, whether an explicit Purview access policy exists granting this user or their group read access to this specific resource, since the fix is either creating/approving that specific access policy grant in Purview, or -- if Purview policy enforcement for this resource was turned on unintentionally or isn't actually meant to be the organization's access control mechanism for this storage account -- disabling policy enforcement for it so native Azure RBAC becomes the sole authorization layer again. The key diagnostic insight is that a 'properties visible in the portal but data read denied' split is a classic signature of a management-plane operation (visible via RBAC) succeeding while a data-plane operation is additionally gated by a second authorization layer that RBAC alone doesn't satisfy.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The detail that jumps out at me is that this storage account has a Purview access policy configured, because that changes the authorization model from 'RBAC alone decides' to 'RBAC and Purview's own policy layer both have to agree.' Turning on policy enforcement for a resource in Purview is a specific, deliberate setting, and once it's on, Purview access policies get a real say in data-plane authorization decisions alongside native RBAC -- so a perfectly valid Storage Blob Data Reader role assignment can still get overridden by a missing or non-matching Purview access policy.

The fact that they can browse the account's properties fine but can't actually read blob data is a pretty clean signature of this -- browsing properties is a management-plane action that RBAC alone covers, while reading the actual blob data is the data-plane action that's additionally gated by whatever policy layer Purview is now enforcing on top. I'd go check whether policy enforcement is actually turned on for this account, and whether there's an approved Purview access policy explicitly covering this user or their group. The fix is either getting that specific access policy approved and granted in Purview, or, if nobody actually intended for this account to be governed by Purview's policy layer, turning enforcement back off so RBAC alone is the authorization decision again.

Not distinguishing a management-plane success (viewing properties) from a data-plane failure (reading blob data)
Assuming registering a storage account in Purview automatically enables policy enforcement on it
Fixing this by granting even broader RBAC roles, which doesn't address a separate Purview policy layer denial
Not checking whether policy enforcement was turned on for this resource intentionally or by accident

Both RBAC and an applicable Purview access policy must permit the action once enforcement is enabled

questions.title: AWS Lake Formation Permissions Are Being Silently Bypassed
questions.prompt: An admin configured AWS Lake Formation permissions carefully to restrict a group to only finance-tagged tables, verified the grants look correct in the Lake Formation console, but discovers that members of that group can still read every table in the underlying S3 buckets directly, completely ignoring the Lake Formation restrictions. Diagnose why Lake Formation's governance isn't actually the enforcement point here.
questions.modelAnswer:
Lake Formation permissions only govern access when Lake Formation is actually the authorization path being used to reach the data -- for queries that go through Lake Formation-integrated services (Athena, Redshift Spectrum, Glue, EMR configured for Lake Formation), Lake Formation's own grants are checked and enforced. But Lake Formation does not retroactively revoke or override direct IAM permissions on the underlying S3 objects -- if the IAM policies attached to the group's role still grant s3:GetObject (or broader S3 permissions) directly on the bucket/prefix where this data lives, members of that group can simply bypass Lake Formation entirely by accessing the S3 objects directly (via the S3 console, AWS CLI, SDK calls to S3 directly) using those still-valid IAM permissions, and Lake Formation has no visibility into or control over that path at all.

This is the single most common Lake Formation governance gap: Lake Formation is a governance layer on top of the data catalog and the services that honor it, not a replacement for correctly scoping the underlying IAM permissions -- for Lake Formation's permission model to be the actual, sole enforcement point, the direct IAM policies granting S3 access to the underlying buckets/prefixes have to be removed from the group's roles (or replaced with Lake Formation's own data access delegation, where Lake Formation manages temporary, scoped credentials for the integrated query services instead of the group's role holding standing S3 permissions). I'd confirm by checking the IAM policies attached to the group's role directly for any S3 permissions scoped to these buckets, and the fix is removing those direct S3 grants so that accessing this data is only possible through a Lake-Formation-integrated service that actually enforces the configured permissions, leaving direct S3 access with no standing grant to fall back on.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The real issue here is that Lake Formation only controls access for the path that actually goes through it -- Athena, Redshift Spectrum, Glue, services that are integrated with Lake Formation and check its permissions. It does nothing to revoke or override whatever IAM permissions are separately sitting on the underlying S3 buckets. So if this group's IAM role still has s3:GetObject or similar permissions directly on those buckets, nothing stops them from just going straight to S3 -- console, CLI, SDK, doesn't matter -- and reading the data with zero awareness that Lake Formation even exists, let alone what it's configured to restrict.

This is probably the single most common way Lake Formation governance quietly fails in practice: people configure Lake Formation carefully and assume that's the whole story, without going and stripping the direct S3 permissions that were there before Lake Formation was set up. I'd go check the group's IAM policies directly for S3 access scoped to these buckets, and the fix is removing that direct access entirely, so the only way to reach this data at all is through a Lake-Formation-integrated service that actually checks and enforces the permissions the admin configured.

Not realizing Lake Formation only governs access through integrated services, not direct S3 access
Verifying only the Lake Formation console's grants without checking the actual IAM policies attached to the group
Assuming Lake Formation automatically revokes or overrides pre-existing IAM permissions on the same resources
Fixing this by tightening Lake Formation permissions further instead of removing the bypassing IAM grants

questions.title: Data Stewards Quietly Stop Maintaining the Glossary and Quality Issues After Launch
questions.prompt: A governance program launched its stewardship program six months ago with enthusiasm -- stewards were trained, glossary terms were drafted, and a data quality issue queue was set up. Today, the glossary hasn't been updated in three months, the issue queue has dozens of stale, unaddressed items, and stewards say they're 'too busy.' Diagnose what actually went wrong with the program design, not just the individual stewards' time management, and propose a fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
'Too busy' is almost never the real root cause of a stewardship program stalling out six months in -- it's usually the symptom of a program design gap that made stewardship an unrewarded, unmeasured, competing priority against stewards' actual day jobs from day one. I'd diagnose this across a few specific, checkable dimensions rather than accepting the time-management explanation at face value.

First, accountability: is steward performance on glossary upkeep and issue resolution actually tracked anywhere, reported to anyone, or tied to any part of their formal role or performance review -- or was stewardship bolted on as an informal, unmeasured 'extra duty' with no consequence either way for doing it or not doing it? If there's no visible accountability mechanism, stewardship will always lose to whatever is actually measured in someone's day job. Second, workload and time allocation: were stewards given explicit, protected time (a percentage of their week, formally acknowledged by their manager) to do this work, or was it simply added on top of an already-full existing role with the assumption they'd find the time? Third, workflow friction: is the issue queue and glossary tooling itself easy to use in the stewards' actual daily workflow, or does updating it require stepping outside their normal tools into something clunky and separate that they have to remember to go do? Fourth, visible value: do stewards ever see any feedback loop showing that their work on the glossary or issue queue actually changed anything downstream, or does it feel like effort disappearing into a system nobody else looks at?

The fix addresses the actual design gaps, not just a reminder email: get explicit, manager-acknowledged time allocation for stewardship work into stewards' formal goals; build a small set of visible KPIs (glossary freshness, issue aging, resolution rate) that get reported up to the governance council regularly, so steward output is actually seen and has a line of sight to consequence; reduce workflow friction by integrating the tooling into stewards' existing systems where possible; and close the feedback loop by periodically showing stewards concrete examples of how their glossary/issue work was actually used downstream, so the effort visibly matters.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't accept 'too busy' as the actual diagnosis -- that's what people say when a program was designed without giving them a real reason or real room to prioritize it, not a genuine time-management failure on their part six months straight. I'd go look at four specific things. Is there any accountability at all -- does anyone actually track or report on steward output, or did we just hope people would do it out of goodwill with zero consequence either way? Was time for this work ever formally carved out and acknowledged by their actual managers, or did we just add it on top of an already-full job and assume it would get done? Is the tooling itself easy to use inside their normal workflow, or is it a separate, clunky system they have to remember to go visit? And do stewards ever see any evidence that their work actually mattered downstream, or does it just vanish into a system nobody else looks at?

My fix is structural, not a reminder email: get explicit, manager-sponsored time allocation written into their actual goals, build a short list of real KPIs -- glossary freshness, issue aging, resolution rate -- that gets reported to the governance council regularly so the work is visible and has weight, reduce the friction of the tools they have to use, and make a point of showing stewards concrete examples where their work changed something real downstream. If none of that changes, the program will keep stalling no matter how many times we remind people they're 'behind.'

Treating this as an individual performance problem rather than a systemic accountability and workload design problem
Fixing it with reminders or re-training instead of structural changes (time allocation, KPIs, tooling, feedback loop)
Not checking whether stewardship work was ever formally acknowledged by stewards' actual managers
Not closing the feedback loop so stewards can see their work actually mattered downstream
keyPoints: A stalled stewardship program is usually a design failure, not an individual time-management failure
Check accountability, protected time allocation, workflow friction, and visible downstream value as the four diagnostic dimensions

The fix is structural: manager-acknowledged time, visible KPIs reported to the governance council, reduced tooling friction, and a feedback loop
