questions.title: When an Indexed View Is Worth the Write Cost
questions.prompt: Your reporting dashboard runs an aggregation query against Production.Product (grouped by subcategory, computing a row count and total list price) hundreds of times per minute during business hours, and the underlying table is only touched by a handful of transactions a day. A teammate suggests materializing this aggregation as an indexed view. Walk through the real requirements for making that work, what SQL Server does differently once it's in place, and the ongoing cost you're trading for speed. Would you recommend it here -- and would your answer change if the table instead took thousands of writes per second?
questions.modelAnswer:
A regular view is just stored SQL text -- it re-runs its underlying SELECT every time it's queried. An indexed view is the one case where that's not true: once you create a unique clustered index on the view, SQL Server physically materializes the computed result set on disk, and queries against the view (or, on Enterprise edition, queries against the base table that the optimizer recognizes as equivalent) can read that pre-computed data directly instead of re-aggregating Production.Product every time.

Getting there has real, non-negotiable requirements: the view must be created WITH SCHEMABINDING, which locks the underlying table's structure so SQL Server can guarantee the view stays consistent with it -- you can't ALTER a schemabound table's referenced columns without dropping dependent objects first. Aggregations must use COUNT_BIG(*), not COUNT(*). A number of T-SQL constructs are disallowed inside the view's definition (TOP, several non-deterministic or imprecise functions, certain outer join shapes). And on non-Enterprise editions, the optimizer won't automatically substitute the indexed view for an equivalent base-table query -- you need the NOEXPAND hint to force it.

The cost is real and ongoing: every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE against Production.Product now has to maintain the materialized aggregate too, on top of the base table write. For this scenario -- read-heavy by a wide margin, with only a dozen or so writes a day -- that tradeoff is clearly worth it: you're paying a trivial amount of extra write overhead a handful of times daily to make hundreds of reads per minute avoid re-aggregating the table from scratch. If the table instead took thousands of writes per second, I'd recommend against it: the indexed view's maintenance cost would be paid on every single one of those writes, compounding exactly where you can least afford it, and I'd look at a separate pre-aggregated reporting table refreshed on a schedule, or a different caching layer, instead.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd frame it for the team: a normal view is free to create because it doesn't store anything -- it's just a saved query. An indexed view is different, and the trigger for that difference is adding a unique clustered index to it; the moment you do, SQL Server actually materializes the result on disk. To even get there you need WITH SCHEMABINDING on the view, COUNT_BIG instead of COUNT, and you have to accept that the view's definition is now more restricted -- no TOP, limited function support. And if we're not on Enterprise, I'd flag that the optimizer won't use it automatically; we'd need NOEXPAND in the query, or it just does the full aggregation anyway and we got nothing for the extra complexity.

The real decision point for me is the read/write ratio. In this case we've got maybe a dozen writes a day against hundreds of reads a minute, so I'd absolutely recommend the indexed view -- we're trading a tiny bit of extra work on writes that barely happen for a big win on reads that happen constantly. But if someone told me this table was taking thousands of writes a second, I'd push back hard on the same idea, because now every one of those writes has to keep the materialized aggregate in sync, and that's exactly the kind of hidden cost that tanks throughput on a hot table. In that case I'd rather build a separate summary table refreshed on a schedule, or push the aggregation into a different layer entirely.
questions.example:
CREATE VIEW dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary
WITH SCHEMABINDING
AS
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID,
       COUNT_BIG(*) AS ProductCount,
       SUM(ListPrice) AS TotalListPrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE ProductSubcategoryID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID;
GO

CREATE UNIQUE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_vw_ProductPriceSummary
ON dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary (ProductSubcategoryID);
GO

-- On Standard edition, force the optimizer to use the materialized data:
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, ProductCount, TotalListPrice
FROM dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary WITH (NOEXPAND);
commonMistakes: Forgetting WITH SCHEMABINDING, which indexed views require
Using COUNT(*) instead of the required COUNT_BIG(*)
Assuming the optimizer auto-uses the indexed view outside Enterprise edition without NOEXPAND
Ignoring write amplification and recommending indexed views for high-write tables
Not accounting for how SCHEMABINDING restricts future ALTER TABLE changes to the base table
keyPoints: Unique clustered index is what actually materializes the view's data
WITH SCHEMABINDING and COUNT_BIG(*) are mandatory requirements
Non-Enterprise editions need the NOEXPAND hint to use the indexed view
Every write to the base table now also maintains the materialized aggregate
Worth it for read-heavy, low-write-ratio reporting aggregations
Not worth it for tables with very high write throughput

questions.title: Defending a Type 2 Slowly Changing Dimension Against a 'Just Overwrite It' Proposal
questions.prompt: The business wants to analyze sales 'as it looked at the time' - attributing a historical sale to the customer's address at the time of purchase - but also wants an easy way to see all sales for a customer regardless of where they lived. A teammate proposes simply overwriting the CustomerAddress column whenever it changes, since it's simpler. Evaluate the proposal and recommend an approach.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd frame this as more than a 'simpler vs more complex' judgment call, because the overwrite approach (Type 1) doesn't just make the first requirement harder - it makes it impossible. If the address column is overwritten in place, every historical fact row's join to the Customer dimension reflects whatever the current address is at query time, regardless of when the sale actually happened; there is no way to recover 'what address was on file when this sale occurred' once the old value has been overwritten, because the history simply no longer exists anywhere in the model. That directly conflicts with the explicit requirement to analyze sales as they looked at the time, so this isn't really a tradeoff to debate - Type 1 fails a stated requirement outright.

I'd recommend a Type 2 design instead: each address change creates a new dimension row with its own surrogate key, an effective date, an expiry date (or null/high-date for the current row), and a current-flag, and each fact row at transaction time joins via the surrogate key representing whichever address was current then - that correctly supports the point-in-time analysis. For the second requirement, 'all sales regardless of address,' I'd make sure the dimension (and ideally the fact table too) also carries the durable, natural CustomerID alongside the surrogate key, so a query can group by that durable identifier across every historical version of the customer's record to get an address-agnostic view, while a query grouping by the surrogate key plus address gives the point-in-time view - both requirements are satisfied simultaneously by choosing which key to aggregate on. I'd be upfront that Type 2 isn't free: the ETL needs explicit change detection and row-expiry logic, the dimension table grows, and every downstream measure needs to be aware of which key it's joining on - but given that Type 1 can't meet the stated requirement at all, that complexity is a justified cost here, not a nice-to-have.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell my teammate directly that this isn't really a 'simpler is fine' situation, because overwriting the address doesn't just make history a little harder to get - it erases it completely. Once we overwrite CustomerAddress, every past sale's dimension join points at whatever address is current today, and there's no way to ask 'what address did this customer have when they bought this' anymore, which is literally the first thing the business asked for. So I'd push for a proper Type 2 design: new dimension row with its own surrogate key every time the address changes, effective and expiry dates, a current flag, and fact rows joining via the surrogate key that was current at transaction time - that gets us accurate point-in-time analysis. For the second ask, seeing all of a customer's sales regardless of address, I'd make sure we keep the durable CustomerID around too, so we can roll up by that across every version of the dimension row when someone wants the address-agnostic view. I wouldn't pretend this is free - it's real ETL work to detect changes and manage row expiry, and it's a bigger dimension table - but given that the overwrite approach can't deliver on one of the two things we were explicitly asked for, that cost isn't optional here.

Implementing Type 2 but forgetting to retain a durable natural key, making the address-agnostic rollup requirement hard to satisfy
Not discussing the real ETL/complexity cost of Type 2 honestly
Confusing a Type 2 dimension with a separate audit/history log table that isn't actually joined to facts
Not considering that Type 2 is the correct answer here specifically because of the stated dual requirement, not as a default best practice
keyPoints: Type 1 overwrite cannot support point-in-time analysis at all - a hard requirement failure, not a tradeoff
Type 2 uses a surrogate key, effective/expiry dates, and a current flag to version history correctly
Retain the durable natural key for customer-level rollups regardless of address history
Both stated requirements are satisfied by choosing which key to aggregate on
Honestly acknowledge the real ETL/complexity cost of Type 2

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies Type 1 as failing the stated requirement outright, not just being less ideal
Recommends Type 2 with correct mechanics

questions.title: Department-Specific Data Marts or One Centralized Warehouse?
questions.prompt: Finance, Marketing, and Supply Chain each want their own fast, purpose-built reporting datasets, and each has proposed building and maintaining an independent data mart with its own ETL rather than working off a shared central warehouse, arguing it's faster for their team to control end-to-end. As the senior analytics engineer, how do you respond, and what architecture do you recommend?
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd start by validating the real concern driving this proposal rather than dismissing it outright: departments want speed and control, and a fully centralized model where one team is the bottleneck for every single change request is a genuine, common failure mode that pushes people toward exactly this kind of workaround - if I just overrule them, I should expect shadow-IT marts to spring up anyway. That said, I'd push back on fully independent, siloed marts with separate ETL per department, because it recreates the problems a shared source of truth exists to prevent: three different definitions of 'Customer' or 'Revenue' that quietly drift apart across Finance's, Marketing's, and Supply Chain's separate pipelines, duplicated extraction load hitting the same source systems three times, and three times the engineering effort maintaining parallel ETL that's mostly doing the same underlying work.

My recommendation is the standard hub-and-spoke compromise: a centrally-owned, conformed layer where shared dimensions - Customer, Product, Date/Calendar - are built once and reused everywhere, feeding department-specific marts (physical tables or virtual views/semantic models) that layer each department's own business logic on top, owned and iterated on by each department's own analysts. This gives departments the speed and autonomy they're actually asking for at the mart layer, while guaranteeing the core shared entities and metrics stay consistent across the organization at the conformed layer underneath. Practically, I'd propose the central team own extraction and the conformed dimension/fact layer with clear SLAs for adding new source data, departments own and can rapidly iterate on their own mart-layer models without waiting on the central team for every change, and a lightweight governance forum where any new shared definition gets vetted into the conformed layer instead of being reinvented three separate times.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just tell them no, because the frustration behind this proposal is legitimate - nobody wants to wait on a central team for every small change, and if I just mandate one fully centralized warehouse with my team as the gatekeeper for everything, I'd expect shadow marts to show up anyway, just without my visibility into them. But I also wouldn't agree to three fully independent marts with their own ETL, because that's exactly how you end up with three different definitions of Revenue quietly drifting apart, plus three pipelines hitting the same source systems and tripling the engineering effort for work that's mostly identical. What I'd actually propose is a hub-and-spoke setup - a centrally-owned conformed layer with shared dimensions like Customer, Product, and Date built once, feeding department-owned marts on top where Finance, Marketing, and Supply Chain can move fast and control their own business logic without needing my team in the loop for every change. They get the speed and autonomy they're asking for at their layer, and we guarantee consistency underneath at the conformed layer. I'd also set up a lightweight process so when someone needs a new shared definition, it gets added to the conformed layer once instead of getting reinvented three separate times.

Agreeing to fully independent per-department marts without addressing definitional drift and duplicated engineering effort
Not knowing the conformed-dimension, hub-and-spoke pattern as the standard resolution to this exact conflict
Not proposing a concrete governance process for how new shared definitions get added to the central layer
Treating this as a purely technical question rather than also an organizational/process design question

Fully independent marts risk definitional drift and duplicated ETL/extraction load
Hub-and-spoke architecture with a centrally-owned conformed dimension/fact layer feeding department-owned marts
Departments get speed and autonomy at the mart layer, consistency is guaranteed at the conformed layer
A lightweight governance process is needed for adding new shared definitions

questions.title: Implementing a Type 2 Slowly Changing Dimension Update in T-SQL
questions.prompt: Given a DimProduct-style dimension with a surrogate ProductKey, a natural/business key ProductAlternateKey, EnglishProductName, StartDate, EndDate, and Status columns, write the T-SQL that correctly expires the current row and inserts a new current row whenever EnglishProductName changes for a given ProductAlternateKey -- preserving every fact table row's link to the historically-correct version of the product. Explain why this design absolutely requires a surrogate key rather than reusing the natural key, and what would break if you used Type 1 (overwrite) instead for this column.
questions.modelAnswer:
A Type 2 SCD update has two required actions, and they have to happen as one atomic unit: expire the old current row (set its EndDate to now and Status to a non-current value), and insert a brand-new row with a new surrogate ProductKey, the updated EnglishProductName, a fresh StartDate, a NULL EndDate, and Status marked current. Both actions share the same ProductAlternateKey, but deliberately do not share the same ProductKey -- that's the entire mechanism.

The surrogate key is non-negotiable because fact table rows join to the dimension by ProductKey, not by the business key. If I instead tried to do this with only the natural key, I'd have to overwrite the single existing row to change its name -- there would be nowhere to put a second, distinct row representing 'the same product, but as it used to be described,' because the natural key is the same for both versions by definition. The surrogate key is what lets two rows coexist that are 'the same real-world product' but represent two different points in time -- old fact rows keep pointing at the old ProductKey (and so report the old name, correctly, for sales that happened under that name), while new fact rows get the new ProductKey going forward.

If I used Type 1 (overwrite in place) for this column instead, the practical consequence is that I lose the ability to report history accurately: every fact row, past and present, would join to the same single DimProduct row and show whatever the current EnglishProductName happens to be right now -- including sales that occurred back when the product had a different name. A report of 'sales by product name, by month, for the last two years' would silently misattribute historical revenue to the product's current name, which is exactly the kind of error that's invisible until someone reconciles against an old static report and the numbers don't match.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd build this: when I detect that EnglishProductName has changed for a given ProductAlternateKey, I do two things in the same transaction -- I update the existing row to set its EndDate to right now and flip its Status off of current, and I insert a brand-new row for that same ProductAlternateKey with a new surrogate ProductKey, the new name, a fresh StartDate, a NULL EndDate, and Status set to current. Both rows share the business key, but they deliberately do not share the surrogate key, and that's really the whole trick.

If someone asked me why the surrogate key matters so much here, I'd say: because fact tables join on ProductKey, not on the business key, having two distinct surrogate keys is what lets two 'versions' of the same real product coexist in the dimension table at the same time. Old sales keep pointing at the old key and keep showing the old name forever; new sales point at the new key. If I only had the natural key to work with, there'd be nowhere to put that second row -- I'd be forced to just overwrite the one row that exists.

And that's exactly what goes wrong with Type 1 here: if I just overwrite the name in place instead, every fact row ever written against this product -- including years-old sales -- now joins to a row showing today's name. Any historical report broken out by product name would be quietly wrong for anything before the rename, and nobody would notice until they tried to reconcile against an old snapshot and the totals didn't match up.
commonMistakes: Reusing the business key as the dimension's join key instead of a dedicated surrogate key
Overwriting the existing row in place (Type 1 behavior) when history needs to be preserved (Type 2)
Forgetting to wrap the expire-and-insert as a single atomic transaction
Not setting EndDate/Status consistently, leaving two rows both marked 'current'
Assuming fact rows automatically re-point to the new surrogate key, when they should keep the old one for historical accuracy

Fact tables join on the surrogate key, enabling two 'versions' of one business entity to coexist
Natural/business key stays the same across versions; surrogate key does not

StartDate/EndDate/Status track which version was active at any point in time

questions.title: Designing a Data Map Scanning Strategy for Hundreds of Sources at Enterprise Scale
questions.prompt: A global enterprise has roughly 400 data sources (Azure SQL databases, ADLS accounts, on-prem SQL Server via self-hosted integration runtime, Snowflake, and dozens of Power BI workspaces) that need to be registered and scanned in a single Purview account. A junior architect proposes one giant scan rule set and one nightly full scan of everything. Design the actual scanning architecture you'd propose instead — collections structure, scan rule set segmentation, credential/identity strategy, and scan scheduling/incremental approach — and explain specifically why the junior architect's plan would fail at this scale.
questions.modelAnswer:
A single giant scan rule set and one nightly full scan of everything fails at this scale for several concrete, compounding reasons: different source types (Azure SQL, ADLS, on-prem SQL Server, Snowflake, Power BI) need fundamentally different scan rule set configurations (different file-type/object-type coverage, different classification relevance -- a classification rule meaningful for structured database columns may be irrelevant or noisy for Power BI metadata), so one shared rule set is either too narrow for some sources or produces irrelevant classification noise on others. A single nightly full scan against 400 sources also doesn't scale operationally: full scans re-read everything every time rather than only what changed, so as data volume grows the nightly window eventually can't finish before business hours, and a single shared schedule gives every source the same cadence regardless of how frequently its data actually changes or how business-critical its freshness is.

The architecture I'd propose: first, a collections hierarchy that mirrors the organization's real structure (top-level collections per business unit or region, sub-collections per source type or team), which lets access control, default classification behavior, and ownership be scoped sensibly rather than flattened into one bucket. Second, scan rule sets segmented by source type at minimum (a SQL-family rule set, an ADLS/file rule set, a Snowflake rule set, separate handling for Power BI's metadata-only scanning), each tuned with only the classifications actually relevant to that source type, which both improves classification precision and keeps each scan's runtime proportional to what it's actually checking. Third, an identity/credential strategy using managed identities wherever the source type supports it (Azure SQL, ADLS) to avoid password-based credentials needing rotation coordination, with a self-hosted integration runtime (properly scaled across multiple nodes for the on-prem SQL Server sources, since a single IR node becomes a throughput bottleneck at this source count) and Key-Vault-backed credentials only where managed identity genuinely isn't supported. Fourth, scan scheduling tiered by business criticality and actual data change frequency -- high-change, high-priority sources on a more frequent incremental schedule, low-change/archival sources on a much less frequent full scan -- combined with incremental scanning (scanning only new/changed assets since the last run) as the default mode everywhere it's supported, reserving full scans for periodic reconciliation rather than every single run. This tiered, segmented approach keeps runtime manageable, keeps classification accuracy high per source type, and lets the scanning cadence actually reflect business priority instead of forcing every source through an identical, one-size-fits-all nightly job.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell the junior architect that the one-rule-set, one-nightly-scan plan works fine at a demo scale and falls over almost immediately at 400 real sources, for a few concrete reasons, not just 'it's bad practice.' Different source types need genuinely different scan configurations -- what's relevant classification-wise for a SQL column isn't the same as what's relevant for Power BI metadata, so one shared rule set ends up either missing things or generating noise. And a full scan every night of everything doesn't scale with data growth -- full scans re-read everything from scratch, so eventually that nightly window just doesn't fit, and giving every source the same schedule ignores that some sources change constantly and some barely change at all.

What I'd actually build: a collections hierarchy that mirrors the real org structure, business unit or region at the top, team or source type underneath, so ownership and default behavior are scoped sensibly instead of dumped into one flat bucket. Scan rule sets segmented by source type at minimum -- SQL family, ADLS/files, Snowflake, Power BI handled separately -- each tuned to only the classifications that are actually relevant there. For identity, managed identity wherever the source supports it so we're not stuck coordinating password rotations across 400 sources, a properly scaled-out self-hosted integration runtime for the on-prem SQL sources so one node isn't a bottleneck, and Key Vault credentials only where managed identity genuinely isn't an option. And for scheduling, I'd tier it by actual business criticality and change frequency -- frequent incremental scans for the sources that matter most and change often, much less frequent full scans for archival or slow-changing sources -- with incremental scanning as the default everywhere it's supported, saving full scans for periodic reconciliation instead of running one every single night.
commonMistakes: Using one shared scan rule set across fundamentally different source types
Running full scans on every schedule instead of defaulting to incremental scanning where supported
Giving every source the same scan cadence regardless of business criticality or actual change frequency
Using password-based credentials everywhere instead of managed identity where the source type supports it
Running on-prem sources through a single self-hosted integration runtime node without scaling it out
Flattening collections into one bucket instead of mirroring real organizational/ownership structure
keyPoints: Scan rule sets should be segmented by source type for both classification accuracy and manageable runtime
A collections hierarchy should mirror real organizational structure, not be a single flat bucket
Managed identity should be used wherever supported; self-hosted IR must be scaled for on-prem source volume
Incremental scanning should be the default, with full scans reserved for periodic reconciliation
Scan scheduling should be tiered by business criticality and actual data change frequency, not uniform

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why a single rule set and uniform full-scan schedule fails at scale
Proposes a sensible collections hierarchy design
Proposes scan rule set segmentation by source type
Proposes a correct identity/credential strategy including IR scaling
Proposes a tiered, incremental-first scheduling approach

questions.title: Designing Business Domains and Collections to Mirror a Multi-Business-Unit Enterprise
questions.prompt: A holding company has three largely independent business units (Retail, Logistics, Financial Services), each with its own data sources, its own data stewards, and its own compliance requirements, but shares a single Purview account across all three for cost reasons. Design how you'd structure business domains and collections so each business unit gets effective autonomy and appropriately scoped governance, without the three units interfering with each other's scans, classifications, or glossaries.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd design a top-level collection per business unit (Retail, Logistics, Financial Services), each acting as the root of that unit's entire footprint in Purview, with every data source registered underneath its unit's collection rather than in a shared top-level bucket -- this is the structural boundary that makes scan configuration, source registration, and most importantly role-based access control scoped per unit, since Purview roles (collection admin, data curator, data reader) can be assigned at a specific collection level and inherit downward, letting each unit's own governance lead manage their own collection tree without needing rights over the other two.

For business domains specifically (the catalog-organizing layer, separate from collections), I'd create one business domain per business unit as well, aligning the domain structure with the collection structure so an asset's domain and its collection consistently reflect the same organizational boundary -- this keeps the Data Catalog's browsing/search experience, glossary term scoping, and data product groupings naturally separated by business unit rather than requiring every search to be manually filtered. Each business unit's stewards would own glossary terms scoped to their domain, and cross-unit term collisions (two units independently defining 'Customer' differently, which is realistic given how different Retail's and Financial Services' definitions of a customer actually are) are handled by deliberately not forcing a single shared glossary across units unless a term is genuinely shared and intentionally governed as a cross-unit concept -- in which case it gets promoted to an explicitly shared/global term with clear ownership, rather than accidentally colliding.

For classification and scanning, scan rule sets and schedules are configured per collection/unit, so Retail's classification needs (PCI-relevant payment card data) and Financial Services' needs (financial compliance-specific classifications) don't bleed into each other's scans or create irrelevant classification noise on sources that don't need those checks. The shared Purview account's cost efficiency is preserved, but because collections and domains both mirror the actual business unit boundaries consistently, each unit effectively operates its own governance space without administrative overhead needing to flow through a single central team for every decision.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd set this up: one top-level collection per business unit, and every single data source for that unit lives under its own collection root, not in some shared top bucket. That's what actually lets each unit manage its own governance independently -- Purview's roles get assigned at the collection level and flow downward, so Retail's governance lead can be a collection admin over Retail's entire tree without having any rights at all over Logistics or Financial Services, and vice versa.

For business domains, which organize the catalog itself rather than access, I'd mirror the same structure -- one domain per business unit, lined up with that unit's collection, so an asset's domain and collection consistently tell the same organizational story. That keeps glossary terms, data products, and catalog browsing naturally scoped per unit instead of needing manual filtering every time. I'd deliberately not force one shared glossary across all three units -- Retail's definition of 'Customer' and Financial Services' definition of 'Customer' are genuinely different things, and trying to make them share one glossary entry would just create confusion. If a term really is shared and meaningfully the same across units, I'd promote that specific term to an explicitly shared, intentionally-owned global term -- but that's the exception, not the default.

Scan rule sets and schedules get configured per collection too, so Retail's PCI-relevant classification needs don't bleed into Financial Services' sources and vice versa. End result: one shared Purview account for cost efficiency, but three business units that each effectively run their own governance space without stepping on each other.
commonMistakes: Registering all sources under one shared top-level collection instead of per-business-unit collection roots
Forcing a single shared glossary across business units with genuinely different definitions for the same term
Using one shared scan rule set across units with different classification needs
Not aligning the business domain structure with the collection structure, causing catalog browsing confusion
Assuming a shared Purview account requires centralized administration rather than delegated per-unit collection roles
keyPoints: Per-business-unit collection roots enable delegated, scoped role-based access control via inheritance
Aligning business domain structure with collection structure keeps the catalog experience consistently scoped
Glossary terms should be scoped per unit by default, with genuine cross-unit terms explicitly promoted and owned
Scan rule sets and schedules configured per collection prevent classification/scan cross-contamination between units
A shared Purview account can still deliver effective per-unit governance autonomy through correct structural design

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes per-business-unit collection roots enabling delegated access control
Proposes aligned business domain structure for catalog organization
Correctly handles glossary term scoping and cross-unit term collisions
Correctly scopes scan rule sets/classification per unit
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Designing a Fabric Domain and Workspace Governance Architecture for an Enterprise Rollout
questions.prompt: A company with four business units (Sales, Marketing, Finance, Operations) is rolling out Microsoft Fabric organization-wide. Each unit needs dozens of workspaces over time as teams spin up new projects, but leadership wants consistent governance defaults, naming, and security posture across the whole tenant without a central team having to manually configure every new workspace. Design the domain and workspace architecture, including how new workspaces inherit governance automatically.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd create one Fabric domain per business unit (Sales, Marketing, Finance, Operations), each with a designated domain admin from that unit who owns day-to-day governance decisions for their domain, while a central platform team retains tenant-level admin rights for cross-cutting settings. The mechanism that actually solves 'new workspaces shouldn't need manual central configuration' is domain-level default settings: each domain can define default workspace settings (and, depending on tenant configuration, default capacity assignment) that automatically apply to any workspace assigned to that domain going forward -- so a new Marketing workspace created next quarter inherits Marketing's domain defaults the moment it's assigned to that domain, without a central team touching it individually.

For this to actually work at scale with 'dozens of workspaces over time,' workspace assignment to the correct domain has to be either automatic or enforced as a required step -- I'd push for automatic domain assignment based on workspace naming convention or creator's business unit attribute where the tenant configuration supports it, and failing that, a lightweight approval/intake process requiring domain assignment before a new workspace is considered provisioned, rather than relying on individual creators remembering to assign it themselves. Naming conventions themselves (a required prefix indicating business unit and environment, like SLS-Prod-CampaignAnalytics) should be documented and ideally validated by whatever intake process exists, since Fabric itself doesn't enforce workspace naming patterns natively.

For consistent security posture specifically, I'd combine domain-level defaults with tenant-level settings that can't be overridden at the domain level for the genuinely non-negotiable items (e.g. external sharing restrictions, sensitivity label requirements) -- tenant settings sit above domain settings in the hierarchy for anything leadership considers mandatory across the whole organization, while domain-level defaults handle the business-unit-specific preferences that are allowed to vary. This layered approach -- tenant settings for non-negotiables, domain defaults for unit-specific but still centrally-defined defaults, applied automatically on domain assignment -- is what lets dozens of new workspaces per unit inherit consistent governance without a central team manually configuring each one.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd set up one domain per business unit, each with its own domain admin who actually owns the day-to-day governance calls for their unit, while the central platform team keeps tenant-level admin rights for the handful of things that genuinely need to be non-negotiable across the whole company. The piece that actually solves the 'don't make the central team configure every new workspace by hand' problem is domain-level default settings -- each domain can define defaults that automatically apply to any workspace assigned into it, so a new workspace in the Marketing domain just inherits Marketing's defaults the instant it's assigned there, with zero manual work from anyone central.

The part that takes real design thought is making sure new workspaces actually get assigned to the right domain reliably, since nothing stops someone from creating a workspace and forgetting that step. I'd push for automatic domain assignment tied to naming convention or the creator's business unit attribute wherever the tenant setup supports it, and if that's not fully available, a lightweight intake process that requires domain assignment before a workspace counts as properly provisioned, rather than trusting individual creators to remember.

For the genuinely non-negotiable stuff -- external sharing rules, sensitivity label requirements -- I'd keep those at the tenant level, above domain settings, so no domain can accidentally or deliberately loosen them. Domain defaults handle everything that's allowed to vary by business unit. That layering is what actually gets dozens of new workspaces per unit inheriting consistent governance automatically, without anyone centrally touching each one.
commonMistakes: Relying on individual workspace creators to remember to assign the correct domain, with no enforcement mechanism
Putting genuinely non-negotiable security settings at the domain level, where they could be loosened per unit
Not using domain-level default settings, requiring manual central configuration of every new workspace
Assuming Fabric natively enforces workspace naming conventions without an intake process
Giving domain admins tenant-level rights instead of scoping their authority to their own domain
keyPoints: One domain per business unit, each with a domain admin owning day-to-day governance for that unit
Domain-level default settings automatically apply to any workspace assigned to that domain
Reliable domain assignment requires automation or an enforced intake process, not reliance on memory
Tenant-level settings should hold non-negotiable governance items above domain-level defaults
This layered model lets new workspaces inherit consistent governance without manual central configuration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes one domain per business unit with appropriately scoped domain admin rights
Correctly identifies domain-level default settings as the auto-inheritance mechanism
Proposes a reliable mechanism for correct domain assignment at scale
Correctly layers tenant-level non-negotiables above domain-level defaults
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Designing a OneLake Security Model for a Sensitive HR Lakehouse
questions.prompt: An HR lakehouse in Fabric holds payroll data, performance review notes, and anonymized workforce analytics, all needed by different audiences: HR business partners need full access to their own department's records, an analytics team needs only the anonymized workforce tables, and executives need a curated summary with no row-level detail at all. Design the full security model combining workspace roles, OneLake data access roles, and sensitivity labels to serve all three audiences correctly from the same lakehouse.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd structure the lakehouse itself with physically or logically separated zones matching the three audiences' needs, since that separation is what makes each layer of security actually enforceable cleanly: a restricted zone holding payroll and performance review tables, an anonymized-analytics zone holding the workforce analytics tables with no directly-identifying fields, and a curated-summary layer (likely a set of pre-aggregated tables or a separate semantic model) serving the executive view with no row-level detail.

For workspace roles, I'd give the broader analytics team and executives Viewer access to the workspace so they can use the items that are meant for them, while HR business partners get access scoped more carefully depending on whether they also need to edit data (Contributor/Member) or just consume it (Viewer) -- workspace roles alone won't achieve the actual data-level separation though, which is where OneLake data access roles come in: a role scoped to the restricted payroll/performance path granting read access only to HR business partners (and, for departmental scoping specifically, if HR business partners should only see their own department's records, a row-level restriction would need to be enforced inside whatever query layer sits on top -- a Warehouse view with row-level security, or a Power BI semantic model's RLS, since OneLake data access roles themselves are path-scoped, not row-scoped, and can't natively restrict to 'your own department's rows' within one table), and a separate role scoped to the anonymized-analytics path granting read access to the analytics team without any path into the restricted zone at all.

For the executive audience specifically, rather than giving them any direct lakehouse access, I'd serve them through a Power BI semantic model built on top of the curated-summary layer, with no OneLake data access role granting them lakehouse-level access at all -- their consumption path is entirely through the report, which has no mechanism to expose row-level detail because the underlying summary tables themselves don't contain it. Finally, I'd apply sensitivity labels (Highly Confidential on the payroll/performance tables, Confidential or General on the anonymized analytics, matching labels on the executive summary reflecting its aggregated nature) both as a classification signal for the organization's broader information-protection policies and, depending on tenant configuration, to drive additional protection actions like encryption or restricting export, layered on top of -- not instead of -- the access-role-based restrictions already in place.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start by physically separating the lakehouse into zones that match the three audiences, because that's what makes every layer of security below actually clean to enforce: a restricted zone for payroll and performance review data, an anonymized zone for the workforce analytics tables with no directly-identifying fields, and a curated summary layer -- probably just a handful of pre-aggregated tables or its own semantic model -- for the executive view.

For access, HR business partners get a OneLake data access role scoped specifically to the restricted zone, and the analytics team gets a completely separate role scoped only to the anonymized zone, with no overlap into the restricted path at all. I'd flag one real limitation here though -- if HR business partners are only supposed to see their own department's records, OneLake data access roles are path-scoped, not row-scoped, so that specific department-level restriction needs to be handled one layer up, in a Warehouse view with row-level security or a Power BI semantic model's RLS sitting on top of the lakehouse data, not inside the data access role itself.

For executives, I wouldn't give them any direct lakehouse access at all -- I'd serve them entirely through a Power BI report built on the curated summary layer, so there's no row-level detail anywhere in their path simply because the underlying tables they're querying don't contain any. And I'd layer sensitivity labels on top of all of this -- Highly Confidential on the restricted zone, something lighter on the anonymized and summary layers -- as both a classification signal for the broader org and, depending on how the tenant's configured, an extra protection mechanism, but always in addition to the access-role restrictions, never as a substitute for them.
commonMistakes: Giving all three audiences access to the same unseparated lakehouse zone and trying to restrict via labels alone
Assuming OneLake data access roles can natively enforce row-level (e.g. per-department) restrictions within one table
Granting executives any direct lakehouse access instead of serving them through a summary-only reporting layer
Treating sensitivity labels as a substitute for access-role restrictions rather than an additional layer
Not separating the anonymized analytics data from the restricted zone at the storage/zone level
keyPoints: Physically/logically separating the lakehouse into zones makes each audience's restriction cleanly enforceable
OneLake data access roles are path-scoped, not row-scoped -- departmental row restriction needs a layer above (RLS)
Executives should be served through a summary-only reporting layer with no direct lakehouse access
Sensitivity labels classify and optionally add protection, layered on top of access-role restrictions, not instead of them
Each audience's access path should have no reachable route into zones not meant for them

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a correctly separated zone structure matching the three audiences
Correctly scopes OneLake data access roles per zone/audience
Correctly identifies the row-level departmental restriction gap and proposes RLS as the fix
Correctly serves executives through a summary-only layer with no direct lakehouse access
Correctly layers sensitivity labels as additive, not substitutive

questions.title: Designing a Unity Catalog Metastore/Catalog/Schema Structure for Multi-Environment, Multi-Business-Unit Databricks
questions.prompt: A company runs Databricks across dev, test, and production environments, and across two business units (Retail and Wholesale) that need some data isolation but also need to share a small set of common reference data (currency rates, calendar dimension). Design the Unity Catalog metastore, catalog, and schema structure, explaining specifically where environment separation and business-unit separation should each live in the hierarchy, and how the shared reference data should be structured so neither unit has to duplicate it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd place environment separation at the metastore level where feasible, or failing that, at the catalog level, and business-unit separation at the catalog level beneath that -- the key design decision is that Unity Catalog metastores are typically one per region/cloud deployment rather than one per environment, so in practice environment separation most often ends up expressed through separate catalogs within a shared metastore (dev_retail, test_retail, prod_retail, dev_wholesale, test_wholesale, prod_wholesale) rather than separate metastores per environment, unless there's a specific regulatory or workspace-binding reason requiring full metastore-level isolation for production.

Within that structure, each business unit gets its own catalog per environment, and schemas within each business unit's catalog organize by subject area or team (sales, inventory, finance) -- this gives Retail and Wholesale genuine data isolation at the catalog level, since catalog-level grants don't automatically cross over, and each unit's own data stewards can be granted USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA/object-level privileges scoped entirely to their own catalog without any standing access to the other unit's catalog.

For the shared reference data (currency rates, calendar dimension), I'd create a dedicated shared catalog per environment (shared_prod, shared_test, shared_dev) separate from either business unit's own catalog, owned and maintained by a central data platform team, with both Retail's and Wholesale's catalogs granted USE CATALOG and SELECT on the relevant shared schemas/tables within that shared catalog. This avoids duplicating currency rates or the calendar dimension inside each business unit's own catalog -- there's exactly one physical copy of each shared reference table, in the shared catalog, and both business units read from it via cross-catalog grants rather than maintaining their own copy that would eventually drift out of sync with the other unit's copy or with the authoritative source.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd lay this out: environment separation lives mostly at the catalog level, not the metastore level, because metastores are usually one per region or cloud deployment rather than one per environment -- so dev, test, and prod end up being separate catalogs within the same metastore unless there's a specific compliance reason to fully isolate production into its own metastore. Business-unit separation then also lives at the catalog level, crossed with environment, so you end up with something like dev_retail, test_retail, prod_retail alongside dev_wholesale, test_wholesale, prod_wholesale -- each business unit's catalog is its own genuinely isolated grant boundary, and schemas inside each one organize by subject area like sales or inventory.

For the shared reference data, I wouldn't let either business unit keep its own copy of currency rates or the calendar dimension -- that's exactly how two copies quietly drift apart from each other. I'd put a dedicated shared catalog per environment, owned by a central platform team, holding just that reference data, and grant both Retail's and Wholesale's catalogs read access into it via cross-catalog USE CATALOG and SELECT grants. So there's one physical copy of the shared data, both units read from the same source, and business-unit isolation at the catalog level is preserved everywhere else.
commonMistakes: Assuming environment separation requires a separate metastore per environment rather than separate catalogs
Duplicating shared reference data (currency rates, calendar) into each business unit's own catalog
Not granting cross-catalog access to the shared catalog, forcing each unit to recreate the data anyway
Mixing business-unit and environment separation at the same level without a clear naming/structural convention
Giving a business unit standing access to the other unit's catalog instead of true catalog-level isolation
keyPoints: Environment separation typically lives at the catalog level, not the metastore level, within a shared regional metastore
Business-unit separation also lives at the catalog level, crossed with environment (e.g. prod_retail, prod_wholesale)
Catalog-level grants provide genuine data isolation between business units with no automatic crossover
Shared reference data lives in its own dedicated shared catalog, owned centrally, with cross-catalog grants to each unit
This avoids duplicated reference data drifting out of sync across business units

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly places environment separation at the catalog level within a shared metastore
Correctly places business-unit separation at the catalog level, crossed with environment
Proposes a dedicated shared catalog for reference data with cross-catalog grants
Explains why this avoids duplicated/drifting reference data
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Scaling PII Protection Across Hundreds of Unity Catalog Tables Without Per-Table Policies
questions.prompt: A Databricks environment has grown to roughly 600 tables across a dozen schemas, with PII scattered across many of them in columns with inconsistent naming. Writing and maintaining a separate row filter and column mask per table is already unsustainable, and new tables are added weekly. Design an architecture using governed tags and attribute-based access control that scales PII protection without hand-writing a policy per table.
questions.modelAnswer:
The architecture has to decouple 'which columns/rows need protection' (a classification/tagging problem, which scales with correct discovery and labeling) from 'what protection rule applies' (a policy problem, which should be written once and reused), which is exactly what Unity Catalog's attribute-based access control model built on governed tags enables. I'd define a small, standardized set of governed tags at the account/metastore level (e.g. a classification tag with values like PII_DIRECT, PII_INDIRECT, FINANCIAL, PUBLIC), then write a small number of masking/row-filter policies -- one per classification value, not one per table -- that reference the tag rather than a specific column or table name directly.

For discovery and tagging at this scale, I'd pair this with an automated classification pass (either Unity Catalog's built-in sensitive-data discovery tooling where available, or a scheduled job using pattern-matching logic against column names and sampled values) that proposes tags for review rather than requiring every column across 600 tables to be manually inspected and tagged by hand -- a human-in-the-loop review step for proposed tags keeps accuracy high without making the initial rollout a fully manual, unsustainable project. Once a column is tagged PII_DIRECT, it automatically picks up whatever masking policy is associated with that tag value -- no per-table policy-writing step is needed, and this applies identically to brand-new tables created next week, as long as the same classification/tagging step (automated proposal plus human review) runs against them as part of onboarding.

For governance sustainability going forward, I'd make tagging a required, enforced step in the table/schema creation process (via a lightweight review gate or a scheduled sweep that flags newly created, untagged tables for review) rather than a one-time cleanup project, since the entire point of this architecture is that protection scales with correct, ongoing classification rather than needing anyone to write new policy logic as the environment grows.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The core move here is separating 'what needs protecting' from 'how it gets protected,' because trying to hand-write a row filter and column mask per table is never going to keep up with 600 tables and weekly additions. I'd define a small, standard set of governed tags at the account level -- something like a classification tag with values for PII_DIRECT, PII_INDIRECT, financial data, and so on -- and write just a handful of masking and row-filter policies, one per classification value, that key off the tag itself rather than any specific table or column name.

For actually getting those tags onto 600 tables' worth of columns, I wouldn't try to do that by hand -- I'd run an automated classification pass, pattern-matching against column names and sampled values, that proposes tags for a human to review and approve rather than requiring someone to manually inspect every single column. Once a column's tagged PII_DIRECT, it's immediately covered by whatever policy is tied to that tag -- no new policy has to be written for that specific table, and the exact same thing happens automatically for a brand-new table created next week, as long as it goes through that same automated-proposal-plus-review step.

The last piece that makes this actually sustainable long-term is making tagging a required part of how new tables get created, not a one-time cleanup project -- either a review gate at creation time or a scheduled sweep that flags any newly created, untagged table. The whole point of this design is that protection scales with correct ongoing classification, not with anyone writing more policy logic as the environment keeps growing.
commonMistakes: Continuing to write a separate row filter/column mask per table instead of tag-driven, reusable policies
Attempting to manually tag 600 tables' worth of columns by hand instead of using automated classification with human review
Treating tagging as a one-time cleanup project rather than an enforced, ongoing part of table creation
Defining too many granular tag values, recreating the per-table maintenance burden at the tag level instead
Not accounting for new tables created weekly needing the same classification/tagging step automatically
keyPoints: Decouple classification/tagging (scales with discovery) from policy logic (written once per tag value, reused everywhere)
A small, standardized set of governed tags at the account/metastore level drives all masking/row-filter policies
Automated classification with human-in-the-loop review makes initial tagging across hundreds of tables sustainable
New tables automatically inherit protection once tagged, with no new per-table policy needed
Tagging must be an enforced, ongoing part of table creation, not a one-time project

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes decoupling classification/tagging from reusable, tag-driven policies
Proposes a scalable automated classification/discovery approach with human review
Explains how new tables automatically inherit protection via tagging
Proposes making tagging an enforced, ongoing process rather than a one-time project
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Designing a Functional-Role vs. Access-Role Hierarchy for a Large Snowflake Organization
questions.prompt: A large organization's Snowflake account has grown to the point where roles have been granted directly and inconsistently to users for two years, and nobody can confidently answer 'who can see what' without manually tracing individual grants. Design a clean role hierarchy architecture (functional roles vs. access roles) that would replace this, and explain how it avoids the same 'nobody can trace it' problem recurring in another two years.
questions.modelAnswer:
The root cause of 'nobody can trace it' after two years is almost always that privileges got granted directly to individual users, or roles got built as one-off, ad hoc bundles mixing 'who someone is' with 'what they can access' in the same role -- both patterns make tracing effective access require manually walking a tangle of individual exceptions rather than reading a clean, intentional structure. The standard architectural fix is separating two distinct kinds of roles: access roles, which each represent one specific, narrow privilege grant on one specific set of objects (e.g. ACCESS_SALES_READ granting SELECT on the sales schema, nothing else), and functional roles, which represent a job function or team (e.g. SALES_ANALYST) and are built purely by composing access roles together via GRANT ROLE access_role TO ROLE functional_role -- users are only ever granted functional roles directly, never access roles, and access roles are never granted directly to users.

This structure makes tracing tractable again because answering 'who can see the sales schema' becomes 'which functional roles have ACCESS_SALES_READ granted to them, and who holds those functional roles' -- a clean, two-hop lookup through an intentional hierarchy, rather than an unstructured tangle of historical exceptions. Avoiding recurrence requires more than just building the clean hierarchy once -- it requires governance discipline going forward: a hard rule (enforced through review, not just documented) that no privilege is ever granted directly to a user or directly bundled into an ad hoc role outside this access-role/functional-role pattern, a lightweight access-request process that only ever grants existing functional roles (never improvises new one-off combinations per request), and periodic access reviews (quarterly or semi-annual) that specifically check for and flag any direct grants to individual users that violate the pattern, since the original problem was created by small, individually-reasonable-seeming exceptions accumulating silently over time -- the review process is what actually catches drift before it becomes two years of untraceable history again.
questions.professionalAnswer:
What caused the original mess is almost certainly that privileges got granted straight to individual users, or roles got built as one-off bundles that mix 'who this person is' with 'what they're allowed to touch' in the same object -- either way, tracing access means manually untangling a pile of individual exceptions instead of reading a structure that was actually designed. The fix is splitting roles into two clean categories: access roles, each one a narrow, specific privilege grant on one set of objects and nothing else, and functional roles, which represent an actual job function and are built entirely by composing access roles together. Users only ever get functional roles directly -- never access roles, never a raw privilege grant.

That alone makes tracing sane again, because 'who can see the sales schema' becomes a two-step lookup -- which functional roles have the sales access role granted to them, and who holds those functional roles -- instead of manually walking two years of accumulated one-off exceptions. But building the clean hierarchy once doesn't prevent this from happening again in two more years -- that takes actual discipline going forward. I'd put in a hard rule that nothing ever gets granted directly to a user or bundled as a new one-off role outside this pattern, make the access-request process only able to hand out existing functional roles rather than improvising new combinations per request, and run a periodic access review specifically looking for direct grants that violate the pattern -- because the original mess didn't happen all at once, it happened one small, reasonable-seeming exception at a time, and that's exactly what a recurring review is built to catch before it becomes untraceable again.
commonMistakes: Granting privileges directly to individual users instead of only through functional roles
Building ad hoc roles that mix specific privilege grants with job-function identity in the same object
Building the clean hierarchy once but not establishing ongoing governance discipline to prevent drift
Allowing the access-request process to improvise new one-off role combinations per request
Not running periodic access reviews specifically designed to catch direct-grant violations of the pattern
keyPoints: Separate access roles (narrow, specific privilege grants) from functional roles (job-function roles composed of access roles)
Users are granted only functional roles; access roles are never granted directly to users
This structure makes 'who can see what' a clean, traceable two-hop lookup instead of an exception tangle
Preventing recurrence requires ongoing governance discipline, not just a one-time clean rebuild
A periodic access review specifically targeting direct-grant violations catches drift before it accumulates again
