Proposes appropriate escalation if resistance persists, rather than forcing or giving up
Maintains a collaborative, non-adversarial tone throughout

questions.title: Owning an Incident Where Ungoverned Data Caused a Reporting Discrepancy
questions.prompt: An executive noticed that a revenue number in a board-level report didn't match a nearly identical number from a different report, both reportedly showing 'the same metric.' Investigation reveals the discrepancy traces back to an ungoverned semantic model built outside the standard pipeline, using a slightly different revenue definition, that nobody in governance knew existed until this incident. You're the governance lead and this happened on your watch. How do you handle the immediate incident and the aftermath?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer takes genuine ownership without either over-apologizing in a way that undermines confidence or deflecting blame onto whoever built the ungoverned model, since an unknown ungoverned model existing is itself a governance program gap, not purely an individual's rule violation. The candidate should describe handling the immediate incident first: identifying which of the two numbers is actually correct (or whether neither fully is, if the definitions genuinely differ for a legitimate reason), communicating a clear, factual explanation to the executive promptly rather than letting the discrepancy sit unexplained, and correcting whichever report is wrong.

For the root cause analysis, the candidate should go beyond 'someone built a model outside the pipeline' to ask why that was possible without governance's awareness — was there no monitoring/discovery mechanism catching ungoverned models, was the standard pipeline too slow or cumbersome such that going around it felt like the only option, was there no clear policy communicated about where revenue definitions must come from — and should be willing to say directly to leadership that the program's own discovery/monitoring gap, not just the individual's choice, is part of what let this happen undetected.

For the aftermath, the response should describe concrete, structural fixes rather than just a one-time correction: establishing or improving a regular discovery/scanning process specifically to catch ungoverned models before they cause an incident rather than after, and addressing why going around the standard pipeline felt necessary in the first place (process friction, unclear policy) rather than just telling people not to do it again. The candidate should also describe communicating the root cause and fix plan transparently to leadership, including honest acknowledgment of the governance program's own gap, since credibility with executives after an incident depends more on a credible fix plan than on minimizing the program's own role in it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move is fixing the actual confusion in front of the executive, fast — figure out which number is right, or whether the two definitions are genuinely both legitimate for different reasons, and give them a clear, factual explanation quickly rather than letting it sit as an unresolved mystery. Then I correct whichever report is actually wrong.

But the harder, more important part is the root cause conversation, and I'd be straight with myself and with leadership that this isn't just 'someone built something outside the rules.' The real question is why governance had zero visibility into this model existing at all — did we not have any discovery or scanning process that would've caught it, was our standard pipeline slow or painful enough that going around it felt like the reasonable move, was the policy on where revenue definitions have to come from ever actually communicated clearly? I'd own that gap directly rather than making this entirely about the individual who built the model.

For the actual fix, I wouldn't settle for 'we corrected the number and told people not to do that again.' I'd put in place a real discovery/monitoring process that catches ungoverned models proactively instead of after they've already caused an executive-visible incident, and I'd look hard at whether our standard pipeline is actually usable enough that people don't feel pushed to route around it. And I'd go back to leadership with the real root cause, including our own monitoring gap, and a credible fix plan — because after something like this, what actually rebuilds trust is leadership seeing that I know exactly what broke and have a real plan, not me trying to make the incident sound smaller than it was.
commonMistakes: Deflecting blame entirely onto the individual who built the ungoverned model, ignoring the program's own visibility gap
Over-apologizing in a way that undermines executive confidence without a credible fix plan
Fixing only the immediate reporting discrepancy without addressing why it went undetected
Not investigating whether pipeline friction or unclear policy contributed to someone going around the standard process
Minimizing the governance program's own role in the incident rather than owning it honestly to leadership
keyPoints: Resolves the immediate discrepancy with a clear, factual, prompt explanation and correction
Takes genuine ownership of the governance program's own discovery/monitoring gap, not just individual blame
Investigates whether pipeline friction or unclear policy contributed to the root cause
Proposes structural fixes (proactive discovery/monitoring, pipeline usability) rather than a one-time correction
Communicates the real root cause and fix plan transparently to leadership to rebuild trust

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Resolves the immediate discrepancy clearly, factually, and promptly
Takes genuine ownership of the program's own visibility/monitoring gap
Investigates root cause beyond blaming the individual (pipeline friction, policy clarity)
Proposes concrete structural fixes rather than a one-time correction
Communicates transparently with leadership to rebuild trust

questions.title: Presenting Governance KPIs to an Executive Steering Committee
questions.prompt: You have 15 minutes with the executive steering committee to present the governance program's quarterly KPIs: catalog coverage is up to 62% from 40%, policy adoption varies widely by platform, and there are 34 open data quality issues, 9 of which are over 90 days old. Some executives in the room are impatient with 'IT metrics' and want to know if the program is actually worth the investment. Walk through how you'd structure this presentation.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer leads with business translation, not raw metrics — the candidate should describe opening with the one or two sentence business answer to the implicit question in the room ('is this worth it') before diving into numbers, since executives impatient with 'IT metrics' are really asking for the metric-to-business-impact translation to be done for them, not asked to do it themselves while staring at a catalog coverage percentage.

For catalog coverage (40% to 62%), the candidate should translate this into what it actually means operationally — more of the data estate is now discoverable and classified, which directly reduces the risk of exactly the kind of ungoverned-model incident that causes executive-visible reporting discrepancies — rather than presenting the percentage as an end in itself. For the varying policy adoption by platform, the candidate should be honest about the gap rather than smoothing it over, framing it as a prioritized remediation plan (which platform's gap carries the most business risk, and what's being done about it) rather than just reporting the number and moving on. For the 34 open issues with 9 aged past 90 days, the candidate should not bury this -- the aged issues are the number most likely to trigger exactly the 'is this worth it' skepticism in the room, so addressing it head-on with a concrete remediation plan and timeline is more credible than hoping it goes unnoticed or gets glossed over.

The response should close by directly answering the ROI/worth-it question with a concrete tie-back: citing a specific risk avoided or incident prevented this quarter (or, if none occurred, the specific exposure that existed before the program and has since been reduced), since a steering committee responds much better to 'here is the specific risk this program is reducing' than to an abstract maturity narrative. Time management for a 15-minute slot should also be explicit: lead with the business answer and a one-page visual summary, keep the detailed metric walkthrough brief, and reserve time for the harder questions (the aged issues, the adoption gap) rather than running out of time before addressing the parts most likely to be challenged.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd open with the actual answer to the question they're really asking, before a single number goes up on the screen: is this worth it, and here's why, in one or two sentences. Executives who are impatient with 'IT metrics' aren't asking me to show them a catalog coverage percentage and let them figure out what it means — they want that translation already done.

For catalog coverage going from 40 to 62 percent, I wouldn't present the number as the win itself — I'd say what it actually means: more of our data estate is now discoverable and classified, which is directly what reduces the risk of another surprise like an ungoverned model causing a board-level reporting discrepancy. For the policy adoption gap across platforms, I'd be straight about it rather than smoothing it over — here's which platform's gap carries the most real risk, and here's the specific plan to close it, not just a number and a shrug.

The 34 open issues, 9 of them over 90 days old — I would not bury that slide or rush past it, because that's exactly the number that's going to trigger the skepticism in the room if I don't address it myself first. I'd own it directly with a concrete remediation plan and a real timeline, because that's more credible than hoping nobody asks.

And I'd close by tying straight back to the worth-it question with something concrete — a specific risk we avoided this quarter, or if nothing dramatic happened, the specific exposure that existed before this program and has measurably shrunk since. A steering committee responds to 'here's the specific risk this is reducing' a lot better than to a vague maturity story. And with only 15 minutes, I'd keep the detailed metric walkthrough tight and make sure I've got time left over for the harder questions instead of running out of time right before the aged-issues slide.
commonMistakes: Leading with raw metrics instead of the business-impact translation executives actually want
Presenting catalog coverage as an end in itself rather than explaining its risk-reduction meaning
Smoothing over or burying the varying policy adoption and aged-issue numbers instead of addressing them directly
Not tying the presentation back to a concrete ROI/risk-avoided answer to the 'worth it' question
Poor time management, running out of time before addressing the most likely-to-be-challenged numbers
keyPoints: Opens with the business-impact translation of the metrics, not the raw numbers themselves
Translates catalog coverage improvement into concrete risk-reduction meaning
Addresses the policy adoption gap and aged issues honestly with a concrete remediation plan, not glossing over them
Closes by directly tying the presentation back to a concrete answer to the 'is this worth it' question
Manages the 15-minute time constraint deliberately, reserving time for the hardest questions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Leads with business-impact translation rather than raw metrics
Correctly translates catalog coverage into concrete risk-reduction meaning
Addresses the policy adoption gap and aged issues directly with a remediation plan
Closes with a concrete tie-back to program ROI/value
Demonstrates deliberate time management for the format constraint

questions.title: Handling a Data Owner Who Won't Sign Off on Classification SLAs
questions.prompt: As part of the governance program, every data owner is supposed to sign off on a 10-business-day SLA for responding to classification review requests on their data. One senior data owner has ignored three separate requests to review and sign off, saying through their assistant that they're 'too busy' and governance 'can just use their best judgment.' Issue requests are starting to pile up waiting on this specific owner's input. How do you handle this?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer resists the tempting shortcut of just using 'best judgment' as the data owner suggested, since classification decisions on data this owner is accountable for need that owner's actual input precisely because the governance team may not have the business context to classify it correctly — accepting the shortcut would also set a precedent that ignoring governance SLAs has no real consequence, which undermines the SLA for every other data owner watching how this plays out.

The candidate should describe first attempting a direct, low-friction re-engagement — a short, specific conversation (not another generic request) framing exactly what's needed, why it can't be done without their input, and the concrete business risk of the pile-up (what's blocked, for how long, affecting whom) rather than assuming the owner understands the downstream impact of their delay. If this genuinely doesn't land after a good-faith direct attempt, the answer should describe an appropriate escalation path — to the data owner's manager or through the governance council, depending on how the program's RACI defines who's accountable for an unresponsive data owner — rather than either continuing to wait indefinitely or quietly working around the SLA's intent.

The response should also address the systemic question: is this SLA breach isolated to one busy executive, or does it reveal that SLA sign-off needs an enforcement mechanism (visibility to the governance council on overdue sign-offs, consequences built into the original policy) rather than relying purely on goodwill compliance — and should note that how this specific case is resolved sets a visible precedent other data owners will notice.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't take the 'just use your best judgment' offer, even though it would make the backlog disappear immediately, because the whole reason we need this specific owner's sign-off is that they have business context we don't have — and quietly accepting that shortcut also tells every other data owner watching that ignoring the SLA has zero real consequence, which kills the SLA for everyone, not just this one person.

First I'd try a real, direct conversation instead of another generic request email — something specific: here's exactly what I need from you, here's why it genuinely can't be decided without your input, and here's what's actually blocked and for how long because of the delay. A lot of the time, a busy executive genuinely doesn't realize the downstream impact of ignoring three requests; they just see 'another governance email' in their inbox.

If that direct, good-faith attempt still doesn't land, I'd escalate it properly — to their manager or through the governance council, whichever our program's own accountability structure says is the right path for an unresponsive data owner — rather than either waiting indefinitely or quietly working around it myself. And I'd also take a step back and ask whether this is really just one busy person, or whether it's telling us our SLA needs an actual enforcement mechanism — visibility to the council on overdue sign-offs, real consequences built into the policy — instead of relying purely on goodwill. However this specific case gets resolved, every other data owner is going to notice how it played out.
commonMistakes: Accepting the 'use your best judgment' shortcut, undermining the SLA's credibility for every other data owner
Sending another generic, non-specific request instead of a direct, concrete re-engagement
Waiting indefinitely without escalating, letting the issue pile-up continue unaddressed
Escalating immediately without a genuine, specific direct attempt first
Not considering whether this reveals a systemic enforcement gap in the SLA rather than an isolated incident
keyPoints: Declines the 'use best judgment' shortcut, since it undermines both correctness and SLA credibility for everyone
Attempts a direct, specific, low-friction re-engagement before escalating
Frames the concrete business impact (what's blocked, for how long) rather than a generic reminder
Escalates appropriately through the correct accountability path if direct engagement fails
Considers whether the SLA needs a real enforcement mechanism rather than relying purely on goodwill

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly declines the 'best judgment' shortcut and explains why
Attempts a direct, specific re-engagement framing concrete business impact
Proposes appropriate escalation if direct engagement fails
Considers the systemic SLA enforcement question, not just this isolated case
Clear, professional, non-adversarial tone throughout

questions.title: Balancing Governance Rigor Against an Analyst Velocity Complaint
questions.prompt: A well-regarded analytics team complains that the new Unity Catalog access-request process -- requiring a documented business justification and a two-step approval for anything touching customer tables -- is 'killing their velocity' and that they were faster before governance existed. They're not wrong that it's slower. How do you respond, and what, if anything, do you change?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer takes the complaint seriously as a real signal rather than dismissing it as resistance to be overcome, since 'slower than before governance existed' is true by definition and isn't itself evidence the process is wrong -- the real question is whether the added friction is proportionate to the risk being managed, and whether the same risk reduction could be achieved with less friction. The candidate should investigate specifically rather than assuming either 'the process is fine, they'll adjust' or 'the process is broken, remove it': how often are requests actually denied or substantively changed as a result of the two-step review (if nearly all requests are approved as-is, the review may be adding delay without adding much actual risk reduction), and what's actually consuming the time -- the justification-writing step, waiting on a specific approver, or the review itself taking long.

The response should distinguish between friction that's doing real risk-reduction work (which should stay, with the business risk explained honestly to the team even if they still dislike it) and friction that's just process overhead without a matching risk benefit (which should be streamlined). Concrete options the candidate might propose: pre-approved request templates for common, well-understood access patterns that skip the full two-step review when the request matches a known-low-risk profile, a faster approval SLA so the delay is bounded and predictable even where review is still required, or delegating one of the two approval steps to the data owner directly rather than routing through governance centrally for lower-risk cases.

The answer should avoid two failure modes: caving entirely and removing the control because a well-regarded team complained (which undermines the governance program's credibility and the actual risk it exists to manage), and dismissing the complaint without genuinely investigating whether the process is well-calibrated (which breeds resentment and workarounds). A good answer closes by committing to a specific, time-boxed review of the actual approval data before deciding what, if anything, changes, rather than deciding reactively in the moment.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd take this seriously rather than writing it off as 'they just don't like governance yet.' They're right that it's slower than before -- that's just true -- but slower isn't automatically wrong; the real question is whether that added time is actually buying real risk reduction, or whether it's friction without much payoff. So before I'd change anything, I'd go look at the actual data: how often does the two-step review actually catch something and deny or change a request, versus just approving almost everything that comes through? If it's nearly always a rubber stamp, that tells me the review step might be adding delay without adding much real protection.

I'd also want to know specifically where the time is going -- is it writing the justification, waiting on a particular approver, or the review itself taking a while -- because the fix is completely different depending on which one it is. If the review genuinely is catching real risk, I'd keep it and be honest with the team about why, even if they still don't love it. But if it's mostly overhead, I'd look at streamlining it -- pre-approved templates for common, well-understood access patterns that skip the full review, a tighter approval SLA so at least the delay is predictable, or letting the data owner directly handle one of the two approval steps for lower-risk cases instead of routing everything centrally.

What I wouldn't do is just cave and remove the control because a well-liked team complained loudly -- that guts the whole point of having it. And I wouldn't dismiss them either, because ignoring a real signal just breeds resentment and people quietly finding workarounds. I'd commit to actually looking at the approval data on a specific timeline before deciding anything, instead of reacting in the moment either way.
commonMistakes: Dismissing the complaint as resistance without investigating whether the process is actually well-calibrated
Caving entirely and removing the control because a well-regarded team complained loudly
Not distinguishing between friction doing real risk-reduction work and friction that's just overhead
Changing the process reactively without looking at actual approval/denial data first
Not considering lower-friction alternatives (templates, faster SLAs, delegated approval) that preserve risk reduction
keyPoints: Takes the velocity complaint seriously as a signal worth investigating, not dismissing as pure resistance
Investigates actual approval/denial data to assess whether the friction is proportionate to risk reduction
Distinguishes friction doing real risk-reduction work from friction that's pure overhead
Proposes concrete lower-friction alternatives that preserve risk reduction where it's genuinely needed
Avoids both caving entirely and dismissing the complaint outright; commits to a data-driven, time-boxed review

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Takes the complaint seriously without dismissing it as mere resistance
Proposes investigating actual approval data to assess proportionality
Correctly distinguishes risk-reducing friction from pure overhead
Proposes concrete, viable lower-friction alternatives
Avoids both caving entirely and dismissing the complaint

questions.title: Leading a Cross-Functional Team Through a Disruptive Unity Catalog Migration
questions.prompt: Your organization is migrating from an unmanaged Hive metastore setup to Unity Catalog, which will change how dozens of downstream dashboards, scheduled jobs, and ad hoc notebooks reference tables across five different teams, none of whom report to you. Several teams are anxious about breakage and one has quietly said they'll 'just deal with it later.' You're accountable for the migration succeeding. How do you lead this?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer recognizes that leading a migration across five teams with no direct authority over any of them is fundamentally an influence and planning problem, not a technical problem alone, and should describe building legitimacy through a concrete, team-specific plan rather than a general mandate. The candidate should describe first inventorying actual impact per team (which specific tables, jobs, dashboards, and notebooks each team owns that will be affected) so each team gets a concrete, specific picture of what changes for them rather than a vague 'this will affect everyone' message that's easy to deprioritize.

For the anxious teams, the response should describe a staged migration approach -- starting with a lower-risk team or workload as a proof point, demonstrating the migration process works and showing what the actual experience looks like, before asking more anxious teams to go through it, rather than asking everyone to move simultaneously on faith. For the team that said they'd 'deal with it later,' the candidate should treat this as a genuine risk to flag rather than ignore, directly and specifically naming the business consequence of their workloads breaking unmigrated (jobs failing, dashboards showing errors) and the actual hard cutover date, rather than assuming goodwill alone will get them to move in time -- and should describe escalating to that team's own leadership if direct engagement doesn't produce a concrete commitment, since a lack of authority over the team doesn't remove accountability for the migration's overall success.

The response should also address practical de-risking: providing a compatibility/transition period or dual-access window where old and new references both work temporarily if the platform supports it, clear documentation and office hours/support channels during the cutover, and a concrete rollback or remediation plan for anything that breaks despite the migration effort -- since leading without direct authority depends heavily on making the migration genuinely easy and low-risk to adopt, not just repeatedly asking people to prioritize it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Since I don't have direct authority over any of these five teams, I know this has to work through a concrete plan and real influence, not a mandate I can't actually enforce. First move is inventorying exactly what's affected per team -- which specific tables, jobs, dashboards, notebooks each one owns that this migration touches -- so every team gets a specific picture of what changes for them, not a vague 'this affects everyone' email that's easy to ignore.

For the anxious teams, I'd migrate a lower-risk team first as a proof point -- show the process actually works, show what the real experience looks like, before asking the more nervous teams to go through it themselves. Nobody wants to be the first one to find out something broke.

For the team that said they'll 'deal with it later' -- I'm not going to let that slide quietly. I'd go to them directly and be specific: here's exactly what breaks and when if you don't migrate by this date, here's the hard cutover, and I need an actual commitment from you, not a vague acknowledgment. If that direct conversation doesn't get me a real commitment, I'd escalate to their leadership, because not having authority over them doesn't mean I'm not still accountable if their workloads break on migration day.

And practically, I'd try to de-risk this as much as possible -- a transition window where old and new references both work if the platform supports it, real documentation and office hours during the cutover, and an actual rollback or remediation plan for anything that breaks despite everyone's best effort. Leading a migration like this without direct authority really comes down to making it genuinely easy and low-risk to go along with, not just repeatedly asking people to make it a priority.
commonMistakes: Sending a vague, non-specific 'this affects everyone' communication instead of a per-team impact inventory
Asking all five teams to migrate simultaneously on faith instead of staging with a proof-point team first
Ignoring or softening the 'deal with it later' team's risk instead of naming the concrete consequence directly
Not escalating to the resistant team's leadership when direct engagement fails to produce a commitment
Relying purely on repeated requests to prioritize the migration instead of actively reducing its risk and friction
keyPoints: Builds legitimacy through a concrete, team-specific impact plan rather than a general mandate
Stages the migration, proving it with a lower-risk team before asking anxious teams to follow
Directly and specifically names the consequence to the 'deal with it later' team rather than ignoring the risk
Escalates to the resistant team's leadership if direct engagement doesn't produce a real commitment
De-risks the migration practically (transition window, documentation, rollback plan) rather than relying on goodwill alone

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Builds a concrete, team-specific impact plan rather than a vague general communication
Proposes a staged migration with a proof-point team for anxious teams
Directly addresses the 'deal with it later' team's risk with specific consequences
Proposes appropriate escalation if direct engagement fails
Proposes concrete de-risking measures (transition window, support, rollback plan)

questions.title: Communicating a Sensitive Data Exposure Found During a Routine Scan
questions.prompt: A routine Purview scan unexpectedly classifies a column in a widely-used customer support table as containing unmasked national ID numbers -- a field nobody realized held that data, and access logs show dozens of support agents have had unrestricted read access to it for over a year. You're the one who first sees this in the scan results. Walk through exactly what you do in the first hour, and how you communicate this to legal/compliance and the business.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats the first hour as containment and verification, not immediate broad alarm-raising, since acting on an unverified classification result as if it's confirmed fact risks both overreacting to a possible false positive and underreacting if it's confirmed -- the candidate should describe first manually verifying the classification is accurate (checking a sample of actual values in the column, not just trusting the automated classification result at face value) before escalating anything, since a false positive escalated as a real exposure wastes the exact urgent response capacity that a real exposure would need.

Once verified as real, the candidate should describe immediate, narrow containment -- restricting access to the specific column (via masking policy, access policy, or revoking the broad read grant, whichever is fastest to execute safely) to stop the ongoing exposure, which should happen essentially in parallel with notification, not after a lengthy investigation, since every additional hour of exposure matters and containment is usually faster to execute than full investigation.

For communication, the candidate should describe escalating to legal/compliance immediately once verified, since unmasked national ID exposure very likely triggers specific regulatory notification obligations that only legal/compliance can correctly assess and that have their own clocks running from the moment of discovery -- this is not a decision the person who found it should make alone or delay on, even informally, while doing more investigation first. The communication itself should be factual and specific (what data, how many records, who had access, for how long, what's already been done to contain it) rather than either minimizing the scope or speculating beyond what's actually known at this point, and should include a clear statement of what's still being investigated versus what's already confirmed, so legal/compliance can make an informed, timely call on notification obligations without being misled by premature certainty in either direction.
questions.professionalAnswer:
In the first hour, my focus is verification and containment, not broadcasting alarm everywhere at once. First I'd manually check a sample of the actual column values myself -- I'm not escalating an automated classification result as a confirmed exposure until I've actually looked and confirmed it's real, because escalating a false positive as a crisis burns the exact response capacity a real one would need.

Once I've confirmed it's real, containment happens essentially right away, in parallel with notifying people, not after a long investigation -- restrict access to that specific column as fast as I safely can, whether that's a masking policy, an access policy, or just revoking the broad read grant, because every additional hour this stays open is additional exposure.

For communication, legal and compliance get told immediately once I've verified it's real -- this isn't something I sit on to investigate further first, because unmasked national ID data exposure very likely has actual regulatory notification clocks running from the moment it was discovered, and only legal and compliance can correctly judge that, not me. What I tell them is specific and factual -- what data, roughly how many records, who's had access and for how long, and what's already been done to contain it -- and I'm explicit about what's confirmed versus what I'm still investigating, because giving them false certainty in either direction, too alarming or too reassuring, makes it harder for them to make the right call on notification obligations.
commonMistakes: Escalating an unverified automated classification result as a confirmed exposure without checking actual values first
Delaying containment until after a full investigation, extending the exposure window unnecessarily
Delaying legal/compliance notification to investigate further first, when regulatory clocks may already be running
Communicating with either excessive alarm or minimization instead of precise, factual, confirmed-vs-still-investigating detail
Making the notification-obligation decision unilaterally instead of deferring that judgment to legal/compliance
keyPoints: Verifies the classification result manually before escalating, to avoid wasted urgent response on a false positive
Executes narrow, immediate containment in parallel with notification, not after a lengthy investigation
Escalates to legal/compliance immediately once verified, since regulatory notification clocks may be running
Communicates factually and specifically, distinguishing confirmed facts from what's still being investigated
Defers the actual regulatory notification decision to legal/compliance rather than deciding unilaterally

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly verifies the classification result before escalating
Executes immediate, narrow containment in parallel with notification
Escalates to legal/compliance immediately once verified, without unnecessary delay
Communicates factually and specifically, distinguishing confirmed vs. still-investigating
Correctly defers the regulatory notification decision to legal/compliance

questions.title: Coaching a Junior Governance Analyst Who Over-Applies Classification Labels
questions.prompt: A junior governance analyst on your team has started tagging almost everything they review as 'Highly Confidential' or 'PII,' including columns that are genuinely public or low-sensitivity, explaining that they'd rather 'be safe than sorry.' Teams are starting to complain that legitimate, harmless reports are getting blocked by overly aggressive labels, and some are quietly asking for exceptions that bypass the analyst's review entirely. How do you coach this analyst?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer recognizes that over-classification is a real governance failure, not a safely conservative default, and should explain this to the analyst in those terms rather than simply telling them to be less cautious -- over-classification has concrete costs: it trains the business to see governance as an obstacle rather than a value-add, it causes exactly the outcome described (teams seeking workarounds/exceptions that bypass review entirely, which is strictly worse for actual data protection than correctly-scoped labels that people respect and work within), and it dilutes the meaning of 'Highly Confidential' so that when something genuinely is highly confidential, it doesn't stand out or get treated with appropriate seriousness.

The coaching approach should be concrete and example-based rather than abstract -- reviewing specific recent cases where the analyst over-classified, walking through the actual classification criteria/decision framework together, and asking the analyst to articulate why they believed a specific over-classified case warranted the label, which usually reveals the actual gap (not understanding the real-world distinguishing criteria between sensitivity tiers, or not trusting their own judgment and defaulting to the most restrictive option out of genuine uncertainty rather than careless) -- the fix differs significantly depending on which one it is.

The response should also address the systemic consequence already appearing: teams asking for exceptions that bypass review entirely is a serious problem on its own, independent of fixing the analyst's classification accuracy, since it represents stakeholders giving up on the review process's legitimacy -- the candidate should describe directly addressing those requests (not granting blanket bypasses, but committing to a faster, more accurate review going forward and discussing with those teams why their legitimate complaint will now actually be addressed) so trust in the review process is rebuilt rather than quietly eroded further while the coaching happens.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start by being direct with the analyst that 'better safe than sorry' isn't actually safe here -- it has real costs. If everything gets tagged Highly Confidential, the business starts treating governance as something to work around instead of trust, teams start quietly asking for exceptions that skip review entirely -- which is worse for real protection than a correctly-scoped label people actually respect -- and when something genuinely is highly confidential, the label doesn't mean anything anymore because it's been slapped on everything.

For the actual coaching, I'd go through specific recent cases with them, not an abstract lecture -- pull up a few things they over-tagged and walk through our actual classification criteria together, and ask them to explain why they thought that specific case warranted the label. That conversation usually tells me what's really going on -- either they don't actually understand the real distinguishing line between sensitivity tiers, or they understand it fine but don't trust their own judgment yet and default to the most restrictive option whenever they're uncertain. Those are two different problems with two different fixes, so I want to know which one it actually is before I decide how to coach them further.

And separately from fixing the analyst's accuracy, I'd deal with the exception requests directly and quickly, because teams asking to bypass review entirely is its own serious problem -- it means they've basically given up on the review process being worth going through. I wouldn't just grant blanket bypasses, but I would go back to those teams, acknowledge their complaint was legitimate, and commit to a faster, more accurate review now, so trust in the process actually gets rebuilt instead of quietly eroding further while I work on coaching.
commonMistakes: Treating over-classification as a harmlessly cautious default rather than a real governance cost
Coaching abstractly instead of walking through specific recent over-classified cases together
Not diagnosing whether the root cause is a criteria-understanding gap or a confidence/judgment-trust gap
Ignoring the teams' exception-bypass requests while only focusing on fixing the analyst
Granting blanket review bypasses instead of committing to faster, more accurate review to rebuild trust
keyPoints: Over-classification is a real governance cost (erodes trust, prompts bypass requests, dilutes label meaning), not a safe default
Coaching should be concrete and example-based, reviewing specific over-classified cases with the analyst
Diagnosing whether the gap is criteria-understanding or judgment-confidence changes the right coaching approach
Teams requesting review bypasses is a serious, separate problem needing direct, prompt attention
Trust should be rebuilt through faster, more accurate review, not by granting blanket bypasses

questions.title: Building a Business Case to Advocate for Governance Program Budget and Headcount
questions.prompt: Your governance program has been running for a year with one person (you) covering Purview, Unity Catalog, and Power BI governance across the whole organization, and it's clearly not sustainable as the data estate grows. You need to make the case to finance and leadership for additional headcount and tooling budget next fiscal year, competing against other departments' funding requests. How do you build and present this case?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer builds the case around quantified risk and opportunity cost rather than 'I'm overworked,' since a funding request competing against other departments' requests needs to be argued in the same terms finance evaluates any other investment, not as a personal workload complaint. The candidate should describe gathering concrete evidence over the current year: specific incidents or near-misses that occurred or were narrowly avoided due to under-resourcing (an ungoverned model that went undetected longer than it should have, a classification backlog that delayed a compliance requirement, access requests sitting unresolved for weeks), the current coverage gap quantified (what percentage of the data estate is realistically being monitored/reviewed with current capacity versus what exists), and a forward-looking growth projection (data estate size, new platform rollouts planned) showing the gap will widen, not stay flat, without additional investment.

The case should be framed as risk mitigation and enablement, not program growth for its own sake: additional headcount and tooling reduce the probability and impact of specific categorized risks (compliance exposure, reporting errors reaching executives, security incidents from stale access) and unblock specific business value currently waiting on governance capacity (faster access provisioning enabling business unit initiatives, broader catalog coverage enabling self-service analytics the business has asked for). The candidate should propose a specific, justified ask -- a defined headcount number tied to a specific coverage gap it closes, and specific tooling costs tied to specific capability gaps -- rather than an open-ended 'more resources' request, since a specific, scoped ask is easier for finance to evaluate and approve than a vague one.

Finally, the response should address the competitive funding reality directly: proposing a phased ask (the most critical piece first, with a defined follow-up ask tied to demonstrated results) if a full ask is unlikely to be approved in one pass, and being prepared to show what happens to the identified risks if the request isn't funded at all -- not as a threat, but as the honest cost-of-inaction case finance needs to weigh it fairly against competing requests.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't walk in and say 'I'm overworked, I need help' -- that's not an argument finance can actually weigh against other departments' requests. I'd build this the same way I'd expect any other investment case to be built: quantified risk and opportunity cost, not a workload complaint. So first I'd pull together real evidence from this past year -- specific incidents or near-misses that happened or were barely avoided because of under-resourcing, what percentage of our actual data estate we're realistically able to monitor and review with just me, and a forward-looking projection showing that gap gets worse, not better, as the data estate keeps growing and we roll out more platforms.

I'd frame the whole ask around risk mitigation and enablement, not 'the program wants to grow.' Additional headcount and tooling reduce specific risks -- compliance exposure, reporting errors reaching executives, security incidents from stale access -- and they unblock specific business value that's currently waiting on governance capacity, like faster access provisioning or broader catalog coverage the business has actually asked for. And I'd make the ask specific, not open-ended -- a defined headcount number tied to a specific coverage gap it closes, and specific tooling costs tied to specific capability gaps, because a scoped ask is just easier for finance to actually evaluate than 'give me more resources.'

Since I'm competing against other departments' requests, I'd also come in with a phased version ready -- the single most critical piece first, with a clear follow-up ask tied to results, in case the full ask isn't going to get approved in one shot. And I'd be ready to lay out honestly what happens to the risks I've identified if this doesn't get funded at all -- not as a threat, just the real cost-of-inaction picture finance needs to weigh fairly against everything else competing for the same budget.
commonMistakes: Framing the case as personal workload complaint instead of quantified risk/opportunity cost
Making an open-ended 'more resources' request instead of a specific, scoped headcount/tooling ask
Not gathering concrete evidence (incidents, coverage gaps, growth projections) to support the case
Ignoring the competitive funding reality and not preparing a phased or prioritized version of the ask
Failing to honestly present the cost-of-inaction if the request isn't funded
